Example: "([]{})" → true. "([)]" → false, because [ was opened last but ) tries to close first.

1Brute force — delete matching pairs until nothing changes

A valid string always has at least one pair like (), [] or {} sitting right next to each other. Remove them and repeat. If the string becomes empty, it was valid.

boolean isValid(String s) {
    String prev = null;
    while (!s.equals(prev)) {              // stop when a round removes nothing
        prev = s;
        s = s.replace("()", "").replace("[]", "").replace("{}", "");
    }
    return s.isEmpty();
}

Time O(n²)Space O(n)

Deeply nested input like "(((...)))" needs about n/2 rounds, and each round copies the whole string.

2Optimal — a stack of the closers we are waiting for
The idea

The bracket opened last must be closed first: that is exactly a stack. When you see an opener, push the closer you now expect. When you see a closer, it must equal the top of the stack; pop it. At the end nothing may be left waiting.

boolean isValid(String s) {
    Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (c == '(') stack.push(')');        // opener: remember which closer we need
        else if (c == '[') stack.push(']');
        else if (c == '{') stack.push('}');
        else if (stack.isEmpty() || stack.pop() != c) return false;  // wrong or no opener
    }
    return stack.isEmpty();                   // leftover openers were never closed
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

One pass; each character is pushed or popped once.

Remember

"Most recent thing must be handled first" → stack. Pushing the expected closer keeps the check to one comparison.

Watch out

Two edge cases: a closer when the stack is empty ("]") must return false, not crash; and leftover openers ("((") mean false, so return stack.isEmpty(), not true.

Pattern notes: Stacks · Open on LeetCode

LC 682Baseball GameEasyStackLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You keep a list of scores. Each operation is either a number (add that score), "+" (add a score equal to the last two added), "D" (add double the last score), or "C" (cancel the last score). Return the sum of the scores left at the end.

Example: ["5", "2", "C", "D", "+"] → 30. Scores go 5, then 5 2, then 5 (2 cancelled), then 5 10, then 5 10 15. Sum = 30.

1Brute force — simulate with a list, sum at the end

Do exactly what the rules say using an ArrayList, always working with its last items, then add everything up.

int calPoints(String[] operations) {
    List<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();
    for (String op : operations) {
        int n = scores.size();
        if (op.equals("+")) scores.add(scores.get(n - 1) + scores.get(n - 2));
        else if (op.equals("D")) scores.add(2 * scores.get(n - 1));
        else if (op.equals("C")) scores.remove(n - 1);
        else scores.add(Integer.parseInt(op));
    }
    int total = 0;
    for (int s : scores) total += s;
    return total;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

This is already optimal: you must read every operation, and you must remember old scores because "C" can cancel back through them. Notice that we only ever touch the end of the list: that is a stack in disguise.

2Cleaner — a real stack plus a running total
The idea

"Cancel the last one" is an undo, and undo is the classic stack job. Use a stack for the scores and keep the total up to date as you go: add when you push, subtract when you pop. Then no second loop is needed.

int calPoints(String[] operations) {
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    int total = 0;
    for (String op : operations) {
        if (op.equals("+")) {
            int top = stack.pop();           // take the top off to see the one below
            int sum = top + stack.peek();
            stack.push(top);                 // put it back
            stack.push(sum);
            total += sum;
        } else if (op.equals("D")) {
            int d = 2 * stack.peek();
            stack.push(d);
            total += d;
        } else if (op.equals("C")) {
            total -= stack.pop();            // undo the last score
        } else {
            int v = Integer.parseInt(op);    // a plain number, may be negative
            stack.push(v);
            total += v;
        }
    }
    return total;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Same big-O as step 1; the stack just says clearly "we only care about the latest scores".

Remember

Undo / cancel the last action → stack. Keeping a running total next to it saves a final pass.

Watch out

Check the letters "+", "D", "C" before calling parseInt, and compare strings with equals, never ==. Scores like "-2" are valid numbers.

Pattern notes: Stacks · Open on LeetCode

LC 844Backspace String CompareEasyStack / Two PointersLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Two strings are typed into text editors. A # means "backspace": delete the character before it (if there is one). Are the two final texts equal?

Example: s = "ab#c", t = "ad#c" → true. Both become "ac".

1Brute force — actually type both strings, then compare

Use a StringBuilder as a stack: append normal characters, delete the last one on #. Build both final strings and compare them.

boolean backspaceCompare(String s, String t) {
    return build(s).equals(build(t));
}

String build(String str) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();          // works like a stack of chars
    for (char c : str.toCharArray()) {
        if (c != '#') sb.append(c);
        else if (sb.length() > 0) sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length() - 1);
    }
    return sb.toString();
}

Time O(n + m)Space O(n + m)

Fast and a great answer to start with. The follow-up asks for O(1) extra space, so we must avoid building new strings.

2Optimal — walk both strings backwards
The idea

Reading forwards, you don't know yet whether a character will be erased. Reading backwards, you do: a # comes before the letter it deletes. So walk from the end, count the #s you pass and skip that many letters. Each time both strings land on a real surviving letter, compare them.

boolean backspaceCompare(String s, String t) {
    int i = s.length() - 1, j = t.length() - 1;
    while (i >= 0 || j >= 0) {
        i = nextChar(s, i);              // jump to the next letter that survives
        j = nextChar(t, j);
        if (i < 0 && j < 0) return true;   // both finished at the same time
        if (i < 0 || j < 0) return false;  // one text is longer
        if (s.charAt(i) != t.charAt(j)) return false;
        i--; j--;
    }
    return true;
}

// Returns the index of the next surviving char at or before i, or -1.
int nextChar(String str, int i) {
    int skip = 0;
    while (i >= 0) {
        if (str.charAt(i) == '#') { skip++; i--; }   // one more letter to erase
        else if (skip > 0)        { skip--; i--; }   // this letter is erased
        else break;                                   // a real, surviving letter
    }
    return i;
}

Time O(n + m)Space O(1)

Each index moves left only, so both strings are read once, and we store just a few ints.

Remember

"Undo" characters → a stack (StringBuilder). If you need O(1) space, process from the end, where you already know what gets undone.

Watch out

A # on an empty text does nothing: "a##c" equals "#a#c" (both are "c"). And #s can chain, so count them with a skip counter rather than jumping back a fixed 2 places.

Pattern notes: Stacks · Open on LeetCode

LC 232Implement Queue using StacksEasyDesign · Two StacksLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Build a queue (first in, first out) with push, pop, peek and empty, but you may only use stacks (last in, first out) inside.

Example: push(1), push(2), peek(), pop(), empty() → 1, 1, false. The first one pushed is the first one out.

1Simple design — keep the stack in queue order on every push

Keep one main stack with the oldest item on top. To push, pour everything into a temp stack, put the new item at the bottom, and pour everything back. Then pop and peek are just the top.

class MyQueue {
    private Deque<Integer> main = new ArrayDeque<>();   // oldest item on top
    private Deque<Integer> temp = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public MyQueue() {}

    public void push(int x) {
        while (!main.isEmpty()) temp.push(main.pop());  // move all out
        main.push(x);                                   // new item goes to the bottom
        while (!temp.isEmpty()) main.push(temp.pop());  // move all back on top of it
    }

    public int pop()  { return main.pop(); }
    public int peek() { return main.peek(); }
    public boolean empty() { return main.isEmpty(); }
}

push O(n)pop / peek O(1)Space O(n)

Correct, but every single push moves the whole queue twice. n pushes cost O(n²) in total.

2Better design — an "in" stack and an "out" stack
The idea

Pouring a stack into another stack reverses it, which turns newest-on-top into oldest-on-top. So push always goes onto in. For pop or peek, read from out, and only when out is empty, pour all of in into out. Each item is poured at most once in its life.

class MyQueue {
    private Deque<Integer> in = new ArrayDeque<>();    // new items land here
    private Deque<Integer> out = new ArrayDeque<>();   // oldest item on top

    public MyQueue() {}

    public void push(int x) { in.push(x); }

    public int pop()  { moveIfNeeded(); return out.pop(); }

    public int peek() { moveIfNeeded(); return out.peek(); }

    public boolean empty() { return in.isEmpty() && out.isEmpty(); }

    private void moveIfNeeded() {
        if (out.isEmpty()) {                             // only pour when out runs dry
            while (!in.isEmpty()) out.push(in.pop());
        }
    }
}

All operations O(1) amortizedSpace O(n)

A single pop can take O(n) when it pours, but each item is poured only once, so n operations cost O(n) in total: O(1) each on average ("amortized").

Remember

Two stacks make a queue: push to in, pop from out, refill out only when it is empty. "Amortized O(1)" means an occasional slow step is paid for by many fast ones.

Watch out

Never pour into out while it still has items: new items would land on top of older ones and break the order. And empty() must check both stacks.

Pattern notes: Queues & Deques · Open on LeetCode

LC 155Min StackMediumDesign · StackLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Build a stack with push, pop, top and one extra: getMin(), which returns the smallest value currently in the stack. Every operation must be O(1).

Example: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), top(), getMin() → -3, 0, -2.

1Simple design — scan the whole stack for the min

Use a normal stack, and when someone asks for the minimum, loop over every item.

class MinStack {
    private Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public MinStack() {}

    public void push(int val) { stack.push(val); }
    public void pop() { stack.pop(); }
    public int top() { return stack.peek(); }

    public int getMin() {
        int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int v : stack) min = Math.min(min, v);   // look at everything
        return min;
    }
}

getMin O(n)others O(1)Space O(n)

Breaks the rule that every operation is O(1). A single variable min doesn't work either: after you pop the minimum, you have no idea what the previous minimum was.

2Better design — every item remembers the min below it
The idea

A stack only changes at the top, so the minimum of "this item and everything under it" never changes while the item sits there. So store each value together with the min at that moment: the pair [val, minSoFar]. getMin just reads the top pair. When you pop, the pair below already knows the old minimum. Like writing "the lowest so far" on each plate as you stack it.

class MinStack {
    private Deque<int[]> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();   // each item: {val, minSoFar}

    public MinStack() {}

    public void push(int val) {
        int min = stack.isEmpty() ? val : Math.min(val, stack.peek()[1]);
        stack.push(new int[]{val, min});
    }

    public void pop() { stack.pop(); }

    public int top() { return stack.peek()[0]; }

    public int getMin() { return stack.peek()[1]; }
}

All operations O(1)Space O(n)

We pay one extra int per item to get the minimum instantly, even after pops.

Remember

If a stack needs a running statistic (min, max), store it with each item. Popping then undoes the statistic for free.

Watch out

Duplicates of the minimum: push 0, 1, 0 then pop; the min must still be 0. Storing a min per item handles this. If you use the "second stack of mins" variant, push onto it when val <= min (with <=, not <), or duplicates break it.

Pattern notes: Stacks · Open on LeetCode

LC 496Next Greater Element IEasyMonotonic StackLeetCode
The problem in easy words

For a number in nums2, its "next greater element" is the first number to its right that is bigger (or -1 if there is none). nums1 is a list of some numbers from nums2 (all numbers are distinct). For each of them, return its next greater element in nums2.

Example: nums1 = [4, 1, 2], nums2 = [1, 3, 4, 2] → [-1, 3, -1]. Nothing bigger comes after 4; after 1 the first bigger is 3; nothing bigger comes after 2.

1Brute force — find it, then look right

For each number in nums1, find where it sits in nums2, then walk to the right until you hit something bigger.

int[] nextGreaterElement(int[] nums1, int[] nums2) {
    int[] res = new int[nums1.length];
    for (int i = 0; i < nums1.length; i++) {
        res[i] = -1;
        int j = 0;
        while (nums2[j] != nums1[i]) j++;            // find its position
        for (j = j + 1; j < nums2.length; j++) {    // scan to the right
            if (nums2[j] > nums1[i]) { res[i] = nums2[j]; break; }
        }
    }
    return res;
}

Time O(n1 · n2)Space O(1)

Fine for this small problem, but each query rescans the array. With many queries, or the harder versions of this problem, it becomes O(n²).

2Optimal — a monotonic stack answers everyone in one pass
The idea

Walk through nums2 once. Keep a stack of numbers that are still waiting for a bigger number. The stack is always in decreasing order (that's what "monotonic" means). When a new number arrives, it is the answer for every smaller number on top of the stack: pop them and record "next greater = this number" in a HashMap. Then push the new number to wait its turn. Picture people in a queue for a view: a tall person arriving blocks everyone shorter in front.

int[] nextGreaterElement(int[] nums1, int[] nums2) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> nextGreater = new HashMap<>();   // number -> its next greater
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();             // numbers still waiting
    for (int num : nums2) {
        while (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() < num) {
            nextGreater.put(stack.pop(), num);   // num is the first bigger one to its right
        }
        stack.push(num);                         // now num waits for its own answer
    }
    int[] res = new int[nums1.length];
    for (int i = 0; i < nums1.length; i++) {
        res[i] = nextGreater.getOrDefault(nums1[i], -1);   // never answered = -1
    }
    return res;
}

Time O(n1 + n2)Space O(n2)

Each number of nums2 is pushed once and popped at most once, so the while loop adds only O(n2) work in total.

Remember

"Next greater / next smaller / how many days until warmer" → monotonic stack. The stack holds items still waiting for an answer, and the newcomer answers them as it pops.

Watch out

Use while, not if: one big number can answer many waiting numbers at once (in [3, 2, 1, 5], the 5 pops 1, 2 and 3). And numbers left in the stack at the end get -1, which getOrDefault handles.

Pattern notes: Monotonic Stack & Queue · Open on LeetCode

Stage 3 — Pointers & halvingLinked lists, binary search and the small math tricks interviewers love.

Linked List

A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds a value and an arrow (next) to the following node. You can't jump to position 5; you have to walk there. The key patterns here: re-pointing arrows in place (reversal), a dummy node in front of the head, two pointers walking side by side, and slow / fast pointers to find the middle or a loop.

LC 206Reverse Linked ListEasyIn-place ReversalLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get the head of a linked list. Turn every arrow around so the list runs backwards, and return the new head.

Example: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1.

1Brute force — copy the values, rebuild backwards

Walk the list and copy every value into an ArrayList. Then build a brand new list by reading that ArrayList from the end to the start.

ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
    List<Integer> vals = new ArrayList<>();
    for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) vals.add(n.val);   // copy values out
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    for (int i = vals.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {                       // rebuild backwards
        tail.next = new ListNode(vals.get(i));
        tail = tail.next;
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

The speed is already fine, but we made a full copy of the list. The interviewer wants you to reverse it in place, using only a few pointers.

2Optimal — flip the arrows one by one with prev / curr
The idea

Walk the list once. At each node, save next, point curr back at prev, then step both forward. prev is the reversed part growing behind you; curr is the node you are fixing. You must save next first, or you lose the rest of the list the moment you flip the arrow.

ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null;          // the part already reversed
    ListNode curr = head;          // the node we are fixing now
    while (curr != null) {
        ListNode next = curr.next; // 1. save the rest of the list
        curr.next = prev;          // 2. flip the arrow backwards
        prev = curr;               // 3. move prev forward
        curr = next;               // 4. move curr forward
    }
    return prev;                   // prev is the new head
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

Every node is visited once and we only ever hold three pointers, no matter how long the list is.

Remember

The four-line dance save next, flip, move prev, move curr is the core of every "reverse part of a list" problem. Learn it by heart.

Watch out

Returning head or curr at the end. After the loop head is the last node and curr is null; the new head is prev.

Pattern notes: In-place Linked List Reversal · Open on LeetCode

LC 21Merge Two Sorted ListsEasyDummy NodeLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get two linked lists, each already sorted from small to big. Join them into one sorted list by re-using their nodes, and return its head.

Example: 1 → 2 → 4 and 1 → 3 → 4 → 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4.

1Brute force — dump everything, sort, rebuild

Copy all values from both lists into one ArrayList, sort it, and build a new list from the sorted values.

ListNode mergeTwoLists(ListNode list1, ListNode list2) {
    List<Integer> vals = new ArrayList<>();
    for (ListNode n = list1; n != null; n = n.next) vals.add(n.val);
    for (ListNode n = list2; n != null; n = n.next) vals.add(n.val);
    Collections.sort(vals);                        // ignores that both are already sorted
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    for (int v : vals) { tail.next = new ListNode(v); tail = tail.next; }
    return dummy.next;
}

Time O((n+m) log(n+m))Space O(n+m)

We throw away the most useful fact we were given: both lists are already sorted. Sorting again is wasted work, and so is the copy.

2Optimal — zip the two lists with a dummy node
The idea

Like merging two sorted piles of cards: look at the top card of each pile and always take the smaller front node, then attach it to the end of your result. A dummy node at the start means the result always has a "last node" to attach to, so the first node needs no special case.

ListNode mergeTwoLists(ListNode list1, ListNode list2) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);   // fake start, so we never special-case the head
    ListNode tail = dummy;              // last node of the merged list
    while (list1 != null && list2 != null) {
        if (list1.val <= list2.val) {   // take the smaller front node
            tail.next = list1;
            list1 = list1.next;
        } else {
            tail.next = list2;
            list2 = list2.next;
        }
        tail = tail.next;
    }
    tail.next = (list1 != null) ? list1 : list2;   // glue on whatever is left
    return dummy.next;
}

Time O(n+m)Space O(1)

Each node is looked at once, and we only re-point arrows, so no extra memory is needed.

Remember

When you build a new list, start with a dummy node and a tail pointer, then return dummy.next. It removes all the "is the result still empty?" checks.

Watch out

Forgetting the leftovers. When one list runs out, the other may still have nodes. You don't need a loop: one line tail.next = rest attaches the whole remaining chain.

Pattern notes: Linked Lists · Open on LeetCode

LC 876Middle of the Linked ListEasyFast & Slow PointersLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Return the middle node of a linked list. If there are two middles (even length), return the second one.

Example: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → node 3. For 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → node 4.

1Brute force — copy nodes into an array

A list has no index, but an array does. Put every node into an ArrayList, then return the one at position size / 2.

ListNode middleNode(ListNode head) {
    List<ListNode> nodes = new ArrayList<>();
    for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) nodes.add(n);   // copy nodes into an array
    return nodes.get(nodes.size() / 2);                             // index n/2 = second middle
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Fast enough, but it stores every node. We can find the middle in one walk with no extra memory.

2Optimal — slow and fast pointers
The idea

Two runners start at the head. Slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps. Fast covers twice the distance, so when fast reaches the end, slow is exactly halfway.

ListNode middleNode(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {   // fast can still take 2 steps
        slow = slow.next;                         // 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next;                    // 2 steps
    }
    return slow;                                  // fast hit the end, slow is halfway
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

One pass, two pointers. For even length, fast lands on null, which leaves slow on the second middle, exactly what the problem asks.

Remember

"Find the middle" or "find something in one pass without knowing the length" → slow moves 1, fast moves 2. You will reuse this in Palindrome Linked List and in cycle detection.

Watch out

The loop check must be fast != null && fast.next != null, in that order. Checking only fast.next crashes with a NullPointerException on even-length lists.

Pattern notes: Fast & Slow Pointers · Open on LeetCode

LC 141Linked List CycleEasyFast & Slow PointersLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Does the list have a loop? That is, does some node's next point back to an earlier node, so walking forward never reaches null? Return true or false.

Example: 3 → 2 → 0 → -4, and -4 points back to 2 → true.

1Brute force — remember every node you visit

Walk the list and put each node into a HashSet. If you ever meet a node that is already in the set, you have gone around a loop.

boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    Set<ListNode> seen = new HashSet<>();      // stores NODES, not values
    for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) {
        if (!seen.add(n)) return true;         // add() returns false if already there
    }
    return false;                              // reached null: no loop
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Correct, but the set can hold every node. LeetCode's follow-up asks for O(1) memory.

2Optimal — Floyd's tortoise and hare
The idea

Think of two runners on a track. If the track is a straight line, the fast one just finishes. If it is a loop, the fast runner eventually laps the slow one and they meet. Each step the gap between them shrinks by 1, so fast can never jump over slow.

boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;          // tortoise: 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next;     // hare: 2 steps
        if (slow == fast) return true;   // same NODE: the hare lapped the tortoise
    }
    return false;                  // hare fell off the end: no loop
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

Without a loop, fast reaches the end in n/2 steps. With a loop, they meet within about one lap. Either way it's linear, with just two pointers.

Remember

"Is there a loop?" → slow and fast pointers; if they ever meet, there is a cycle. No memory needed.

Watch out

Compare the nodes (slow == fast), not the values. Two different nodes can hold the same number. Also move first, then compare: both start on the head, so checking before moving would say "cycle" straight away.

Pattern notes: Fast & Slow Pointers · Open on LeetCode

LC 83Remove Duplicates from Sorted ListEasyPointer WalkLeetCode
The problem in easy words

The list is sorted, so equal values sit next to each other. Delete the extra copies so each value appears only once, and return the head.

Example: 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 3 → 1 → 2 → 3.

1Brute force — collect unique values, rebuild

Put every value into a LinkedHashSet (a set that remembers insertion order) to drop repeats, then build a fresh list from the set.

ListNode deleteDuplicates(ListNode head) {
    Set<Integer> seen = new LinkedHashSet<>();          // keeps first-seen order
    for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) seen.add(n.val);
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    for (int v : seen) { tail.next = new ListNode(v); tail = tail.next; }
    return dummy.next;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

This would work even on an unsorted list, which is a hint that we are not using the "sorted" gift. Sorted means copies are neighbours, so we can just unlink them.

2Optimal — compare each node with its neighbour
The idea

Stand on a node and look at the next one. If it has the same value, skip over it by pointing curr.next one further, and stay where you are (there might be a third copy). If it's different, step forward.

ListNode deleteDuplicates(ListNode head) {
    ListNode curr = head;
    while (curr != null && curr.next != null) {
        if (curr.val == curr.next.val) {
            curr.next = curr.next.next;   // skip the copy, but DON'T move yet
        } else {
            curr = curr.next;             // next value is new, step forward
        }
    }
    return head;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

One walk, no extra structure. The head never changes because the first node is always kept.

Remember

To delete a node in a singly linked list, stand on the node before it and write curr.next = curr.next.next. "Sorted" usually means "the things you care about are neighbours".

Watch out

Moving curr forward right after deleting. With 1 → 1 → 1 you would remove one copy, step onto the second 1, and never compare it with the third. Only move when the values differ.

Pattern notes: Linked Lists · Open on LeetCode

LC 203Remove Linked List ElementsEasyDummy NodeLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Remove every node whose value equals val, and return the new head. The head itself might need removing, even several times in a row.

Example: 1 → 2 → 6 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6, val = 6 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. And 7 → 7 → 7 → 7, val = 7 → empty list.

1Brute force — copy the values you keep, rebuild

Walk the list, copy every value that is not val into an ArrayList, then build a new list from it.

ListNode removeElements(ListNode head, int val) {
    List<Integer> keep = new ArrayList<>();
    for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) {
        if (n.val != val) keep.add(n.val);          // copy only the good values
    }
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    for (int v : keep) { tail.next = new ListNode(v); tail = tail.next; }
    return dummy.next;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

It builds a whole second list. We can unlink the bad nodes in place instead.

2Optimal — dummy node, then unlink in place
The idea

To delete a node you need the node before it. The head has no node before it, so we give it one: a dummy node placed in front of the head. Now every real node, the head included, has a predecessor and one simple rule handles them all.

ListNode removeElements(ListNode head, int val) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);   // sits before the real head
    ListNode curr = dummy;                    // we always look at curr.next
    while (curr.next != null) {
        if (curr.next.val == val) {
            curr.next = curr.next.next;       // unlink it, stay put
        } else {
            curr = curr.next;                 // keep it, move on
        }
    }
    return dummy.next;                        // the head may have changed
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

One pass, and only one extra node no matter how long the list is.

Remember

Whenever the head might be deleted or changed, put a dummy node in front and return dummy.next. It turns a special case into the normal case.

Watch out

Returning head instead of dummy.next. In 6 → 1 → 6 with val = 6, the old head was removed, so returning head gives back a deleted node.

Pattern notes: Linked Lists · Open on LeetCode

LC 160Intersection of Two Linked ListsEasyTwo PointersLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Two lists may merge into one shared tail, like two roads joining. Return the first node they share (the same node object, not just the same value), or null if they never join.

Example: A = 4 → 1 → 8 → 4 → 5, B = 5 → 6 → 1 → 8 → 4 → 5, sharing the tail from node 8 → the node with value 8.

1Brute force — check every pair of nodes

For each node in A, walk all of B and see if any node in B is the very same node.

ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
    for (ListNode a = headA; a != null; a = a.next) {
        for (ListNode b = headB; b != null; b = b.next) {
            if (a == b) return a;          // same node object, not just same value
        }
    }
    return null;
}

Time O(m·n)Space O(1)

Two lists of 30,000 nodes means 900 million comparisons. (A HashSet of A's nodes gets O(m+n) time but costs O(m) memory.)

2Optimal — swap lists at the end so both walk the same distance
The idea

The lists have different lengths, so walking them side by side doesn't line up. Fix it with a trick: when pointer a finishes A, it jumps to the start of B, and b jumps to the start of A. Now each pointer walks A-only + B-only + shared, the same total, so they arrive at the join point together. If there is no join, they both reach null together.

ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
    ListNode a = headA, b = headB;
    while (a != b) {                       // stop when they point at the same node (or both null)
        a = (a == null) ? headB : a.next;  // A finished? jump to B's start
        b = (b == null) ? headA : b.next;  // B finished? jump to A's start
    }
    return a;                              // the meeting node, or null if none
}

Time O(m+n)Space O(1)

Each pointer walks at most m + n nodes, and we only store two pointers. The loop always ends: in the worst case both become null at the same moment.

Remember

When two walks have different lengths, make them equal by having each one also walk the other's path. Same distance, same speed, same arrival time.

Watch out

Comparing values instead of nodes. In the example both lists contain a 1, but they are different nodes; the real answer is 8. Always compare with a == b on the node references.

Pattern notes: Two Pointers · Open on LeetCode

LC 234Palindrome Linked ListEasyFast & Slow + ReversalLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Does the list read the same forwards and backwards? Return true or false.

Example: 1 → 2 → 2 → 1 → true. 1 → 2 → false.

1Brute force — copy into an array, check from both ends

A list can't walk backwards, but an array can. Copy the values into an ArrayList, then compare the first with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on.

boolean isPalindrome(ListNode head) {
    List<Integer> vals = new ArrayList<>();
    for (ListNode n = head; n != null; n = n.next) vals.add(n.val);   // copy into an array
    int i = 0, j = vals.size() - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        if (!vals.get(i).equals(vals.get(j))) return false;   // equals, not == on Integer
        i++; j--;
    }
    return true;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Simple and a fine first answer, but LeetCode's follow-up asks for O(1) extra space.

2Optimal — find the middle, reverse the second half, compare
The idea

This combines two tricks you already know. Use slow / fast (LC 876) to reach the middle, then reverse (LC 206) the second half. Now the second half reads backwards, so you can walk both halves forward and compare node by node.

boolean isPalindrome(ListNode head) {
    // 1. find the middle with slow / fast
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }
    // 2. reverse the second half (same code as LC 206)
    ListNode prev = null, curr = slow;
    while (curr != null) {
        ListNode next = curr.next;
        curr.next = prev;
        prev = curr;
        curr = next;
    }
    // 3. compare first half with reversed second half
    ListNode left = head, right = prev;
    while (right != null) {
        if (left.val != right.val) return false;
        left = left.next;
        right = right.next;
    }
    return true;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

Three linear walks, still O(n) total, and only a handful of pointers. (In an interview, mention that this changes the input list; you could reverse the half back afterwards.)

Remember

Harder list problems are often small patterns glued together: find the middle + reverse + walk two pointers. Master the pieces and you can build the whole.

Watch out

Loop on right != null, not left != null. The first half still links into the middle node, so it is the longer one; the reversed half is the one that ends cleanly at null. In the brute force, comparing two Integer objects with == fails for values above 127, so use .equals.

Pattern notes: Fast & Slow Pointers · Open on LeetCode

Binary Search

Binary search finds something in a sorted range by checking the middle and throwing away the half that can't hold the answer, like opening a dictionary in the middle instead of reading from page 1. Each check halves the range, so a billion items take only about 30 checks. The key pattern: ONE template (lo, hi, while (lo <= hi), mid, move lo or hi past mid), used either to find an exact match or, with an ans variable, to find the first or last value that passes a yes/no test.

LC 704Binary SearchEasyBinary SearchLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get a sorted array of distinct numbers and a target. Return the index of the target, or -1 if it's not there. It must run in O(log n).

Example: nums = [-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], target = 9 → 4. With target = 2 → -1.

1Brute force — check every number

Walk from left to right and stop when you see the target.

int search(int[] nums, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] == target) return i;
    }
    return -1;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

This ignores that the array is sorted, and the problem explicitly demands O(log n).

2Optimal — the binary search template
The idea

Keep a range [lo, hi] where the answer could be. Look at the middle. Because the array is sorted, one comparison tells you which half to throw away: if nums[mid] is too small, everything to its left is too small too.

int search(int[] nums, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;          // the answer lives in [lo, hi]
    while (lo <= hi) {                         // range not empty yet
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;          // middle, without overflow
        if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;   // found it
        else if (nums[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1;   // too small: throw away left half
        else hi = mid - 1;                     // too big: throw away right half
    }
    return -1;                                 // range became empty: not there
}

Time O(log n)Space O(1)

The range halves every round, so for n = 1,000,000 it takes at most about 20 rounds.

Remember

This is the template for the whole topic: lo = 0, hi = n - 1, while (lo <= hi), mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2, then lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid - 1. Always +1 / -1, because mid has already been checked.

Watch out

Writing while (lo < hi) with this template skips the last one-cell range, so [5] with target 5 wrongly returns -1. And lo = mid (no +1) can loop forever when lo and hi are neighbours.

Pattern notes: Binary Search · Open on LeetCode

LC 35Search Insert PositionEasyBinary SearchLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Sorted array of distinct numbers and a target. If the target is there, return its index. If not, return the index where it would go to keep the array sorted. O(log n).

Example: nums = [1, 3, 5, 6]: target 5 → 2, target 2 → 1, target 7 → 4.

1Brute force — find the first number that is big enough

Both cases have the same answer: the first index whose number is >= target. If there is none, the target goes at the very end.

int searchInsert(int[] nums, int target) {
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (nums[i] >= target) return i;   // first spot that is big enough
    }
    return nums.length;                    // bigger than everything: goes at the end
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

Correct, but linear. The array is sorted, so we can binary search for that "first big enough" spot.

2Optimal — same template, plus an ans variable
The idea

Ask a yes/no question at each index: "is nums[i] >= target?" The answers look like no no no yes yes, and we want the first yes. When mid says yes, write it down as the best answer so far, then keep looking to the left for an earlier yes.

int searchInsert(int[] nums, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;
    int ans = nums.length;                 // default: insert at the end
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] >= target) {         // mid is a valid spot...
            ans = mid;                     // ...remember it
            hi = mid - 1;                  // ...but look for an earlier one
        } else {
            lo = mid + 1;                  // mid too small: go right
        }
    }
    return ans;
}

Time O(log n)Space O(1)

Exactly the LC 704 loop. The only change: instead of returning on a match, we record ans and keep shrinking.

Remember

"Find the first position where something becomes true" → template + ans = mid; hi = mid - 1 when true. This is the most useful binary search variant of all.

Watch out

Forgetting the default. If the target is bigger than every number, mid never says yes, so ans must start at nums.length, not 0 or -1.

Pattern notes: Binary Search · Open on LeetCode

LC 278First Bad VersionEasyBinary SearchLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Versions 1..n of a product were released. Once one version is bad, every later version is bad too. Using the given API isBadVersion(v), find the first bad version with as few calls as possible.

Example: n = 5, first bad is 4: isBadVersion(3) = false, isBadVersion(4) = true → 4.

1Brute force — test versions one by one

Ask the API about version 1, 2, 3, ... and return the first one that says bad.

int firstBadVersion(int n) {
    for (int v = 1; v <= n; v++) {
        if (isBadVersion(v)) return v;     // first one that says "bad"
    }
    return n;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

n can be about 2 billion, so this can mean 2 billion API calls. Too slow (Time Limit Exceeded).

2Optimal — binary search for the first "bad"
The idea

The answers look like good good good bad bad: sorted, even though there is no array. That is all binary search needs. It's the same "first yes" question as LC 35, where "yes" now means isBadVersion(mid).

int firstBadVersion(int n) {
    int lo = 1, hi = n;
    int ans = n;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;      // NOT (lo + hi) / 2: that can overflow
        if (isBadVersion(mid)) {
            ans = mid;                     // mid is bad: a candidate
            hi = mid - 1;                  // maybe an earlier one is bad too
        } else {
            lo = mid + 1;                  // mid is good: first bad is to the right
        }
    }
    return ans;
}

Time O(log n)Space O(1)

For n = 2,126,753,390 this makes 31 API calls instead of about 2 billion.

Remember

Binary search doesn't need an array. It works on any range where a yes/no test flips only once (all no, then all yes). This is called "binary search on the answer".

Watch out

(lo + hi) / 2 overflows when both are near 2 billion: the sum goes past Integer.MAX_VALUE and turns negative. This is the classic failing test on this problem. Always write lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

Pattern notes: Binary Search · Open on LeetCode

LC 69Sqrt(x)EasyBinary SearchLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Return the square root of x, rounded down to a whole number. You may not use Math.sqrt or pow. In other words: the biggest k with k × k <= x.

Example: x = 4 → 2. x = 8 → 2 (the real root is 2.83..., rounded down).

1Brute force — count up until the square is too big

Try 1, 2, 3, ... and stop just before the square passes x.

int mySqrt(int x) {
    long i = 0;
    while ((i + 1) * (i + 1) <= x) i++;    // grow while the next square still fits
    return (int) i;
}

Time O(√x)Space O(1)

For the biggest int that is about 46,000 steps. It passes, but binary search needs only about 31.

2Optimal — binary search for the last k that fits
The idea

Ask "does k × k <= x?" for k = 0, 1, 2, ... The answers are yes yes yes no no. We want the last yes, the mirror image of LC 35. So when mid fits, save it, then look to the right for a bigger one.

int mySqrt(int x) {
    int lo = 0, hi = x;
    int ans = 0;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if ((long) mid * mid <= x) {       // long: mid * mid can overflow int
            ans = mid;                     // mid fits: a candidate
            lo = mid + 1;                  // try a bigger one
        } else {
            hi = mid - 1;                  // too big: go left
        }
    }
    return ans;
}

Time O(log x)Space O(1)

Same template again. "First yes" saves and goes left; "last yes" saves and goes right. That's the only difference.

Remember

"Biggest value that still works" → template + ans = mid; lo = mid + 1 when it works. Many "find the max/min k such that..." problems are this exact shape.

Watch out

mid * mid with int overflows once mid passes 46,340, turns negative, and looks "small enough". Cast to long before multiplying: (long) mid * mid. Test x = 2147483647 → 46340.

Pattern notes: Binary Search · Open on LeetCode

LC 367Valid Perfect SquareEasyBinary SearchLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Given a positive number num, return true if it is a perfect square (some whole number times itself), without using Math.sqrt.

Example: num = 16 → true (4 × 4). num = 14 → false.

1Brute force — try every k while k × k fits

Check 1 × 1, 2 × 2, 3 × 3, ... If one equals num, it is a square. Once the square passes num, stop.

boolean isPerfectSquare(int num) {
    for (long i = 1; i * i <= num; i++) {
        if (i * i == num) return true;
    }
    return false;
}

Time O(√n)Space O(1)

Fine for small numbers, but it walks one by one through a sorted range, which is exactly what binary search avoids.

2Optimal — exact-match binary search on k
The idea

The squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ... are sorted, so this is LC 704 in disguise: search k in [1, num] for k × k == num. Too small, go right; too big, go left; equal, done.

boolean isPerfectSquare(int num) {
    int lo = 1, hi = num;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        long sq = (long) mid * mid;        // long, so it can't overflow
        if (sq == num) return true;        // exact hit
        else if (sq < num) lo = mid + 1;
        else hi = mid - 1;
    }
    return false;
}

Time O(log n)Space O(1)

At most about 31 rounds even for the largest int, and no floating-point rounding to worry about.

Remember

Before coding, decide which of the three shapes you need: exact match (return inside the loop), first yes (save, go left), or last yes (save, go right). The loop itself never changes.

Watch out

Overflow again: mid * mid must be computed as long. With int, a huge mid can wrap around and accidentally equal num or look smaller than it.

Pattern notes: Binary Search · Open on LeetCode

Recursion, Bits & Math

Small problems about numbers that teach you how a computer thinks. You will learn recursion and memoization (a function that calls itself, plus a notebook so it never repeats work), bit tricks like n & (n - 1) that remove the lowest 1-bit, and peeling digits off a number with % 10 and / 10.

LC 509Fibonacci NumberEasyRecursion + MemoLeetCode
The problem in easy words

The Fibonacci numbers start 0, 1, and every next number is the sum of the two before it: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, .... Given n, return the n-th one, F(n).

Example: n = 4 → 3, because F(4) = F(3) + F(2) = 2 + 1 = 3.

1Brute force — plain recursion, straight from the definition

The definition already says how to compute it: F(n) = F(n-1) + F(n-2), and the answer is known for n = 0 and n = 1 (the base cases, where the recursion stops).

int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;              // base cases: F(0) = 0, F(1) = 1
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);    // two smaller calls
}

Time O(2ⁿ)Space O(n)

Every call makes two more calls, so the number of calls roughly doubles each level. fib(40) makes over 300 million calls, and most of them compute things that were already computed.

2Optimal — memoization: remember every answer once
The idea

Look at the tree below: f(3) and f(2) are solved again and again. Keep a notebook (an array memo). Before computing F(k), check the notebook; after computing it, write it down. Now each value from 0 to n is computed only once.

int fib(int n) {
    int[] memo = new int[n + 1];
    Arrays.fill(memo, -1);              // -1 means "not computed yet"
    return solve(n, memo);
}

int solve(int n, int[] memo) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    if (memo[n] != -1) return memo[n];  // already in the notebook
    memo[n] = solve(n - 1, memo) + solve(n - 2, memo);
    return memo[n];                     // write it down, then return
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Each F(k) is computed once and then reused, so the work drops from exponential to a straight line. (You can even drop the array and keep only the last two values: see LC 70 below.)

Remember

If a recursion tree has the same call appearing many times, add a memo. That single change is the doorway into Dynamic Programming.

Watch out

Forget the base case (or write only n == 1) and fib(0) recurses into negative numbers forever, ending in a StackOverflowError. Always ask "where does this stop?" first.

Pattern notes: Recursion & the Call Stack · Open on LeetCode

LC 231Power of TwoEasyBit ManipulationLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Given an integer n, return true if it is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...), otherwise false.

Example: n = 16 → true (2⁴). n = 3 → false.

1Brute force — keep dividing by 2

A power of two is 2 × 2 × ... × 2. So divide by 2 while the number is even. If you end up at exactly 1, it was a power of two.

boolean isPowerOfTwo(int n) {
    if (n <= 0) return false;           // 0 and negatives are never powers of two
    while (n % 2 == 0) n /= 2;          // strip every factor of 2
    return n == 1;
}

Time O(log n)Space O(1)

This is already fast (at most 31 divisions for an int). But there is a one-line answer that interviewers love, and it teaches a bit trick you will reuse.

2Optimal — one bit trick
The idea

In binary, a power of two has exactly one 1-bit: 8 is 1000. Subtracting 1 flips that bit to 0 and every bit below it to 1: 7 is 0111. So n & (n - 1) is 0 only when n has a single 1-bit.

boolean isPowerOfTwo(int n) {
    // n > 0 rules out 0 and negatives; the AND checks "exactly one 1-bit"
    return n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0;
}

Time O(1)Space O(1)

One subtraction and one AND, no loop at all.

Remember

n & (n - 1) removes the lowest 1-bit of n. "Is it 0 now?" means "was there only one 1-bit?". You will use the same trick in LC 191 right below.

Watch out

Do not skip n > 0. For n = 0, 0 & -1 is 0 and you would wrongly say true. For Integer.MIN_VALUE (only the sign bit set) the AND is also 0. Also note the brackets: == binds tighter than & in Java.

Pattern notes: Bit Manipulation · Open on LeetCode

LC 191Number of 1 BitsEasyBit ManipulationLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Given a number, count how many 1s appear in its binary form (this count is called the "Hamming weight").

Example: n = 11 → 3, because 11 in binary is 1011.

1Brute force — check all 32 bits one by one

An int has 32 bits. Shift each bit down to the last position and look at it with & 1.

int hammingWeight(int n) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) {
        if (((n >>> i) & 1) == 1) count++;   // is bit i a 1?
    }
    return count;
}

Time O(32)Space O(1)

Always 32 steps, even for n = 128 which has a single 1-bit. We waste time looking at zeros.

2Optimal — jump straight from one 1-bit to the next
The idea

From LC 231: n &= n - 1 deletes the lowest 1-bit. Keep deleting until n is 0 and count the deletions. The loop runs once per 1-bit, and never visits a 0.

int hammingWeight(int n) {
    int count = 0;
    while (n != 0) {
        n &= n - 1;      // remove the lowest 1-bit
        count++;         // one 1-bit gone
    }
    return count;
}

Time O(number of 1s)Space O(1)

At most 32 turns, and far fewer when the number has few 1s. (Java also has Integer.bitCount(n), but interviewers want to see the trick.)

Remember

To loop over only the 1-bits of a number, repeat n &= n - 1. It is called Brian Kernighan's trick.

Watch out

In the brute force, use >>> (unsigned shift), not >>. If you shift n itself with >> in a while (n != 0) loop, a negative number keeps copying its sign bit and the loop never ends.

Pattern notes: Bit Manipulation · Open on LeetCode

LC 338Counting BitsEasyBits + DPLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Given n, return an array ans of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1-bits in i, for every i from 0 to n.

Example: n = 5 → [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2] (0 = 0, 1 = 1, 2 = 10, 3 = 11, 4 = 100, 5 = 101).

1Brute force — count the bits of each number separately

For every i, peel off its bits one at a time and count the 1s, exactly like LC 191.

int[] countBits(int n) {
    int[] ans = new int[n + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        int x = i, count = 0;
        while (x != 0) {
            count += x & 1;   // last bit
            x >>= 1;          // drop it
        }
        ans[i] = count;
    }
    return ans;
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(1) extra

Each number costs about log n steps. The problem's follow-up asks for a single pass in O(n).

2Optimal — reuse the answer for i / 2
The idea

i >> 1 (i divided by 2) is just i with its last bit chopped off. That smaller number is already in the array. So ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1): the bits of the front part, plus 1 if the last bit is 1.

int[] countBits(int n) {
    int[] ans = new int[n + 1];          // ans[0] = 0 already
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        // bits of i = bits of (i without last bit) + the last bit
        ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1);
    }
    return ans;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1) extra

Because i >> 1 is always smaller than i, its answer is ready when we need it. This is a tiny Dynamic Programming problem.

Remember

When you need an answer for every number from 0 to n, ask: "can I build the answer for i from a smaller one I already have?" That question is the heart of DP.

Watch out

The array has size n + 1, not n, because 0 and n are both included. Also bracket (i & 1): in Java + binds tighter than &, so ans[i >> 1] + i & 1 means something else.

Pattern notes: Bit Manipulation · Open on LeetCode

LC 9Palindrome NumberEasyMath / DigitsLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Return true if an integer reads the same forwards and backwards. Negative numbers never do, because of the minus sign.

Example: 121 → true. -121 → false (backwards it is 121-). 10 → false (backwards 01).

1Brute force — turn it into a String

Convert the number to text, then compare the first and last characters, moving inward with two pointers.

boolean isPalindrome(int x) {
    String s = String.valueOf(x);
    int l = 0, r = s.length() - 1;
    while (l < r) {
        if (s.charAt(l) != s.charAt(r)) return false;
        l++; r--;
    }
    return true;
}

Time O(d)Space O(d)

Here d is the number of digits. It works, but the follow-up asks: "could you solve it without converting the integer to a string?"

2Optimal — reverse only the second half of the digits
The idea

x % 10 gives the last digit and x / 10 removes it. Move digits from the end of x onto a new number rev. Stop when rev is at least as big as what is left of x: you have reversed half the digits. Now just compare the two halves. Reversing only half also means rev can never overflow.

boolean isPalindrome(int x) {
    // negatives, and numbers ending in 0 (except 0 itself), can't be palindromes
    if (x < 0 || (x % 10 == 0 && x != 0)) return false;
    int rev = 0;
    while (x > rev) {
        rev = rev * 10 + x % 10;   // move the last digit of x onto rev
        x /= 10;                   // and remove it from x
    }
    // even length: x == rev; odd length: the middle digit sits at the end of rev
    return x == rev || x == rev / 10;
}

Time O(d)Space O(1)

We look at only half the digits and store just two ints, with no String and no overflow risk.

Remember

% 10 reads the last digit, / 10 removes it, and rev * 10 + digit appends a digit. These three moves solve most "digits of a number" problems.

Watch out

Numbers that end in 0, like 10, break the half-reverse: the reversed half would start with 0, and a leading 0 simply vanishes, so 10 would wrongly return true. That is why the first line returns false for them (but keeps 0, which is a palindrome).

Pattern notes: Math & Number Theory · Open on LeetCode

Stage 4 — Trees & graphsThink recursively: trees, heaps and your first graph traversals.

Trees

A binary tree is a family tree of nodes: each node holds a value and points to at most two children, left and right. Almost every tree problem is solved the same way: ask each child for an answer, then combine the answers at the parent (recursive DFS). The problems below teach the traversal orders (preorder, inorder), "return something up to the parent" (depth, diameter), walking two trees together (same / symmetric), and the BST rule (smaller left, bigger right) that lets you skip half the tree at every step.

LC 94Binary Tree Inorder TraversalEasyTree DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Visit every node of a binary tree in inorder: first the whole left side, then the node itself, then the whole right side. Return the values in that order.

Example: root = [1, null, 2, 3] (1 has a right child 2, and 2 has a left child 3) → [1, 3, 2].

1First way — recursion

The definition is already recursive: "left side, me, right side". So write a helper that does exactly that and let Java's call stack remember where to come back to.

List<Integer> inorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    walk(root, out);
    return out;
}

void walk(TreeNode node, List<Integer> out) {
    if (node == null) return;        // empty spot: nothing to do
    walk(node.left, out);            // 1. whole left side first
    out.add(node.val);               // 2. then me
    walk(node.right, out);           // 3. then whole right side
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

This is already O(n) and perfectly fine. LeetCode's follow-up asks: "can you do it iteratively?" On a very deep tree (h close to n) recursion can overflow Java's stack, and interviewers like to see that you know what the recursion is doing behind the scenes.

2Iterative — your own stack
The idea

Recursion secretly uses a stack. Do it by hand: slide left as far as you can, pushing every node. When you hit null, pop a node, visit it, then jump to its right child and repeat. The stack holds the "parents I still have to come back to", exactly like the call stack did.

List<Integer> inorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
        while (cur != null) {          // slide left as far as possible,
            stack.push(cur);           // saving each node for later
            cur = cur.left;
        }
        cur = stack.pop();             // leftmost unvisited node
        out.add(cur.val);              // visit it
        cur = cur.right;               // then handle its right side
    }
    return out;
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Same big-O as recursion (be honest about that in an interview). The win is control: no risk of a StackOverflowError, and the same loop shape solves "kth smallest in a BST" and "BST iterator".

Remember

Inorder = left, me, right. On a BST, inorder gives the values in sorted order, which is why this traversal matters so much.

Watch out

The outer loop needs both conditions: cur != null || !stack.isEmpty(). With only !stack.isEmpty() you stop too early right after popping the root, before its right side is visited.

Pattern notes: Tree BFS & DFS · Open on LeetCode

LC 144Binary Tree Preorder TraversalEasyTree DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Visit every node in preorder: the node itself first, then its whole left side, then its whole right side. Return the values in that order.

Example: root = [1, null, 2, 3] → [1, 2, 3].

1First way — recursion

Same helper as inorder, only the "visit me" line moves to the top.

List<Integer> preorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    walk(root, out);
    return out;
}

void walk(TreeNode node, List<Integer> out) {
    if (node == null) return;
    out.add(node.val);               // 1. me first
    walk(node.left, out);            // 2. then left side
    walk(node.right, out);           // 3. then right side
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Already O(n). As with inorder, the follow-up is "do it without recursion", which shows you understand the stack underneath.

2Iterative — push right, then left
The idea

Pop a node and visit it straight away (that is "me first"). Then push its children. A stack is last-in-first-out, so push the right child first and the left child second: the left one comes out next, just like preorder wants.

List<Integer> preorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return out;
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(root);
    while (!stack.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = stack.pop();
        out.add(node.val);                              // visit on pop
        if (node.right != null) stack.push(node.right); // push RIGHT first...
        if (node.left != null) stack.push(node.left);   // ...so LEFT pops first
    }
    return out;
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Same O(n) as recursion, with an explicit stack instead of the call stack. Swap the stack for a queue and you get level-order (BFS) instead.

Remember

Preorder = me, left, right. It is the order you use to copy or serialize a tree, because each parent is written before its children.

Watch out

Pushing left before right gives [1, 3, 2]-style wrong orders: the stack reverses things. Also guard root == null before pushing, or you pop a null and crash on node.val.

Pattern notes: Tree BFS & DFS · Open on LeetCode

LC 104Maximum Depth of Binary TreeEasyTree DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

How many nodes are on the longest path from the root down to a leaf? That count is the tree's maximum depth.

Example: root = [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] → 3 (the path 3 → 20 → 15 has three nodes).

1First way — count the levels (BFS)

Walk the tree one floor at a time with a queue, like counting floors in a building. Each time you finish a whole level, add one.

int maxDepth(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return 0;
    Queue<TreeNode> queue = new LinkedList<>();
    queue.add(root);
    int levels = 0;
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int size = queue.size();          // nodes on this level
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            TreeNode node = queue.poll();
            if (node.left != null) queue.add(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) queue.add(node.right);
        }
        levels++;                         // finished one whole level
    }
    return levels;
}

Time O(n)Space O(w)

Correct and O(n), where w is the widest level. It just takes a lot of code for a simple question. Recursion says the same thing in three lines.

2Cleaner — ask the children (recursive DFS)
The idea

Every node asks its two children "how deep are you?" and answers its own parent with 1 + the bigger of the two answers. An empty spot answers 0. The answers bubble up from the leaves to the root.

int maxDepth(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return 0;                 // empty tree has depth 0
    int left = maxDepth(root.left);             // ask the left child
    int right = maxDepth(root.right);           // ask the right child
    return 1 + Math.max(left, right);           // me + the deeper side
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Both ways are O(n) time: every node must be seen once. The recursive version is shorter and uses O(h) stack instead of O(w) queue memory.

Remember

The core tree template: handle null, ask left, ask right, combine. Depth, size, sum, balanced check and diameter are all this same shape.

Watch out

The base case returns 0 for null, not 1. Returning 1 for null makes every answer one too big. And an empty tree (root = []) must return 0.

Pattern notes: Binary Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 226Invert Binary TreeEasyTree DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Turn the tree into its mirror image: at every node, the left child and the right child trade places. Return the root.

Example: root = [4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, 9] → [4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 1].

1First way — build a mirrored copy

Make a brand new tree: each new node gets the mirror of the old right side as its left, and the mirror of the old left side as its right.

TreeNode invertTree(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return null;
    TreeNode copy = new TreeNode(root.val);
    copy.left = invertTree(root.right);    // new left = mirrored old right
    copy.right = invertTree(root.left);    // new right = mirrored old left
    return copy;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

It works, but it allocates n new nodes. There's no need: we can just rewire the existing tree.

2Optimal — swap in place
The idea

At each node, swap the two child pointers, then do the same for each child. Like flipping a photo: flip the big picture, and every small part inside is flipped too.

TreeNode invertTree(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return null;
    TreeNode temp = root.left;        // swap my two children
    root.left = root.right;
    root.right = temp;
    invertTree(root.left);            // then fix each subtree the same way
    invertTree(root.right);
    return root;
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Still O(n) time (every node must be swapped), but no new nodes: only the recursion stack, O(h).

Remember

A tree operation that applies "to every node" = do it here, then recurse on both children. Swapping with a temp variable is the same as swapping two array cells.

Watch out

Don't write root.left = invertTree(root.right); root.right = invertTree(root.left);. The second line reads root.left after you already overwrote it. Save one side in a temp first.

Pattern notes: Binary Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 100Same TreeEasyTree DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get two trees, p and q. Are they exactly the same, meaning the same shape and the same value in every position?

Example: p = [1, 2, 3], q = [1, 2, 3] → true. p = [1, 2], q = [1, null, 2] → false (2 is a left child in one and a right child in the other).

1Brute force — turn both trees into strings

Write each tree out as text in preorder, marking empty spots with #, then compare the two strings.

boolean isSameTree(TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    return serialize(p).equals(serialize(q));
}

String serialize(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return "#";                  // mark empty spots!
    return node.val + "," + serialize(node.left) + "," + serialize(node.right);
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

It builds two whole strings (and lots of temporary ones along the way) even when the roots already differ. We can compare directly and stop at the first difference.

2Optimal — walk both trees together
The idea

Put one finger on each tree and move them in lockstep. At each pair of spots: both empty is fine, one empty is a mismatch, different values is a mismatch. Otherwise, check the left pair and the right pair the same way.

boolean isSameTree(TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (p == null && q == null) return true;     // both empty: same
    if (p == null || q == null) return false;    // only one empty: different
    if (p.val != q.val) return false;            // different values
    return isSameTree(p.left, q.left)            // left sides must match
        && isSameTree(p.right, q.right);         // and right sides too
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Worst case still visits every node (when the trees are equal), but it uses only the recursion stack and quits early on the first mismatch.

Remember

"Compare two trees" = recurse on pairs of nodes. The three base cases (both null, one null, values differ) come first, in that order.

Watch out

Check the null cases before reading p.val, or you get a NullPointerException. In the string version, forgetting the # markers makes [1, 2] and [1, null, 2] look identical.

Pattern notes: Binary Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 101Symmetric TreeEasyTree DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Is the tree a mirror of itself around a vertical line through the root? Fold it down the middle: every node on the left should land on an equal node on the right.

Example: root = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3] → true. root = [1, 2, 2, null, 3, null, 3] → false.

1Brute force — every level must read the same both ways

Go level by level with a queue, write down each level's values (with null for gaps), and check each level is a palindrome.

boolean isSymmetric(TreeNode root) {
    Queue<TreeNode> queue = new LinkedList<>();
    queue.add(root);
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int size = queue.size();
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            TreeNode node = queue.poll();
            if (node == null) { level.add(null); continue; }   // keep gaps!
            level.add(node.val);
            queue.add(node.left);
            queue.add(node.right);
        }
        for (int i = 0, j = level.size() - 1; i < j; i++, j--) {
            if (!Objects.equals(level.get(i), level.get(j))) return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Correct, but it stores whole levels (including null placeholders) and always finishes a level before checking. The recursive mirror check is shorter and stops at the first mismatch.

2Optimal — compare the two halves as mirrors
The idea

It's "Same Tree" with a twist: compare the left subtree with the right subtree, but outside with outside, inside with inside. So a.left pairs with b.right, and a.right pairs with b.left.

boolean isSymmetric(TreeNode root) {
    return isMirror(root.left, root.right);
}

boolean isMirror(TreeNode a, TreeNode b) {
    if (a == null && b == null) return true;
    if (a == null || b == null) return false;
    return a.val == b.val
        && isMirror(a.left, b.right)     // outside pair
        && isMirror(a.right, b.left);    // inside pair
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Each node is compared once with its mirror partner. Memory is just the recursion depth.

Remember

Symmetric = "Same Tree" between the two halves, with the children crossed. Learn the pair-recursion shape once and reuse it.

Watch out

Checking only that the left child's value equals the right child's value at each node is not enough. [1, 2, 2, null, 3, null, 3] passes that test but is not a mirror: you must compare across the two halves.

Pattern notes: Binary Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 112Path SumEasyTree DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Is there a path from the root down to a leaf (a node with no children) whose values add up to targetSum?

Example: root = [5, 4, 8, 11, null, 13, 4, 7, 2, null, null, null, 1], targetSum = 22 → true, because 5 + 4 + 11 + 2 = 22.

1Brute force — collect every path sum

Walk every root-to-leaf path, write each total into a list, and at the end ask the list whether it contains the target.

boolean hasPathSum(TreeNode root, int targetSum) {
    List<Integer> sums = new ArrayList<>();
    collect(root, 0, sums);
    return sums.contains(targetSum);
}

void collect(TreeNode node, int soFar, List<Integer> sums) {
    if (node == null) return;
    soFar += node.val;
    if (node.left == null && node.right == null) sums.add(soFar);  // a leaf: path done
    collect(node.left, soFar, sums);
    collect(node.right, soFar, sums);
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

It stores one number per leaf (up to about n/2) and always walks the entire tree, even if the very first path already hits the target.

2Optimal — subtract as you go down
The idea

Think of the target as a budget. Each node you step on pays its value out of the budget. If you reach a leaf with exactly 0 left, you found a path. || stops as soon as one side says yes.

boolean hasPathSum(TreeNode root, int targetSum) {
    if (root == null) return false;                  // no path here
    int remaining = targetSum - root.val;            // pay for this node
    if (root.left == null && root.right == null) {   // leaf: path ends here
        return remaining == 0;
    }
    return hasPathSum(root.left, remaining)          // try left...
        || hasPathSum(root.right, remaining);        // ...or right (stops at first true)
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Worst case it still visits every node, but it keeps no list and returns the moment a good path is found.

Remember

Pass information down the tree as a parameter (here: the remaining budget). Pass answers up with the return value.

Watch out

The check must happen at a leaf, not at null. For root = [1, 2], targetSum = 1 the answer is false: node 1 has a child, so it is not a leaf, and the empty right spot does not count as a path end.

Pattern notes: Binary Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 543Diameter of Binary TreeEasyTree DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

The diameter is the longest path between any two nodes, counted in edges (the lines between nodes). The path may or may not pass through the root.

Example: root = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] → 3. The path 4 → 2 → 1 → 3 has three edges.

1Brute force — at every node, measure both heights

Any longest path "bends" at some top node. So for every node, compute the height of its left side plus the height of its right side, and keep the largest. Height is computed from scratch each time.

int diameterOfBinaryTree(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return 0;
    int throughMe = height(root.left) + height(root.right);   // path bending at root
    int best = Math.max(diameterOfBinaryTree(root.left),
                        diameterOfBinaryTree(root.right));   // or entirely inside a subtree
    return Math.max(throughMe, best);
}

int height(TreeNode node) {          // counts nodes on the longest way down
    if (node == null) return 0;
    return 1 + Math.max(height(node.left), height(node.right));
}

Time O(n²)Space O(h)

Each call to height re-walks a whole subtree, and we call it at every node. On a long skinny tree that's about n²/2 steps: the same heights get recomputed over and over.

2Optimal — one pass: return height, record diameter
The idea

The height function already knows the left and right heights of every node. So while computing heights, also check left + right at each node and remember the best in a field. The function returns one thing (height) but records another (diameter).

private int best = 0;                    // longest path found so far (in edges)

int diameterOfBinaryTree(TreeNode root) {
    height(root);
    return best;
}

int height(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int left = height(node.left);        // how far down on the left
    int right = height(node.right);      // how far down on the right
    best = Math.max(best, left + right); // path that bends at this node
    return 1 + Math.max(left, right);    // tell my parent my height
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Every node is visited exactly once, and each height is computed once and reused by the parent.

Remember

When a tree answer needs info from both children, return what the parent needs (height) and track the global answer on the side (diameter). This "return one thing, record another" trick also solves Balanced Tree and Max Path Sum.

Watch out

The longest path does not have to pass through the root, so "left height of root + right height of root" alone is wrong. Also count edges, not nodes: left + right (heights in nodes) already equals the edge count of the bent path.

Pattern notes: Binary Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 108Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search TreeEasyDivide & ConquerLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get a sorted array. Build a height-balanced BST from it: smaller values to the left, bigger to the right, and the two sides of every node differ in height by at most 1.

Example: nums = [-10, -3, 0, 5, 9] → [0, -3, 9, -10, null, 5]. [0, -10, 5, null, -3, null, 9] is also accepted: any balanced BST is fine.

1First way — split the array into copies

The middle value must be the root (half the values are smaller, half bigger). Then do the same for the left half and the right half, making a new small array for each.

TreeNode sortedArrayToBST(int[] nums) {
    if (nums.length == 0) return null;
    int mid = nums.length / 2;
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(nums[mid]);
    root.left = sortedArrayToBST(Arrays.copyOfRange(nums, 0, mid));                // new array
    root.right = sortedArrayToBST(Arrays.copyOfRange(nums, mid + 1, nums.length)); // new array
    return root;
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n log n)

The idea is right, but every level of recursion copies about n numbers in total, and there are log n levels. Copying is wasted work: the numbers are already sitting in the original array.

2Optimal — same idea, with index bounds
The idea

Instead of copying halves, pass two indexes, lo and hi, that say which slice of the original array you are working on. Middle of the slice becomes the node, left slice builds its left subtree, right slice its right subtree.

TreeNode sortedArrayToBST(int[] nums) {
    return build(nums, 0, nums.length - 1);
}

TreeNode build(int[] nums, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo > hi) return null;                 // empty range: no node
    int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;             // middle = root of this range
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(nums[mid]);
    root.left = build(nums, lo, mid - 1);     // left half builds left subtree
    root.right = build(nums, mid + 1, hi);    // right half builds right subtree
    return root;
}

Time O(n)Space O(log n)

Each value becomes exactly one node. Because we always split in the middle, the recursion is only log n deep.

Remember

Middle of a sorted range = balanced root. And whenever you are tempted to copy a sub-array into recursion, pass lo and hi indexes instead.

Watch out

Inserting the values one by one in sorted order into a BST gives a straight line (every new value is bigger, so it always goes right). That is a valid BST but not balanced, so it is wrong here.

Pattern notes: Binary Search Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 700Search in a Binary Search TreeEasyBSTLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Find the node with value val in a BST and return it (its whole subtree comes with it). If it isn't there, return null.

Example: root = [4, 2, 7, 1, 3], val = 2 → [2, 1, 3]. With val = 5 → [] (null).

1Brute force — search everywhere

Treat it like any binary tree: check this node, then search the left side, and if that fails search the right side.

TreeNode searchBST(TreeNode root, int val) {
    if (root == null) return null;
    if (root.val == val) return root;
    TreeNode found = searchBST(root.left, val);   // look left...
    if (found != null) return found;
    return searchBST(root.right, val);            // ...and right, no matter what
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

It ignores the one thing that makes a BST special: its ordering. It can end up looking at every node.

2Optimal — follow the BST rule down one path
The idea

In a BST, everything left of a node is smaller and everything right is bigger. So at each node go left if val is smaller, right if it's bigger. It's binary search on a tree: one comparison throws away a whole side.

TreeNode searchBST(TreeNode root, int val) {
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null && cur.val != val) {
        cur = (val < cur.val) ? cur.left : cur.right;   // throw away the wrong half
    }
    return cur;   // the node, or null if we fell off the tree
}

Time O(h)Space O(1)

We follow a single path from the root, so the cost is the tree's height: about log n for a balanced BST. The loop needs no stack at all.

Remember

BST problems = compare, then go one way. Search, insert, floor/ceiling and LCA in a BST all walk a single root-to-leaf path in O(h).

Watch out

O(h) is only log n if the tree is balanced. A BST built from sorted inserts is a straight line with h = n, so the worst case is still O(n).

Pattern notes: Binary Search Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 235Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search TreeMediumBSTLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Given two nodes p and q in a BST, find their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both of them below it (a node counts as its own ancestor).

Example: root = [6, 2, 8, 0, 4, 7, 9, null, null, 3, 5]. With p = 2, q = 8 → 6. With p = 2, q = 4 → 2 (2 is an ancestor of 4, and of itself).

1Brute force — the general binary-tree method

Ignore the BST order. Search both sides of every node: if p is found on one side and q on the other, this node is where they split, so it's the answer.

TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (root == null || root == p || root == q) return root;
    TreeNode left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q);
    TreeNode right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
    if (left != null && right != null) return root;   // p and q on different sides
    return left != null ? left : right;               // pass up whatever was found
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

This works for any binary tree (it's LC 236), but it may visit every node. The BST ordering tells us which way to go without looking.

2Optimal — walk down until p and q split
The idea

Start at the root. If p and q are both smaller, they both live on the left, so go left. If both bigger, go right. Otherwise they are on different sides (or one of them is this node): the first node where they split is the answer.
