Start the reversal with prev = groupNext instead of null: the first node of the group then points straight at the rest of the list, so the right side is glued for free.

ListNode reverseKGroup(ListNode head, int k) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
    ListNode groupPrev = dummy;                  // node just before the current group
    while (true) {
        ListNode kth = groupPrev;                // walk k steps: is there a full group?
        for (int i = 0; i < k && kth != null; i++) kth = kth.next;
        if (kth == null) break;                  // fewer than k nodes left: stop
        ListNode groupNext = kth.next;           // first node after the group

        // reverse the group (LC 206), but point the first node at groupNext
        ListNode prev = groupNext, cur = groupPrev.next;
        while (cur != groupNext) {
            ListNode nxt = cur.next;
            cur.next = prev;
            prev = cur;
            cur = nxt;
        }
        ListNode oldFirst = groupPrev.next;      // it is now the group's last node
        groupPrev.next = kth;                    // kth is the new first node
        groupPrev = oldFirst;                    // move on to the next group
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

Every node is visited twice (once while looking for kth, once while reversing), and only a few pointers are kept.

Remember

To reverse many pieces of a list, keep a dummy in front and a pointer to the node before each piece. Starting the reversal with prev = nodeAfterPiece reconnects the tail automatically.

Watch out

Check that a full group exists before reversing. If you reverse first and count later, the short tail (5 in the k = 2 example) gets reversed too and you must undo it. Also save groupPrev.next (the old first node) before overwriting it: it is where the next group starts.

Pattern notes: In-place Linked List Reversal · Open on LeetCode

LC 148Sort ListMediumMerge Sort on a ListLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Sort a linked list in ascending order and return the new head. Aim for O(n log n) time. The follow-up asks for O(1) extra memory.

Example: 4→2→1→3 → 1→2→3→4. -1→5→3→4→0 → -1→0→3→4→5.

How to spot the pattern

"Sort" plus "linked list" plus "O(n log n)" points to merge sort. Quick sort and heap sort need jumping to any index, which a list can't do. Merge sort only needs "split in half" and "merge two sorted lists", and a list is great at both: finding the middle is LC 876, merging is LC 21, and merging needs no extra array.

1Brute force — copy out, sort the array, write back

Put all values into an ArrayList, sort it with the library, then walk the list again and overwrite the values in order.

ListNode sortList(ListNode head) {
    List<Integer> vals = new ArrayList<>();
    for (ListNode p = head; p != null; p = p.next) vals.add(p.val);  // copy out
    Collections.sort(vals);                                           // sort the array
    ListNode p = head;
    for (int v : vals) { p.val = v; p = p.next; }                     // write back
    return head;
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)

The time is already fine; the problem is the O(n) copy and that it rewrites values instead of sorting the nodes. An interviewer will ask you to sort the list itself.

2Optimal — top-down merge sort on the nodes
The idea

Two Beginner problems glued with recursion: LC 876 (middle of the list) to split, LC 21 (merge two sorted lists) to join. The extra insight is cut the list at the middle by setting slow.next = null, so each half is a real, separate list you can sort on its own.

Start fast at head.next (not head) so that on a 2-node list slow stops on the first node and the split is 1 + 1, not 2 + 0.

ListNode sortList(ListNode head) {
    if (head == null || head.next == null) return head;  // 0 or 1 node: sorted
    // 1. find the middle (LC 876); slow stops at the END of the left half
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head.next;
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }
    ListNode right = slow.next;
    slow.next = null;                                    // 2. cut into two lists
    ListNode left = sortList(head);                      // 3. sort each half
    right = sortList(right);
    return merge(left, right);                           // 4. merge (LC 21)
}

ListNode merge(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0), tail = dummy;
    while (a != null && b != null) {
        if (a.val <= b.val) { tail.next = a; a = a.next; }
        else                { tail.next = b; b = b.next; }
        tail = tail.next;
    }
    tail.next = (a != null) ? a : b;                     // glue the leftover
    return dummy.next;
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(log n)

There are log n levels of halving, and each level does O(n) work in total (finding middles plus merging). The only extra memory is the recursion stack, log n calls deep.

3Follow-up — bottom-up merge sort, O(1) space

The recursion stack is the only thing that is not O(1). Remove it by working bottom-up: first merge neighbouring runs of size 1, then of size 2, 4, 8... until one run covers the list. cut detaches the next size nodes and returns what follows.

size 1: 4 | 2 | 1 | 3 -> 2 4 | 1 3 size 2: 2 4 | 1 3 -> 1 2 3 4 size 4: size >= n, stop
ListNode sortList(ListNode head) {
    int n = 0;
    for (ListNode p = head; p != null; p = p.next) n++;
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
    for (int size = 1; size < n; size *= 2) {       // sorted runs of 1, 2, 4, ...
        ListNode tail = dummy, cur = dummy.next;
        while (cur != null) {
            ListNode left = cur;
            ListNode right = cut(left, size);       // left = first 'size' nodes
            cur = cut(right, size);                 // right = next 'size' nodes
            tail.next = merge(left, right);         // same merge as above
            while (tail.next != null) tail = tail.next;
        }
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

ListNode cut(ListNode node, int size) {             // keep 'size' nodes, return the rest
    for (int i = 1; node != null && i < size; i++) node = node.next;
    if (node == null) return null;
    ListNode rest = node.next;
    node.next = null;
    return rest;
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(1)

Same merges as step 2, just in a loop instead of a call stack. Worth knowing; top-down is usually enough in an interview.

Remember

Sorting a linked list = merge sort: middle with fast/slow, cut, sort both halves, merge. For O(1) space, merge runs of size 1, 2, 4, ... bottom-up.

Watch out

If you start fast = head, a 2-node list splits into "2 nodes + nothing" and the recursion never gets smaller: a stack overflow. Start fast = head.next, and don't forget slow.next = null, or the left half still runs into the right half.

Pattern notes: Sorting · Open on LeetCode

Trees

Hard tree problems are still one DFS, but the recursive function has to return one thing to its parent while recording a different thing globally, or return a small state instead of a number. Template: decide what a node must tell its parent, compute it from the children's answers (post-order), and update the global answer on the way. What is harder than Intermediate: the value you return is not the answer itself (path sum, cameras), you may need to encode a whole tree as text, or sort nodes by (column, row, value) positions.

LC 124Binary Tree Maximum Path SumHardTree DFS (return vs record)LeetCode
The problem in easy words

A path is any chain of connected nodes, each used at most once. It does not have to go through the root and can go up then down (like an upside-down V). Node values can be negative. Return the largest possible sum of a path (at least one node).

Example: root = [-10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] → 42, the path 15 → 20 → 7.

How to spot the pattern

"Path between any two nodes, not necessarily through the root" is the shape of LC 543 (Diameter of Binary Tree) from Beginner: every path has one highest node where it bends. "Maximum sum" with negative values adds one twist: a subtree may be worth skipping.

1Brute force — try every node as the top of the path

Every path has a highest node (its "top"). For each node as the top, the best path is: its value, plus the best downward chain on the left (if positive), plus the best downward chain on the right (if positive). Compute those chains with a separate recursion every time.

int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    // best path whose TOP (highest node) is root: root plus the good downward chains
    int here = root.val + Math.max(0, down(root.left)) + Math.max(0, down(root.right));
    // ...or the top is somewhere below: try every node as the top
    return Math.max(here, Math.max(maxPathSum(root.left), maxPathSum(root.right)));
}

int down(TreeNode node) {           // best chain that starts at node and goes down
    if (node == null) return 0;
    return node.val + Math.max(0, Math.max(down(node.left), down(node.right)));
}

Time O(n²)Space O(h)

For every node we re-walk its whole subtree to find chains. On a skewed tree with the maximum 3 × 10⁴ nodes that is about 4.5 × 10⁸ steps, which times out.

2Optimal — one post-order DFS that returns a chain and records a path
The idea

This is LC 543 (Diameter) with sums instead of lengths. The helper gain(node) returns the best chain going down from node (one side only, because a parent can extend a chain, not a V). While it has both children's gains, it also checks the path that bends at node. The extra insight: clamp negative gains to 0, meaning "don't take that side at all".

int best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;       // best full path seen anywhere

int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) {
    gain(root);
    return best;
}

// returns the best chain going DOWN from node (can be handed to the parent)
int gain(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;
    int left = Math.max(0, gain(node.left));    // a negative chain? take nothing
    int right = Math.max(0, gain(node.right));
    best = Math.max(best, node.val + left + right);  // path that bends at node
    return node.val + Math.max(left, right);    // parent may use only ONE side
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

Each node is visited once and does O(1) work; the stack is as deep as the tree's height h.

Remember

"Best path anywhere in a tree": the DFS returns the best one-sided chain to the parent and records the best two-sided path in a global. Return and record are different values.

Watch out

Start best at Integer.MIN_VALUE, not 0: in an all-negative tree like [-3] the answer is -3. And never return left + right + node.val to the parent: that is a V shape, and the parent can't attach to the middle of a V.

Pattern notes: Tree BFS & DFS · Open on LeetCode

LC 297Serialize and Deserialize Binary TreeHardPreorder with null markersLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Write a class with two methods: serialize(root) turns a tree into a string, and deserialize(data) turns that string back into the exact same tree (same shape, same values). You choose the format. Values can repeat and be negative.

Example: root = [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4, 5] → some string → [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4, 5] again.

How to spot the pattern

"Turn a tree into text and back" means: pick a traversal order and write down enough to know where each subtree ends. A plain preorder list is ambiguous (1, 2 could be 2 on the left or the right). Recording the null children fixes that. You already rebuilt a tree from two traversals in LC 105; here one traversal plus null markers is enough.

1Brute force — store it like a heap array

Number the slots like a binary heap: root at slot 0, children of slot i at 2i+1 and 2i+2. Make an array big enough for a full tree of the same height, fill in the values, write # in empty slots.

public class Codec {
    // store the tree like a heap: node at slot i, children at 2i+1 and 2i+2
    public String serialize(TreeNode root) {
        int h = height(root);
        String[] slots = new String[(1 << h) - 1];     // 2^h - 1 slots
        Arrays.fill(slots, "#");                        // '#' = no node here
        fill(root, 0, slots);
        return String.join(",", slots);
    }

    void fill(TreeNode node, int i, String[] slots) {
        if (node == null) return;
        slots[i] = String.valueOf(node.val);
        fill(node.left, 2 * i + 1, slots);
        fill(node.right, 2 * i + 2, slots);
    }

    int height(TreeNode node) {
        return node == null ? 0 : 1 + Math.max(height(node.left), height(node.right));
    }

    public TreeNode deserialize(String data) {
        if (data.isEmpty()) return null;
        return build(data.split(","), 0);
    }

    TreeNode build(String[] slots, int i) {
        if (i >= slots.length || slots[i].equals("#")) return null;
        TreeNode node = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(slots[i]));
        node.left = build(slots, 2 * i + 1);
        node.right = build(slots, 2 * i + 2);
        return node;
    }
}

Time O(2ʰ)Space O(2ʰ)

Fine for bushy trees, hopeless for tall ones: a chain of just 31 nodes needs 2³¹ − 1 (about 2 billion) slots, and the problem allows 10⁴ nodes. The size should depend on the number of nodes, not the height.

2Optimal — preorder with "#" for null, read back in the same order
The idea

Write the tree in preorder (node, left subtree, right subtree) and write # for every null child. To read it back, use the same recursion: take one token; # means null, a number means "make a node, then read its left subtree, then its right subtree". The extra insight: the # markers tell the reader exactly where each subtree stops, so no sizes or second traversal are needed.

public class Codec {
    // preorder, writing "#" for every null child
    public String serialize(TreeNode root) {
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        write(root, sb);
        return sb.toString();
    }

    void write(TreeNode node, StringBuilder sb) {
        if (node == null) { sb.append("#,"); return; }
        sb.append(node.val).append(',');        // root first...
        write(node.left, sb);                   // ...then the whole left subtree
        write(node.right, sb);                  // ...then the whole right subtree
    }

    public TreeNode deserialize(String data) {
        Deque<String> tokens = new ArrayDeque<>(Arrays.asList(data.split(",")));
        return read(tokens);
    }

    TreeNode read(Deque<String> tokens) {       // read in the SAME order we wrote
        String t = tokens.poll();
        if (t.equals("#")) return null;
        TreeNode node = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(t));
        node.left = read(tokens);               // consumes exactly the left subtree
        node.right = read(tokens);
        return node;
    }
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

n nodes plus n + 1 null markers, each written once and read once. The string and the recursion stack are both O(n) at worst.

Remember

Preorder + null markers uniquely describes a binary tree. Deserialize with the same recursion shape as serialize, reading from a shared queue (or an index) of tokens.

Watch out

Use a separator (,): values like -12 or 100 are more than one character. And the reader must share one position across all calls (a queue or a field), not a local index that each recursive call copies.

Pattern notes: Binary Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 987Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary TreeHardDFS + Sort by positionLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Give every node a position: the root is at (row 0, column 0), a left child is one row down and one column left, a right child one row down and one column right. Return the values column by column, left to right. Inside a column, go top to bottom; if two nodes share the same row and column, the smaller value comes first.

Example: root = [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 5, 7] → [[4], [2], [1, 5, 6], [3], [7]]. 5 and 6 are both at row 2, column 0, so 5 goes first.

How to spot the pattern

"Column", "row" and a tie-break by value mean each node has a 3-part sort key (column, row, value). Collecting positions is a plain DFS that passes row + 1 and col ± 1 to children; the Hard part is only getting the order right, which a sort does for you.

1Brute force — one full walk per column

First find the leftmost and rightmost column. Then, for each column, walk the whole tree collecting the nodes in that column, and sort just those by (row, value).

int minCol, maxCol;

List<List<Integer>> verticalTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    span(root, 0);                                    // how wide is the tree?
    List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int c = minCol; c <= maxCol; c++) {          // one full walk PER column
        List<int[]> here = new ArrayList<>();         // {row, val}
        collect(root, 0, 0, c, here);
        here.sort((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? a[0] - b[0] : a[1] - b[1]);
        List<Integer> col = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int[] p : here) col.add(p[1]);
        result.add(col);
    }
    return result;
}

void span(TreeNode n, int col) {
    if (n == null) return;
    minCol = Math.min(minCol, col);
    maxCol = Math.max(maxCol, col);
    span(n.left, col - 1);
    span(n.right, col + 1);
}

void collect(TreeNode n, int row, int col, int want, List<int[]> out) {
    if (n == null) return;
    if (col == want) out.add(new int[]{row, n.val});
    collect(n.left, row + 1, col - 1, want, out);
    collect(n.right, row + 1, col + 1, want, out);
}

Time O(n · W)Space O(n)

W is the number of columns, which can be close to n (a zig-zag tree), so this is O(n²). With the limit of 1000 nodes it still passes, but it walks the tree W times for no reason.

2Optimal — one DFS, one sort on (col, row, val)
The idea

It is a normal DFS from Intermediate (like LC 199 / LC 102, but carrying coordinates), plus one extra insight: turn every node into a triple (col, row, val) and sort all triples once. The sort puts columns in order, rows in order inside a column, and breaks ties by value, which are exactly the three rules of the problem. Then cut the sorted list wherever the column changes.

List<List<Integer>> verticalTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<int[]> nodes = new ArrayList<>();            // {col, row, val}
    dfs(root, 0, 0, nodes);
    // sort by column, then row (top first), then value (small first)
    nodes.sort((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? a[0] - b[0]
                       : a[1] != b[1] ? a[1] - b[1]
                       : a[2] - b[2]);
    List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    int prevCol = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
    for (int[] t : nodes) {
        if (t[0] != prevCol) {                        // a new column starts
            result.add(new ArrayList<>());
            prevCol = t[0];
        }
        result.get(result.size() - 1).add(t[2]);
    }
    return result;
}

void dfs(TreeNode n, int row, int col, List<int[]> out) {
    if (n == null) return;
    out.add(new int[]{col, row, n.val});
    dfs(n.left, row + 1, col - 1, out);               // left child: one column left
    dfs(n.right, row + 1, col + 1, out);              // right child: one column right
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)

The DFS is O(n); sorting n triples is O(n log n) and dominates.

Remember

When the output order has several rules ("by column, then row, then value"), collect tuples and sort with a comparator that checks the rules in that order. One sort beats nested maps.

Watch out

A BFS by column with a plain list (the LC 314 approach) is wrong here: it keeps same-row, same-column nodes in visiting order (6 before 5), not sorted by value. You need the value in the sort key.

Pattern notes: Tree BFS & DFS · Open on LeetCode

LC 968Binary Tree CamerasHardGreedy DFS (3 states)LeetCode
The problem in easy words

You can put cameras on tree nodes. A camera watches its own node, its parent and its children. What is the fewest cameras so that every node is watched?

Example: root = [0, 0, null, 0, 0] → 1: one camera on the root's left child watches all four nodes.

How to spot the pattern

"Minimum number of things placed on a tree" where each thing covers its neighbours. Trying all placements is exponential. On a tree you can decide bottom-up: a node's best choice only depends on what its children report, so a post-order DFS with a few states works, like the "what do I tell my parent" DFS in LC 124.

1Brute force — try every set of camera nodes

List all nodes and remember each one's parent. For every subset (a bitmask), check that each node is watched by itself, its parent or a child. Keep the smallest valid subset.

List<TreeNode> nodes = new ArrayList<>();
Map<TreeNode, TreeNode> parent = new HashMap<>();

int minCameraCover(TreeNode root) {
    collect(root, null);
    int n = nodes.size(), best = n;
    for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {   // every subset of nodes
        Set<TreeNode> cams = new HashSet<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if ((mask >> i & 1) == 1) cams.add(nodes.get(i));
        boolean allCovered = true;
        for (TreeNode v : nodes) {                    // is v watched by someone?
            if (!cams.contains(v) && !cams.contains(parent.get(v))
                    && !cams.contains(v.left) && !cams.contains(v.right)) {
                allCovered = false;
                break;
            }
        }
        if (allCovered) best = Math.min(best, cams.size());
    }
    return best;
}

void collect(TreeNode node, TreeNode par) {
    if (node == null) return;
    nodes.add(node);
    parent.put(node, par);
    collect(node.left, node);
    collect(node.right, node);
}

Time O(2ⁿ · n)Space O(n)

Already 25 nodes means about 8 × 10⁸ checks, and the problem allows 1000 nodes. It is only useful to test the fast version on tiny trees.

2Optimal — post-order greedy with three states
The idea

A tree DFS (as in LC 124) where each node returns a state instead of a number: NOT_COVERED, HAS_CAMERA or COVERED. The extra insight is a greedy rule: never put a camera on a leaf; put it on the leaf's parent. The parent's camera covers the leaf too, plus the parent and grandparent, so it is never worse.

From the bottom: a null child counts as COVERED (it needs nothing, and it must not force a camera onto a leaf). If any child is NOT_COVERED, this node must hold a camera. Else if any child has a camera, this node is COVERED. Otherwise it is NOT_COVERED and waits for its parent.

static final int NOT_COVERED = 0, HAS_CAMERA = 1, COVERED = 2;
int cameras = 0;

int minCameraCover(TreeNode root) {
    if (dfs(root) == NOT_COVERED) cameras++;   // nobody above the root to help
    return cameras;
}

int dfs(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return COVERED;          // null needs nothing, wants no camera
    int left = dfs(node.left);                 // post-order: children decide first
    int right = dfs(node.right);
    if (left == NOT_COVERED || right == NOT_COVERED) {
        cameras++;                             // a child is exposed: I MUST watch it
        return HAS_CAMERA;
    }
    if (left == HAS_CAMERA || right == HAS_CAMERA) {
        return COVERED;                        // a child's camera watches me
    }
    return NOT_COVERED;                        // leave me for my parent
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

One post-order pass. The order of the checks matters: "a child is exposed" wins over "a child has a camera".

Remember

Covering / placing problems on trees: go bottom-up and return a small state to the parent. Delay every decision as high as possible (leaf → parent), because a higher camera covers more.

Watch out

Two classic bugs: returning NOT_COVERED for null (then every leaf gets a camera), and forgetting the root. The root has no parent to cover it, so if the DFS returns NOT_COVERED for the root, add one more camera (a single node [0] needs 1).

Pattern notes: Greedy · Open on LeetCode

LC 99Recover Binary Search TreeMediumIn-order DFSLeetCode
The problem in easy words

In a binary search tree, the values of exactly two nodes were swapped by mistake. Fix the tree without changing its shape (swap the two values back).

Example: root = [3, 1, 4, null, null, 2] → [2, 1, 4, null, null, 3]: 3 and 2 were swapped.

How to spot the pattern

"BST" plus "something is out of order" → look at the in-order traversal, which must be sorted (LC 98, Validate BST). Two swapped values make the sorted sequence go down once or twice. Finding those "drops" finds the two nodes.

1Brute force — in-order list, sort, write back

Collect the nodes in in-order position, take their values, sort them, and write the sorted values back into the nodes in the same in-order positions.

void recoverTree(TreeNode root) {
    List<TreeNode> nodes = new ArrayList<>();
    inorder(root, nodes);                            // nodes in in-order position
    List<Integer> vals = new ArrayList<>();
    for (TreeNode n : nodes) vals.add(n.val);
    Collections.sort(vals);                          // what the values SHOULD be
    for (int i = 0; i < nodes.size(); i++) nodes.get(i).val = vals.get(i);
}

void inorder(TreeNode n, List<TreeNode> out) {
    if (n == null) return;
    inorder(n.left, out);
    out.add(n);
    inorder(n.right, out);
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)

Correct, but it sorts everything to fix only two values and stores the whole tree in a list. The follow-up asks for O(1) extra space.

2Optimal — spot the drops during in-order
The idea

Same in-order walk with a prev pointer as LC 98 (Validate BST). The extra insight is what the drops mean: at the first drop the bigger value (prev) is wrong; at the last drop the smaller value (node) is wrong. If the swapped nodes are neighbours in the in-order, there is only one drop, and it gives both.

TreeNode first, second, prev;

void recoverTree(TreeNode root) {
    inorder(root);
    int tmp = first.val;                        // swap the two values back
    first.val = second.val;
    second.val = tmp;
}

void inorder(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return;
    inorder(node.left);
    if (prev != null && prev.val > node.val) {  // a "drop" in the sorted order
        if (first == null) first = prev;        // 1st drop: the bigger one is wrong
        second = node;                          // last drop: the smaller one is wrong
    }
    prev = node;
    inorder(node.right);
}

Time O(n)Space O(h)

One in-order pass, then one swap. The only memory is the recursion stack, as deep as the tree.

3Follow-up — Morris traversal, O(1) space

To drop the stack, use Morris in-order: before going left, make the rightmost node of the left subtree point back to cur (a temporary "thread"). When you come back up the thread, the left side is finished, so you visit cur, remove the thread and go right. The visit check is the same as in step 2.

TreeNode first, second, prev;

void recoverTree(TreeNode root) {
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null) {
        if (cur.left == null) { visit(cur); cur = cur.right; }
        else {
            TreeNode pred = cur.left;               // rightmost node of the left subtree
            while (pred.right != null && pred.right != cur) pred = pred.right;
            if (pred.right == null) {               // first visit: leave a thread back to cur
                pred.right = cur;
                cur = cur.left;
            } else {                                // came back up the thread: left is done
                pred.right = null;                  // remove the thread (tree restored)
                visit(cur);
                cur = cur.right;
            }
        }
    }
    int tmp = first.val; first.val = second.val; second.val = tmp;
}

void visit(TreeNode node) {                         // same check as step 2
    if (prev != null && prev.val > node.val) {
        if (first == null) first = prev;
        second = node;
    }
    prev = node;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

Each edge is walked at most a few times, and every thread is removed, so the tree ends up unchanged except for the fix.

Remember

BST problems → think of the sorted in-order sequence. Two swapped items in a sorted list: first = bigger value at the first drop, second = smaller value at the last drop.

Watch out

Update second at every drop, not only when first is already set, or the neighbour case (one drop, like 1 3 2 4) leaves second null. And swap values, not nodes: moving nodes would change the shape.

Pattern notes: Binary Search Trees · Open on LeetCode

Design

Design problems ask for a class where every method is fast. Template: list the operations and their target cost, then combine structures so each one covers another's weak spot (a HashMap for "find it", a linked list or LinkedHashSet for "order", a heap for "best of many"). What is harder than Intermediate (LRU Cache, LC 146): you track two orders at once (how often and how recently), or you merge data from many users on every call.

LC 460LFU CacheHardHashMap + Frequency BucketsLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Build a cache with a fixed capacity. get(key) returns the value or -1. put(key, value) inserts or updates. When the cache is full and a new key arrives, remove the key used the fewest times; if several keys tie, remove the one used least recently. Both get and put count as a use. Both must run in O(1) on average.

Example: capacity 2: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1) → 1, put(3,3) evicts key 2 (used once, key 1 used twice), get(2) → -1, get(3) → 3, put(4,4) evicts key 1 (1 and 3 both used twice, 1 is older), get(1) → -1, get(3) → 3, get(4) → 4.

How to spot the pattern

"Cache", "capacity", "evict", "O(1)" is the LRU Cache family (LC 146). "Least frequently used, ties by least recently used" means two keys of order. You can't keep one list sorted by both in O(1), so group keys by frequency and keep an LRU order inside each group.

1Brute force (naive design) — one map, scan to evict

Store key → {value, freq, lastUsed} with a global clock. get and updates are O(1). To evict, scan every key and pick the smallest freq, breaking ties by the smallest lastUsed.

class LFUCache {
    private final int capacity;
    private int time = 0;                               // a clock: bigger = more recent
    private Map<Integer, int[]> map = new HashMap<>();  // key -> {value, freq, lastUsed}

    public LFUCache(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

    public int get(int key) {
        int[] e = map.get(key);
        if (e == null) return -1;
        e[1]++;                                         // one more use
        e[2] = ++time;
        return e[0];
    }

    public void put(int key, int value) {
        if (capacity == 0) return;
        int[] e = map.get(key);
        if (e != null) { e[0] = value; e[1]++; e[2] = ++time; return; }
        if (map.size() == capacity) {                   // scan EVERY key for the victim
            int victim = -1;
            int[] worst = null;
            for (Map.Entry<Integer, int[]> en : map.entrySet()) {
                int[] c = en.getValue();
                if (worst == null || c[1] < worst[1]
                        || (c[1] == worst[1] && c[2] < worst[2])) {
                    worst = c;
                    victim = en.getKey();
                }
            }
            map.remove(victim);
        }
        map.put(key, new int[]{value, 1, ++time});
    }
}

Time O(capacity) per put when fullSpace O(capacity)

With capacity 10⁴ and up to 2 × 10⁵ calls, eviction scans can reach about 2 × 10⁹ steps, and the problem explicitly asks for O(1).

2Optimal — one LRU list per frequency, plus minFreq
The idea

This is LRU Cache (LC 146) from Intermediate, one per frequency. buckets[f] is a LinkedHashSet of the keys used exactly f times, oldest first (a LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order and removes in O(1)). On every use, move the key from bucket f to the end of bucket f+1. The extra insight: keep minFreq; it only changes in two easy ways. It becomes 1 when a new key is inserted, and it goes up by 1 when a use empties bucket minFreq. To evict, remove the first key of buckets[minFreq].

class LFUCache {
    private final int capacity;
    private int minFreq = 0;                                  // smallest freq in the cache
    private Map<Integer, Integer> vals = new HashMap<>();     // key -> value
    private Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();     // key -> how many uses
    // freq -> keys with that freq, oldest first (a tiny LRU list per frequency)
    private Map<Integer, LinkedHashSet<Integer>> buckets = new HashMap<>();

    public LFUCache(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

    public int get(int key) {
        if (!vals.containsKey(key)) return -1;
        touch(key);
        return vals.get(key);
    }

    public void put(int key, int value) {
        if (capacity == 0) return;
        if (vals.containsKey(key)) {                          // update = a use, too
            vals.put(key, value);
            touch(key);
            return;
        }
        if (vals.size() == capacity) {                        // evict: least freq, then oldest
            LinkedHashSet<Integer> lowest = buckets.get(minFreq);
            int victim = lowest.iterator().next();            // first = least recently used
            lowest.remove(victim);
            vals.remove(victim);
            freq.remove(victim);
        }
        vals.put(key, value);
        freq.put(key, 1);
        buckets.computeIfAbsent(1, f -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);
        minFreq = 1;                                          // a brand-new key has freq 1
    }

    private void touch(int key) {                             // move key from bucket f to f+1
        int f = freq.get(key);
        freq.put(key, f + 1);
        buckets.get(f).remove(key);
        if (f == minFreq && buckets.get(f).isEmpty()) minFreq++;
        buckets.computeIfAbsent(f + 1, x -> new LinkedHashSet<>()).add(key);  // goes to the END = newest
    }
}

Time O(1) average, get and putSpace O(capacity)

Every step is a HashMap or LinkedHashSet operation, all O(1) on average. No scanning, no sorting.

Remember

Two orders (frequency, then recency) in O(1): bucket by the first order, keep the second order inside each bucket, and track the smallest non-empty bucket with a pointer that only moves in predictable ways.

Watch out

Evict before inserting the new key, and only when the key is new: updating an existing key never evicts. Set minFreq = 1 after evicting, since the victim is found through the old minFreq. Handle capacity = 0 (older test cases) by ignoring puts.

Pattern notes: Design Problems · Open on LeetCode

LC 895Maximum Frequency StackHardStack per FrequencyLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Build a stack-like class. push(val) adds a value. pop() removes and returns the most frequent value in the stack; if several values tie, return the one closest to the top (pushed most recently).

Example: push 5, 7, 5, 7, 4, 5, then pop four times → 5, 7, 5, 4.

How to spot the pattern

"Most frequent, ties by most recent" is the same two-order puzzle as LFU, flipped (take the max, not the min). Frequencies only go up or down by 1 on each push or pop, which hints that you can keep a stack per frequency level and a maxFreq pointer instead of a heap.

1Brute force (naive design) — plain stack, recount on pop

Keep a normal list. On pop, count every value, find the maximum count, then scan from the top for the first value with that count and remove it.

class FreqStack {
    private List<Integer> stack = new ArrayList<>();         // plain stack, top = end

    public void push(int val) { stack.add(val); }

    public int pop() {
        Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();       // recount everything
        int maxFreq = 0;
        for (int v : stack) {
            count.merge(v, 1, Integer::sum);
            maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, count.get(v));
        }
        for (int i = stack.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {        // from the top down
            if (count.get(stack.get(i)) == maxFreq) {        // first most-frequent one
                return stack.remove(i);                      // shifts the rest: O(n)
            }
        }
        return -1;                                           // never happens
    }
}

Time O(n) per popSpace O(n)

With up to 2 × 10⁴ calls, pops can cost around 10⁸ steps in total. Too slow for the O(1) the interviewer expects.

2Optimal — a stack for each frequency level
The idea

Keep freq[val] and a stack group[f] for each frequency f. When val reaches frequency f, push it onto group[f]. The extra insight: a value with count 3 lives in group 1, 2 AND 3 at the same time. Popping from group[maxFreq] removes only its top copy; the lower copies are still in the right place. Each group is a normal stack, so "newest first" breaks ties for free.

class FreqStack {
    private Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();          // value -> count now
    private Map<Integer, Deque<Integer>> group = new HashMap<>();  // f -> values that reached f
    private int maxFreq = 0;

    public void push(int val) {
        int f = freq.getOrDefault(val, 0) + 1;
        freq.put(val, f);
        maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, f);
        group.computeIfAbsent(f, x -> new ArrayDeque<>()).push(val);  // val's f-th copy
    }

    public int pop() {
        Deque<Integer> top = group.get(maxFreq);   // most frequent values, newest on top
        int val = top.pop();
        freq.put(val, freq.get(val) - 1);          // its lower copies stay in lower groups
        if (top.isEmpty()) maxFreq--;              // next level down always has something
        return val;
    }
}

Time O(1) per push and popSpace O(n)

If group[maxFreq] becomes empty, group[maxFreq − 1] can't be empty (every value there also passed through it), so maxFreq-- is always correct.

Remember

When a count changes by exactly 1 at a time, buckets indexed by count plus a max/min pointer replace a heap and give O(1). Keeping a value in every level it passed through removes all bookkeeping on pop.

Watch out

Don't move the value from group f−1 to group f on push; leave the old copy there. If you move it, then after a pop you would have to put it back in the lower group at the right position, which breaks the "newest first" order.

Pattern notes: Design Problems · Open on LeetCode

LC 355Design TwitterMediumDesign + K-way MergeLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Build a tiny Twitter: postTweet(userId, tweetId), follow(a, b), unfollow(a, b), and getNewsFeed(userId), which returns the 10 most recent tweet ids from the user and everyone they follow, newest first.

Example: postTweet(1, 5), getNewsFeed(1) → [5], follow(1, 2), postTweet(2, 6), getNewsFeed(1) → [6, 5], unfollow(1, 2), getNewsFeed(1) → [5].

How to spot the pattern

"Most recent 10" taken from several people's timelines, where each timeline is already in time order, is merge k sorted lists. That means a heap holding one candidate per list, like the heap tricks in LC 378 (Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix).

1Brute force (naive design) — one global list of all tweets

Store every tweet ever posted in one list. For a feed, walk it from the newest end and keep tweets whose author is the user or someone they follow, until you have 10.

class Twitter {
    private List<int[]> allTweets = new ArrayList<>();            // {userId, tweetId}, oldest first
    private Map<Integer, Set<Integer>> follows = new HashMap<>();

    public void postTweet(int userId, int tweetId) {
        allTweets.add(new int[]{userId, tweetId});
    }

    public List<Integer> getNewsFeed(int userId) {
        Set<Integer> mine = follows.getOrDefault(userId, Set.of());
        List<Integer> feed = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = allTweets.size() - 1; i >= 0 && feed.size() < 10; i--) {  // newest first
            int author = allTweets.get(i)[0];
            if (author == userId || mine.contains(author)) feed.add(allTweets.get(i)[1]);
        }
        return feed;
    }

    public void follow(int followerId, int followeeId) {
        follows.computeIfAbsent(followerId, k -> new HashSet<>()).add(followeeId);
    }

    public void unfollow(int followerId, int followeeId) {
        follows.getOrDefault(followerId, new HashSet<>()).remove(followeeId);
    }
}

Time O(T) per feedSpace O(T + follows)

T is the number of tweets by everyone. It passes LeetCode's small limits, but a quiet user following nobody active still scans the whole platform's history on every feed.

2Optimal — per-user timelines, merged with a max-heap
The idea

Each user keeps their own tweets in posting order, stamped with a global time. For a feed, the extra insight is only look at the people involved, and merge their timelines with a heap: put each person's newest tweet in a max-heap by time, pop the newest, push the next-older tweet from the same person, and stop after 10 pops.

class Twitter {
    private int time = 0;                                           // global clock
    private Map<Integer, List<int[]>> tweets = new HashMap<>();     // user -> {time, tweetId}, oldest first
    private Map<Integer, Set<Integer>> follows = new HashMap<>();

    public void postTweet(int userId, int tweetId) {
        tweets.computeIfAbsent(userId, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(new int[]{time++, tweetId});
    }

    public List<Integer> getNewsFeed(int userId) {
        Set<Integer> people = new HashSet<>(follows.getOrDefault(userId, Set.of()));
        people.add(userId);                                         // my own tweets count too
        // max-heap of {time, tweetId, userId, index in that user's list}
        PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> b[0] - a[0]);
        for (int u : people) {                                      // each user's NEWEST tweet
            List<int[]> list = tweets.get(u);
            if (list != null && !list.isEmpty()) {
                int i = list.size() - 1;
                heap.add(new int[]{list.get(i)[0], list.get(i)[1], u, i});
            }
        }
        List<Integer> feed = new ArrayList<>();
        while (!heap.isEmpty() && feed.size() < 10) {
            int[] top = heap.poll();                                // newest tweet overall
            feed.add(top[1]);
            int u = top[2], i = top[3] - 1;                         // that user's next-older tweet
            if (i >= 0) {
                int[] t = tweets.get(u).get(i);
                heap.add(new int[]{t[0], t[1], u, i});
            }
        }
        return feed;
    }

    public void follow(int followerId, int followeeId) {
        if (followerId == followeeId) return;
        follows.computeIfAbsent(followerId, k -> new HashSet<>()).add(followeeId);
    }

    public void unfollow(int followerId, int followeeId) {
        Set<Integer> s = follows.get(followerId);
        if (s != null) s.remove(followeeId);
    }
}

Time O(F + 10 log F) per feedSpace O(T + follows)

F is the number of people in the feed (followees + 1). Building the heap touches each once; then only 10 pops and pushes. Post, follow and unfollow are O(1).

Remember

"Top k newest across many sorted streams" = k-way merge: a heap of one pointer per stream, pop the best, advance that stream. Store data per owner so a query only touches what it needs.

Watch out

Tweet ids are not times: sort by a global counter you increment on every post. A user must see their own tweets even without following themselves, and unfollow of someone never followed (or of yourself) must not crash.

Pattern notes: Top K Elements & K-way Merge · Open on LeetCode

Tries

Tries: a tree of letters (or bits) where words that share a beginning share one path. Template: insert everything once, then walk the trie letter by letter (or bit by bit) and stop the moment the path breaks. What is harder than Intermediate (LC 208, LC 211): the trie is now a helper inside another algorithm. It steers a grid DFS, it stores numbers as 0/1 paths so you can greedily build the biggest XOR, or it stores words backwards so you can find mirror images fast.

LC 212Word Search IIHardTrie + backtrackingLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get a letter grid and a list of words. Return every word that can be spelled by a path of neighbouring cells (up, down, left, right), without using the same cell twice in one word.

Example: board oaan / etae / ihkr / iflv, words = ["oath", "pea", "eat", "rain"] → ["eat", "oath"].

How to spot the pattern

"Grid", "adjacent cells", "same cell not used twice" is Word Search (LC 79) backtracking. "A list of many words" is the new part: you don't want to run the search once per word. Many words that share beginnings is exactly what a trie is for, so one DFS can follow the trie and chase every word at once.

1Brute force — run LC 79 once per word

For each word, try every start cell and backtrack letter by letter, exactly like Word Search I.

List<String> findWords(char[][] board, String[] words) {
    List<String> found = new ArrayList<>();
    for (String w : words) {
        if (exist(board, w)) found.add(w);    // LC 79, once per word
    }
    return found;
}

boolean exist(char[][] b, String w) {
    for (int r = 0; r < b.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < b[0].length; c++)
            if (dfs(b, w, 0, r, c)) return true;
    return false;
}

boolean dfs(char[][] b, String w, int k, int r, int c) {
    if (k == w.length()) return true;          // matched every letter
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= b.length || c >= b[0].length
            || b[r][c] != w.charAt(k)) return false;
    char saved = b[r][c];
    b[r][c] = '#';                             // used on this path
    boolean ok = dfs(b, w, k + 1, r + 1, c) || dfs(b, w, k + 1, r - 1, c)
              || dfs(b, w, k + 1, r, c + 1) || dfs(b, w, k + 1, r, c - 1);
    b[r][c] = saved;                           // undo
    return ok;
}

Time O(W · m·n · 3ᴸ)Space O(L)

W words, an m×n board, words up to L letters. With 30,000 words on a 12×12 board that is already 4.3 million DFS starts before any branching. Worse, words like "oatha", "oathb", "oathc" walk the same o-a-t-h path again and again. That's a time out.

2Optimal — one DFS that walks the grid and the trie together
The idea

This is Word Search (LC 79) plus the Trie from LC 208. Put all words into one trie. Then DFS from every cell, and move to a neighbour only if the trie has a child for that letter. The trie tells you instantly when no word at all can continue this path, so the DFS stops there.

Two small extras make it fast: store the whole word on its last node (no need to rebuild strings), set it to null once found (no duplicates), and cut a node off the trie once it has no word and no children left, so later searches don't walk into dead branches.

class Node {
    Node[] next = new Node[26];
    String word;                               // set on the node where a word ends
}

List<String> findWords(char[][] board, String[] words) {
    Node root = new Node();
    for (String w : words) {                   // 1. all words into ONE trie
        Node cur = root;
        for (char ch : w.toCharArray()) {
            int i = ch - 'a';
            if (cur.next[i] == null) cur.next[i] = new Node();
            cur = cur.next[i];
        }
        cur.word = w;
    }
    List<String> found = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)     // 2. one DFS per cell finds
        for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)  //    every word at once
            dfs(board, r, c, root, found);
    return found;
}

void dfs(char[][] b, int r, int c, Node parent, List<String> found) {
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= b.length || c >= b[0].length) return;
    char ch = b[r][c];
    if (ch == '#' || parent.next[ch - 'a'] == null) return;  // no word goes this way
    Node node = parent.next[ch - 'a'];
    if (node.word != null) {                   // a whole word is spelled
        found.add(node.word);
        node.word = null;                      // never report it twice
    }
    b[r][c] = '#';                             // used on this path
    dfs(b, r + 1, c, node, found);
    dfs(b, r - 1, c, node, found);
    dfs(b, r, c + 1, node, found);
    dfs(b, r, c - 1, node, found);
    b[r][c] = ch;                              // undo
    if (node.word == null && isEmpty(node))  // branch fully used up:
        parent.next[ch - 'a'] = null;          // cut it off the trie
}

boolean isEmpty(Node node) {
    for (Node child : node.next) if (child != null) return false;
    return true;
}

Time O(m·n · 4·3ᴸ⁻¹)Space O(total letters in words)

The worst case looks the same as one Word Search, but now it is paid once for all words, not once per word, and the pruning cuts most paths after one or two letters. Building the trie costs one step per letter of input.

Remember

"Search for many words in the same place" → put the words in a trie and let one search walk the trie alongside the data. The trie says "stop" the moment no word can continue.

Watch out

Don't return when you find a word: "oath" and "oaths" can share a path, so keep searching below. And set node.word = null after adding it, or a word reachable from two different start cells is reported twice.

Pattern notes: Tries · Open on LeetCode

LC 421Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an ArrayMediumBit trieLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Pick two numbers from the array (they may be the same position) so that a XOR b is as large as possible. Return that value. XOR gives a 1 in every bit where the two numbers differ.

Example: nums = [3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8] → 28, from 5 XOR 25 (00101 XOR 11001 = 11100).

How to spot the pattern

"Maximum XOR of a pair" with up to 200,000 numbers. XOR is decided bit by bit, and a bigger number is decided by its highest bit first. A trie over the bits (only two children: 0 and 1) lets you ask "is there a number whose next bit is the opposite of mine?" in one step per bit.

1Brute force — XOR every pair

Two loops, keep the best XOR. (A pair of the same number gives 0, so starting at 0 is fine.)

int findMaximumXOR(int[] nums) {
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++)
            best = Math.max(best, nums[i] ^ nums[j]);   // try every pair
    return best;
}

Time O(n²)Space O(1)

With n = 200,000 that's about 2·10¹⁰ pairs. It will time out.

2Optimal — greedy walk down a 0/1 trie
The idea

This is the Trie from LC 208, with an alphabet of just {0, 1}, plus one greedy insight: a 1 in a high bit is worth more than all lower bits together (10000 = 16 > 01111 = 15). So for each number x, walk from the top bit down and always try to go the opposite way from x's bit. If that child exists, this XOR bit becomes 1. If not, you are forced to follow the same bit and this XOR bit is 0.

Insert all numbers as 31-bit paths first (values fit in 31 bits), then run this walk for every number and keep the best.

class Node {
    Node[] child = new Node[2];                // child[0] = bit 0, child[1] = bit 1
}

int findMaximumXOR(int[] nums) {
    Node root = new Node();
    for (int x : nums) {                       // 1. insert every number, top bit first
        Node cur = root;
        for (int b = 30; b >= 0; b--) {
            int bit = (x >> b) & 1;
            if (cur.child[bit] == null) cur.child[bit] = new Node();
            cur = cur.child[bit];
        }
    }
    int best = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {                       // 2. best partner for each x
        Node cur = root;
        int xor = 0;
        for (int b = 30; b >= 0; b--) {
            int bit = (x >> b) & 1;
            int want = 1 - bit;                // the opposite bit makes this XOR bit 1
            if (cur.child[want] != null) {
                xor |= 1 << b;
                cur = cur.child[want];
            } else {
                cur = cur.child[bit];          // no choice: this XOR bit is 0
            }
        }
        best = Math.max(best, xor);
    }
    return best;
}

Time O(31 · n)Space O(31 · n)

Every insert and every walk is exactly 31 steps, so the whole thing is linear in n. The trie has at most 31 new nodes per number.

Remember

"Best XOR partner" → store the numbers as bit paths in a trie (top bit first) and greedily take the opposite bit whenever it exists. Higher bits always win over lower ones.

Watch out

Insert and query from the top bit (bit 30) down, never from bit 0 up: the greedy choice is only safe when the most valuable bit is decided first. Also use the same number of bits for every number, or short numbers end at different depths.

Pattern notes: Tries · Open on LeetCode

LC 336Palindrome PairsHardHash map + palindrome splitLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get a list of different words. Find every ordered pair of positions [i, j] (i ≠ j) such that words[i] + words[j] reads the same forwards and backwards.

Example: ["abcd", "dcba", "lls", "s", "sssll"] → [[0,1], [1,0], [3,2], [2,4]]: "abcddcba", "dcbaabcd", "slls", "llssssll".

How to spot the pattern

"Pairs" out of up to 5,000 words means the n² pair loop is too slow, so for each word you want to look up its partner directly, like Two Sum. The partner of a word is (roughly) its reverse, and any extra letters must be a palindrome by themselves. Words of up to 300 letters means you can afford to try every cut point of each word.

1Brute force — glue every pair and check

Try every ordered pair, build the joined string and test it with two pointers.

List<List<Integer>> palindromePairs(String[] words) {
    List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < words.length; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < words.length; j++)
            if (i != j && isPal(words[i] + words[j]))   // glue and check
                res.add(List.of(i, j));
    return res;
}

boolean isPal(String s) {
    for (int lo = 0, hi = s.length() - 1; lo < hi; lo++, hi--)
        if (s.charAt(lo) != s.charAt(hi)) return false;
    return true;
}

Time O(n² · k)Space O(k)

n words of length up to k. With n = 5,000 and k = 300 that is 25 million pairs, each building and checking up to 600 characters: around 10¹⁰ steps. Time out.

2Optimal — cut each word, look up the mirror half
The idea

This is Two Sum's "look up the partner in a HashMap", plus one insight about palindromes. Cut word w into left | right at every position:

w + other is a palindrome if other is the reverse of left and right is a palindrome on its own (it sits in the middle). other + w works if other is the reverse of right and left is a palindrome. So store every word reversed in a map, and for each cut do two lookups.

List<List<Integer>> palindromePairs(String[] words) {
    Map<String, Integer> rev = new HashMap<>();   // reversed word -> its index
    for (int i = 0; i < words.length; i++)
        rev.put(new StringBuilder(words[i]).reverse().toString(), i);

    List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < words.length; i++) {
        String w = words[i];
        for (int cut = 0; cut <= w.length(); cut++) {
            String left = w.substring(0, cut), right = w.substring(cut);
            // w + other: other reversed == left, and right is a palindrome
            Integer j = rev.get(left);
            if (j != null && j != i && isPal(right)) res.add(List.of(i, j));
            // other + w: other reversed == right, and left is a palindrome
            j = rev.get(right);
            if (cut > 0 && j != null && j != i && isPal(left)) res.add(List.of(j, i));
        }
    }
    return res;
}

boolean isPal(String s) {
    for (int lo = 0, hi = s.length() - 1; lo < hi; lo++, hi--)
        if (s.charAt(lo) != s.charAt(hi)) return false;
    return true;
}

Time O(n · k²)Space O(n · k)

Each word has k + 1 cuts, and each cut costs O(k) for the substring, the lookup and the palindrome check. That is about 5,000 · 300² ≈ 4.5·10⁸ simple steps in the worst case, versus 10¹⁰ before.

3Trie version — the same idea, words stored backwards

Insert every word reversed into a trie. While inserting, each node remembers which words have a palindrome left over from that point (palBelow). Then walk each word forwards: if a shorter word ends on the way and the rest of w is a palindrome, that is a pair; when w is used up, every word in palBelow pairs with it.

class Node {
    Node[] next = new Node[26];
    int word = -1;                             // index of the word that ends here
    List<Integer> palBelow = new ArrayList<>(); // words whose leftover here is a palindrome
}

List<List<Integer>> palindromePairs(String[] words) {
    Node root = new Node();
    for (int i = 0; i < words.length; i++) {   // insert every word BACKWARDS
        String w = words[i];
        Node cur = root;
        for (int k = w.length() - 1; k >= 0; k--) {
            if (isPal(w, 0, k)) cur.palBelow.add(i);   // leftover w[0..k] reads the same both ways
            int c = w.charAt(k) - 'a';
            if (cur.next[c] == null) cur.next[c] = new Node();
            cur = cur.next[c];
        }
        cur.word = i;
        cur.palBelow.add(i);                   // empty leftover is a palindrome too
    }
    List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < words.length; i++) {   // walk each word FORWARDS
        String w = words[i];
        Node cur = root;
        for (int k = 0; k < w.length() && cur != null; k++) {
            if (cur.word >= 0 && cur.word != i && isPal(w, k, w.length() - 1))
                res.add(List.of(i, cur.word)); // other is shorter; rest of w is a palindrome
            cur = cur.next[w.charAt(k) - 'a'];
        }
        if (cur == null) continue;
        for (int j : cur.palBelow)             // other is as long or longer
            if (j != i) res.add(List.of(i, j));
    }
    return res;
}

boolean isPal(String s, int lo, int hi) {
    for (; lo < hi; lo++, hi--)
        if (s.charAt(lo) != s.charAt(hi)) return false;
    return true;
}

Time O(n · k²)Space O(n · k)

Same complexity, but no substrings are built, so it runs faster in practice. The map version is easier to get right in an interview.

Remember

Two strings glued into a palindrome: one is the reverse of part of the other, and the leftover part is a palindrome by itself. Try every cut and look up the reverse in a map (or a reversed trie).

Watch out

Duplicates: for "abcd" and "dcba" the pair [0, 1] is found by "abcd" at cut = length (first check) and again by "dcba" at cut 0 (second check), so skip the second check when cut == 0. And don't forget the empty string: "" pairs with every palindrome word, in both orders.

Pattern notes: Tries · Open on LeetCode

Segment Trees & Fenwick Trees

Range trees: when the array keeps changing and you keep asking for sums (or counts) over ranges. A prefix-sum array answers a range in O(1), but one change forces you to rewrite every prefix after it. Template: split the array into pre-summed blocks of size 1, 2, 4, 8…, so an update touches only log n blocks and a query adds only log n blocks. What is harder than Intermediate: the tree is stored in a plain array, and for counting problems (LC 315, LC 493) you first turn "how many smaller to my right" into "sum over a range of values".

LC 307Range Sum Query - MutableMediumSegment tree / BITLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Build a class over an integer array with two methods: update(index, val) changes one number, and sumRange(left, right) returns the sum from left to right (both included). Both are called many times, mixed together.

Example: nums = [1, 3, 5]: sumRange(0, 2) → 9, update(1, 2), sumRange(0, 2) → 8.

How to spot the pattern

"Sum of a range" says prefix sums (LC 303, LC 560). But the word "update" mixed with many queries says the array changes between questions, and prefix sums hate change. Many point updates + many range queries is the textbook signal for a segment tree or a Fenwick tree (BIT).

1Brute force — plain array, loop on every query

Keep the array as it is. Updates are instant, queries add up the range one by one.

class NumArray {
    private int[] nums;

    public NumArray(int[] nums) {
        this.nums = nums;
    }

    public void update(int index, int val) {
        nums[index] = val;                     // O(1)
    }

    public int sumRange(int left, int right) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (int i = left; i <= right; i++) sum += nums[i];   // O(n) every time
        return sum;
    }
}

update O(1)sumRange O(n)Space O(1)

With n = 30,000 and 30,000 queries that is up to 9·10⁸ additions. The opposite choice doesn't help either. Here is why a prefix array breaks as soon as a value changes:

nums = 5 2 7 1 4 3 6 8 prefix = 5 7 14 15 19 22 28 36 sumRange is O(1): prefix[r] - prefix[l-1] update(1, 10): nums[1] goes from 2 to 10 (+8) prefix = 5 15 22 23 27 30 36 44 7 of the 8 prefixes changed: update is O(n)

Every prefix after the changed spot contains that number, so all of them go stale. One side is always O(n).

2Optimal — segment tree: pre-summed halves, quarters, eighths
The idea

This is prefix sums plus divide and conquer. Instead of one sum per prefix, keep one sum per block: the whole array, its two halves, their halves, down to single numbers. Each number sits in only log n blocks (one per level), so an update fixes log n sums, and any range is glued from at most about 2·log n whole blocks.

What the tree buys you: both operations become O(log n). No side is O(n) any more.

Storage trick: node 1 is the whole array, and node i has children 2i and 2i + 1, just like a heap, so a plain int[4n] is enough.

class NumArray {
    private int n;
    private int[] tree;                        // tree[node] = sum of that node's range

    public NumArray(int[] nums) {
        n = nums.length;
        tree = new int[4 * n];                 // 4n is always enough room
        build(nums, 1, 0, n - 1);              // node 1 = the whole array
    }

    private void build(int[] nums, int node, int lo, int hi) {
        if (lo == hi) { tree[node] = nums[lo]; return; }    // leaf: one element
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        build(nums, 2 * node, lo, mid);                     // left child
        build(nums, 2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi);             // right child
        tree[node] = tree[2 * node] + tree[2 * node + 1];
    }

    public void update(int index, int val) {
        update(1, 0, n - 1, index, val);
    }

    private void update(int node, int lo, int hi, int i, int val) {
        if (lo == hi) { tree[node] = val; return; }
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        if (i <= mid) update(2 * node, lo, mid, i, val);    // go to the half holding i
        else update(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, i, val);
        tree[node] = tree[2 * node] + tree[2 * node + 1];   // fix sums on the way up
    }

    public int sumRange(int left, int right) {
        return query(1, 0, n - 1, left, right);
    }

    private int query(int node, int lo, int hi, int l, int r) {
        if (r < lo || hi < l) return 0;                 // no overlap: ignore
        if (l <= lo && hi <= r) return tree[node];      // fully inside: use stored sum
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;                        // partly inside: ask both kids
        return query(2 * node, lo, mid, l, r) + query(2 * node + 1, mid + 1, hi, l, r);
    }
}

update O(log n)sumRange O(log n)Space O(n)

Building is O(n) (each node summed once). The query code has only three cases: no overlap, full overlap, partial overlap. Learn those three and you can write a segment tree for min, max or gcd too.

3Shorter — Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree)

A BIT only stores prefix-like blocks: bit[i] holds the sum of the last lowbit(i) numbers ending at position i (1-based), where lowbit(i) = i & -i is the lowest 1-bit of i. A prefix sum hops down by stripping that bit; an update hops up by adding it. Both take at most log n hops.

class NumArray {
    private int[] nums;                        // current values (to know the change)
    private int[] bit;                         // Fenwick tree, 1-indexed

    public NumArray(int[] nums) {
        this.nums = new int[nums.length];
        bit = new int[nums.length + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) update(i, nums[i]);
    }

    public void update(int index, int val) {
        int delta = val - nums[index];
        nums[index] = val;
        for (int i = index + 1; i < bit.length; i += i & -i)  // climb to every box
            bit[i] += delta;                                  // that covers index
    }

    public int sumRange(int left, int right) {
        return prefix(right + 1) - prefix(left);
    }

    private int prefix(int i) {                // sum of the first i numbers
        int sum = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i) sum += bit[i];   // strip the lowest 1-bit each step
        return sum;
    }
}

update O(log n)sumRange O(log n)Space O(n)

Same speed as the segment tree with a third of the code. A BIT only answers things you can subtract (sums, counts); for range min or max, use the segment tree.

Remember

Point updates + range sums: prefix sums make one side O(n). Store sums of blocks instead (segment tree or BIT) and both sides become O(log n). The BIT loops are two lines: i += i & -i going up, i -= i & -i going down.

Watch out

A BIT is 1-indexed: position 0 would give 0 & -0 = 0 and loop forever, so shift every index by one. And update sets a new value, but the BIT only knows how to add, so keep the old values and add val − old.

Pattern notes: Segment Trees & Fenwick Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 315Count of Smaller Numbers After SelfHardBIT + compressionLeetCode
The problem in easy words

For every position i, count how many numbers to its right are strictly smaller than nums[i]. Return those counts as a list.

Example: nums = [5, 2, 6, 1] → [2, 1, 1, 0]. To the right of 5 are 2 and 1 (two smaller), to the right of 2 is only 1, and so on.

How to spot the pattern

"How many smaller numbers to the right" for every element, with n up to 100,000. That is a counting question over a range of values ("values below mine") on a set that grows as you walk. A growing set + "how many below x" is exactly LC 307's point update + prefix sum, with the values as the positions.

1Brute force — look to the right from every position
List<Integer> countSmaller(int[] nums) {
    List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++)   // look at everything to the right
            if (nums[j] < nums[i]) count++;
        res.add(count);
    }
    return res;
}

Time O(n²)Space O(1) extra

With n = 100,000 that is about 5·10⁹ comparisons. Time out.

2Optimal — walk from the right, count seen values in a BIT
The idea

This is the BIT from LC 307, but indexed by value instead of by position. Walk from right to left. Everything already visited is exactly "the numbers to my right". Keep a BIT where bit position r counts how many seen numbers have rank r. Then "how many to my right are smaller" = prefix sum of ranks below mine, and afterwards you add 1 at your own rank.

The extra step is coordinate compression: values can be negative or huge, so sort the distinct values and use each value's position in that sorted list (its rank, 1..m) as the BIT index. Only the order matters, not the actual values.

List<Integer> countSmaller(int[] nums) {
    // 1. coordinate compression: value -> rank 1..m (smallest value = rank 1)
    int[] sorted = Arrays.stream(nums).distinct().sorted().toArray();
    int m = sorted.length;
    int[] bit = new int[m + 1];                // bit counts how many of each rank we've seen

    Integer[] res = new Integer[nums.length];
    for (int i = nums.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {             // 2. walk from the RIGHT
        int rank = Arrays.binarySearch(sorted, nums[i]) + 1;
        int smaller = 0;
        for (int k = rank - 1; k > 0; k -= k & -k) smaller += bit[k];  // seen with rank < mine
        res[i] = smaller;
        for (int k = rank; k <= m; k += k & -k) bit[k]++;              // now I am "seen"
    }
    return Arrays.asList(res);
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)

Sorting for the ranks is O(n log n); then each of the n numbers does one binary search, one BIT query and one BIT update, all O(log n).

3Alternative — merge sort that counts

During merge sort, when a left-half item is placed, every right-half item placed before it is smaller and was to its right. So add j − (mid + 1) to its count. Sort the indices, not the values, so you know whose count to increase.

int[] count;                                   // answer, by original index

List<Integer> countSmaller(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    count = new int[n];
    int[] idx = new int[n];                    // sort INDICES, so we remember who is who
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) idx[i] = i;
    sort(nums, idx, new int[n], 0, n - 1);
    List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int c : count) res.add(c);
    return res;
}

void sort(int[] nums, int[] idx, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    sort(nums, idx, tmp, lo, mid);
    sort(nums, idx, tmp, mid + 1, hi);
    int i = lo, j = mid + 1, k = lo;
    while (i <= mid || j <= hi) {
        if (j > hi || (i <= mid && nums[idx[i]] <= nums[idx[j]])) {
            count[idx[i]] += j - (mid + 1);    // right-half items already placed are smaller
            tmp[k++] = idx[i++];
        } else {
            tmp[k++] = idx[j++];
        }
    }
    for (k = lo; k <= hi; k++) idx[k] = tmp[k];
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)

No compression needed. The same "count while merging" trick solves LC 493 below.

Remember

"How many smaller / larger on one side" → walk from that side and keep a BIT over value ranks: query below your rank, then add yourself. Compress values to ranks first so the BIT stays size n.

Watch out

"Strictly smaller" means query up to rank − 1, not rank, or equal values count each other. In the merge sort version the same rule shows up as <= in the comparison: an equal right-half item must be placed after the left one.

Pattern notes: Segment Trees & Fenwick Trees · Open on LeetCode

LC 493Reverse PairsHardMerge sort countLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Count the pairs i < j where nums[i] > 2 · nums[j]: an earlier number that is more than double a later one.

Example: nums = [2, 4, 3, 5, 1] → 3: the pairs (4, 1), (3, 1) and (5, 1).

How to spot the pattern

"Count pairs i < j" with a comparison between the two values, and n up to 50,000. That is an inversion count in disguise. Merge sort splits every pair into "both on the left", "both on the right" or "one on each side", and the last kind is easy to count once both halves are sorted.

1Brute force — check every pair
int reversePairs(int[] nums) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++)
            if ((long) nums[i] > 2L * nums[j]) count++;   // long: 2 * nums[j] can overflow
    return count;
}

Time O(n²)Space O(1)

With n = 50,000 that is about 1.25·10⁹ pair checks. Time out.

2Optimal — merge sort, count before you merge
The idea

This is merge sort plus a two-pointer count (the same trick as LC 315, step 3). Recursively count pairs inside each half and sort each half. Now every left item is before every right item, so only the values matter. Because both halves are sorted, the pointer j into the right half only moves forward: if a[i] > 2 · a[j], then any bigger a[i] later on also beats that a[j]. Add j − (mid + 1) for each i, then do an ordinary merge.

Counting and merging are two separate loops, because the count uses 2 · a[j] but the sort uses a[j].

int reversePairs(int[] nums) {
    return sort(nums, new int[nums.length], 0, nums.length - 1);
}

int sort(int[] a, int[] tmp, int lo, int hi) {
    if (lo >= hi) return 0;
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    int count = sort(a, tmp, lo, mid) + sort(a, tmp, mid + 1, hi);  // pairs inside each half

    // both halves are sorted now: count pairs with i on the left, j on the right
    int j = mid + 1;
    for (int i = lo; i <= mid; i++) {
        while (j <= hi && (long) a[i] > 2L * a[j]) j++;   // j only moves forward
        count += j - (mid + 1);                           // a[mid+1 .. j-1] all qualify
    }

    // ordinary merge, so the caller gets a sorted range
    int i = lo, k = lo;
    j = mid + 1;
    while (i <= mid && j <= hi) tmp[k++] = a[i] <= a[j] ? a[i++] : a[j++];
    while (i <= mid) tmp[k++] = a[i++];
    while (j <= hi) tmp[k++] = a[j++];
    for (k = lo; k <= hi; k++) a[k] = tmp[k];
    return count;
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)

log n levels, and on each level the count loop and the merge loop are both linear. A BIT over compressed values of nums and 2·nums also works, like LC 315, but needs more setup.

Remember

"Count pairs i < j with some comparison" → merge sort. Inside each merge the halves are sorted, so one forward-only pointer counts all cross pairs in O(n). Count first, merge second.

Watch out

Overflow: nums[j] can be up to 2³¹ − 1, so 2 * nums[j] overflows an int. Write 2L * a[j]. And don't merge while counting with the 2· rule: the merge must still compare plain values.

Pattern notes: Divide & Conquer · Open on LeetCode

Stage 4 — GraphsImplicit graphs, weighted shortest paths, MST, Euler paths, bridges and bitmask BFS.

Advanced Graphs

Advanced graphs are still the BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, union-find and topological sort you used in Intermediate (LC 200, 994, 207, 210, 684, 743). The template: decide what a node is, what an edge is and what an edge costs, then pick the algorithm that fits those costs. What is harder here: the graph is often hidden (words, bus routes, grid cells, even "node + set of visited nodes"), the path cost can be a maximum instead of a sum, and a few problems need a named classic (Bellman-Ford, Prim, Hierholzer, Tarjan) that is short once you have seen it.

If the problem says…UseProblems below
Fewest steps, every move costs the sameBFS, level by level127, 815
Fewest steps, but "where you have been" mattersBFS over (node, extra state), e.g. a bitmask847
Cheapest path, costs ≥ 0 (sum or max along the path)Dijkstra with a min-heap1631, 778
Cheapest path with at most k edgesBellman-Ford, k + 1 rounds787
Longest path, moves only go "uphill" (no cycles)DFS + memo, or topological order329
Connect everything for the least total costMinimum spanning tree: Prim (dense) or Kruskal (sparse)1584
Use every edge exactly onceHierholzer (Eulerian path)332
Which edges, if cut, split the graphTarjan low-link (bridges)1192
LC 127Word LadderHardBFS on implicit graphLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You start at beginWord and want to reach endWord. Each move changes exactly one letter, and every word you step on (except the first) must be in wordList. Return the number of words in the shortest ladder, counting both ends, or 0 if there is none.

Example: hit → cog with [hot, dot, dog, lot, log, cog] → 5 (hit → hot → dot → dog → cog). Without cog in the list the answer is 0.

How to spot the pattern

"Shortest sequence", "change one letter at a time": each word is a node, a one-letter change is an edge, and every edge costs 1. Fewest equal-cost moves is BFS, like Rotting Oranges (LC 994). Nobody hands you the edges, so the real work is finding the neighbours fast.

1Brute force — BFS that compares against every word

Run a normal BFS. To find the neighbours of a word, loop over the whole list and keep the words that differ in exactly one position.

int ladderLength(String beginWord, String endWord, List<String> wordList) {
    Queue<String> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
    q.add(beginWord);
    seen.add(beginWord);
    for (int steps = 1; !q.isEmpty(); steps++) {       // steps = words in the ladder so far
        for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            String w = q.poll();
            if (w.equals(endWord)) return steps;
            for (String next : wordList) {             // scan the WHOLE list every time
                if (!seen.contains(next) && oneApart(w, next)) {
                    seen.add(next);
                    q.add(next);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

boolean oneApart(String a, String b) {
    int diff = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length(); i++)
        if (a.charAt(i) != b.charAt(i)) diff++;
    return diff == 1;
}

Time O(N² · L)Space O(N)

Each of the N words is compared with all N words, letter by letter. With the limits (N = 5000 words of length L = 10) that is about 250 million letter checks: too slow.

2Optimal — BFS with wildcard buckets
The idea

This is the BFS you know, plus one trick for the neighbours: group words by a pattern with one letter blanked out. hot, dot and lot all land in the bucket *ot. Two words are neighbours exactly when they share a bucket, so a word's neighbours are just the contents of its L buckets. No more scanning the whole list.

Bonus: once a bucket has been expanded, every word in it is already queued, so we delete the bucket and never read it again.

int ladderLength(String beginWord, String endWord, List<String> wordList) {
    if (!wordList.contains(endWord)) return 0;
    int L = beginWord.length();
    Map<String, List<String>> buckets = new HashMap<>();   // "h*t" -> [hot, hit, ...]
    for (String w : wordList)
        for (int i = 0; i < L; i++)
            buckets.computeIfAbsent(w.substring(0, i) + '*' + w.substring(i + 1),
                                    k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(w);

    Queue<String> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>();
    q.add(beginWord);
    seen.add(beginWord);
    for (int steps = 1; !q.isEmpty(); steps++) {
        for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            String w = q.poll();
            if (w.equals(endWord)) return steps;
            for (int i = 0; i < L; i++) {
                String key = w.substring(0, i) + '*' + w.substring(i + 1);
                for (String next : buckets.getOrDefault(key, List.of()))
                    if (seen.add(next)) q.add(next);  // add() is false if already seen
                buckets.remove(key);                  // bucket used up: never scan it again
            }
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Time O(N · L²)Space O(N · L²)

Every word makes L keys, and building each key costs L. For N = 5000 and L = 10 that is about half a million steps instead of 250 million.

Remember

When the graph is hidden, ask "how do I list a node's neighbours without checking every other node?" A shared key (here the wildcard pattern) turns an all-pairs scan into hash lookups.

Watch out

The answer counts words, not moves: hit → hot is 2, so BFS starts at steps = 1. And if endWord is not in wordList, return 0 immediately, even if it is one letter away.
