LC 815Bus RoutesHardBFS over routesLeetCode
The problem in easy words

routes[i] lists the stops bus i visits (it loops forever). You stand at stop source and want to reach stop target. What is the fewest buses you must ride? Return -1 if you can't get there.

Example: routes = [[1,2,7],[3,6,7]], source = 1, target = 6 → 2. Take bus 0 to stop 7, change to bus 1, ride to stop 6.

How to spot the pattern

"Fewest buses" is a shortest path where every bus ride costs 1, no matter how many stops it passes. So BFS, but the thing that costs 1 is a bus, not a stop. When the cost is counted in something other than the obvious nodes, make that thing the node.

1Brute force — BFS over stops, scanning every bus

BFS level by level over stops. For each stop in the current level, look through every route to see if it stops there; if so, all its stops join the next level.

int numBusesToDestination(int[][] routes, int source, int target) {
    if (source == target) return 0;
    Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>(List.of(source));
    List<Integer> level = List.of(source);              // stops reachable with 'buses' rides
    for (int buses = 1; !level.isEmpty(); buses++) {
        List<Integer> next = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int stop : level)
            for (int[] route : routes) {                // check EVERY bus at EVERY stop
                if (!contains(route, stop)) continue;
                for (int s : route) {
                    if (s == target) return buses;
                    if (seen.add(s)) next.add(s);
                }
            }
        level = next;
    }
    return -1;
}

boolean contains(int[] route, int stop) {
    for (int s : route) if (s == stop) return true;
    return false;
}

Time O(S · T)Space O(S)

S is the number of different stops and T the total length of all routes. Both can be about 10⁵, so the worst case is around 10¹⁰ steps, far too slow. It also rides the same bus again from every stop on it.

2Optimal — BFS where the nodes are buses
The idea

This is plain BFS (Intermediate), plus a change of view: a node is a bus, and two buses are connected if they share a stop. A map stop → buses gives the connections. Start with every bus that stops at source (level 1), and the level where some bus reaches target is the answer.

Each bus is boarded once (taken[]), and each stop's list of buses is read once (seenStop), so no work is repeated.

int numBusesToDestination(int[][] routes, int source, int target) {
    if (source == target) return 0;
    Map<Integer, List<Integer>> busesAt = new HashMap<>();   // stop -> buses that stop there
    for (int r = 0; r < routes.length; r++)
        for (int s : routes[r])
            busesAt.computeIfAbsent(s, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(r);

    boolean[] taken = new boolean[routes.length];            // bus already boarded?
    Set<Integer> seenStop = new HashSet<>();
    Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int r : busesAt.getOrDefault(source, List.of())) {  // level 1: buses at the source
        taken[r] = true;
        q.add(r);
    }
    for (int buses = 1; !q.isEmpty(); buses++) {
        for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            int r = q.poll();
            for (int s : routes[r]) {                        // ride bus r to every stop
                if (s == target) return buses;
                if (!seenStop.add(s)) continue;              // this stop's buses already queued
                for (int nr : busesAt.get(s))
                    if (!taken[nr]) { taken[nr] = true; q.add(nr); }
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

Time O(T)Space O(T)

Every route is ridden once and every stop's bus list is read once, so the total work is the total length of all routes.

Remember

Pick as a node the thing whose count you minimise. Here the answer counts buses, so BFS over buses; stops are only the "glue" between them.

Watch out

If source == target the answer is 0, even when no bus stops there: check it first. And mark a stop as used after reading its buses once; without that, a stop shared by many buses makes you re-read its long list again and again.

LC 329Longest Increasing Path in a MatrixHardDFS + memoLeetCode
The problem in easy words

In a grid of numbers you can step up, down, left or right, but only onto a strictly bigger number. How long is the longest such path (counting cells)?

Example: [[9,9,4],[6,6,8],[2,1,1]] → 4, the path 1 → 2 → 6 → 9.

How to spot the pattern

"Longest path" on a grid, but only "strictly increasing" moves. Increasing moves can never loop back, so the grid is a DAG (a graph with no cycles). Longest path in a DAG = DFS with a memo, or process cells in topological order like Course Schedule II (LC 210).

1Brute force — DFS from every cell, no memory

From each cell, try all four bigger neighbours recursively and keep the longest. No visited set is needed, because you can never step back onto a smaller number.

int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};

int longestIncreasingPath(int[][] matrix) {
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < matrix.length; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < matrix[0].length; j++)
            best = Math.max(best, walk(matrix, i, j));   // try every start cell
    return best;
}

int walk(int[][] m, int i, int j) {                      // longest path starting at (i, j)
    int best = 1;
    for (int[] d : DIRS) {
        int x = i + d[0], y = j + d[1];
        if (x >= 0 && y >= 0 && x < m.length && y < m[0].length && m[x][y] > m[i][j])
            best = Math.max(best, 1 + walk(m, x, y));    // recomputed again and again
    }
    return best;
}

Time exponentialSpace O(m · n)

The same cell is re-solved from every path that reaches it. On a 200 × 200 grid laid out as a long zig-zag staircase, the number of paths explodes and this never finishes.

2Optimal — the same DFS with a memo
The idea

This is grid DFS from Intermediate, plus one insight: "increasing only" means no cycles, so the answer from a cell never changes. Store it in memo[i][j] the first time and reuse it. That is exactly top-down DP.

State: memo[i][j] = longest increasing path that starts at (i, j).
Recurrence: 1 + max(memo of each strictly bigger neighbour), or 1 if there is none.
Base case: a peak (no bigger neighbour) has length 1.

int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};

int longestIncreasingPath(int[][] matrix) {
    int rows = matrix.length, cols = matrix[0].length, best = 0;
    int[][] memo = new int[rows][cols];                  // 0 = not computed yet
    for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++)
            best = Math.max(best, walk(matrix, i, j, memo));
    return best;
}

int walk(int[][] m, int i, int j, int[][] memo) {
    if (memo[i][j] != 0) return memo[i][j];              // already solved: reuse
    int best = 1;
    for (int[] d : DIRS) {
        int x = i + d[0], y = j + d[1];
        if (x >= 0 && y >= 0 && x < m.length && y < m[0].length && m[x][y] > m[i][j])
            best = Math.max(best, 1 + walk(m, x, y, memo));
    }
    return memo[i][j] = best;                            // save before returning
}

Time O(m · n)Space O(m · n)

Each cell is computed once and looks at 4 neighbours. The recursion can go m·n deep on a staircase grid, which Java handles at these sizes.

3Also good — peel the grid in topological order

No recursion at all: count for each cell how many smaller neighbours it has (its in-degree). Cells with 0 are "valleys" and start the queue. Peel layer by layer like Kahn's algorithm in LC 210; the number of layers is the longest path.

int longestIncreasingPath(int[][] matrix) {
    int rows = matrix.length, cols = matrix[0].length;
    int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
    int[][] smaller = new int[rows][cols];               // in-degree: smaller neighbours
    Queue<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++) {
            for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                int x = i + d[0], y = j + d[1];
                if (x >= 0 && y >= 0 && x < rows && y < cols && matrix[x][y] < matrix[i][j])
                    smaller[i][j]++;
            }
            if (smaller[i][j] == 0) q.add(new int[]{i, j});   // valleys start
        }
    int layers = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {                               // peel one layer per round
        layers++;
        for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            int[] c = q.poll();
            for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                int x = c[0] + d[0], y = c[1] + d[1];
                if (x >= 0 && y >= 0 && x < rows && y < cols
                        && matrix[x][y] > matrix[c[0]][c[1]] && --smaller[x][y] == 0)
                    q.add(new int[]{x, y});
            }
        }
    }
    return layers;                                       // number of layers = longest path
}

Time O(m · n)Space O(m · n)

Remember

"Only move to strictly bigger" = no cycles = memo is safe. Longest path is hard in general graphs, but easy in a DAG: DFS + memo, or topological order.

Watch out

Use strictly greater (>). With >=, two equal neighbours point at each other, the recursion loops forever and the memo is wrong. Also, don't add a visited set: it is not needed and it breaks the memo.

Pattern notes: Topological Sort · Open on LeetCode

LC 787Cheapest Flights Within K StopsMediumBellman-Ford k roundsLeetCode
The problem in easy words

There are n cities and one-way flights [from, to, price]. Find the cheapest way from src to dst that uses at most k stops in between (so at most k + 1 flights). Return -1 if there is none.

Example: flights 0→1 (100), 1→2 (100), 2→0 (100), 1→3 (600), 2→3 (200), src = 0, dst = 3, k = 1 → 700 (0 → 1 → 3). The route 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 costs only 400, but it has 2 stops.

How to spot the pattern

"Cheapest price" says shortest path with weights, but "at most k stops" limits the number of edges. Plain Dijkstra (LC 743) only tracks cost and may throw away a pricier path with fewer stops. A limit on edges points to Bellman-Ford, where round i finds the best paths with at most i edges.

1Brute force — try every route up to k + 1 flights

DFS from src, taking every flight out of the current city, until the flight budget runs out. Keep the cheapest cost that reaches dst.

int best;

int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
    List<List<int[]>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (int[] f : flights) adj.get(f[0]).add(new int[]{f[1], f[2]});
    best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    fly(adj, src, dst, k + 1, 0);                  // k stops = at most k + 1 flights
    return best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : best;
}

void fly(List<List<int[]>> adj, int city, int dst, int flightsLeft, int cost) {
    if (city == dst) { best = Math.min(best, cost); return; }
    if (flightsLeft == 0) return;
    for (int[] f : adj.get(city))                  // try every flight out of this city
        fly(adj, f[0], dst, flightsLeft - 1, cost + f[1]);
}

Time O(nᵏ⁺¹)Space O(n + E)

Each level can branch into up to n − 1 flights. With n = 100 and k up to 99 the number of routes is astronomical.

2Optimal — Bellman-Ford for exactly k + 1 rounds
The idea

This is shortest paths from Intermediate, plus one insight: one round of "try every flight once" = one more flight allowed. After round i, cost[c] is the cheapest price to reach c with at most i flights. So run exactly k + 1 rounds.

The key detail: in each round, read from the old array and write to a copy. Otherwise a price updated in this round could be used again in the same round, which sneaks in an extra flight.

int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
    final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    int[] cost = new int[n];                       // cheapest price using the rounds so far
    Arrays.fill(cost, INF);
    cost[src] = 0;
    for (int round = 0; round <= k; round++) {     // k stops = k + 1 flights = k + 1 rounds
        int[] next = cost.clone();                 // read OLD, write NEW
        for (int[] f : flights) {
            int from = f[0], to = f[1], price = f[2];
            if (cost[from] != INF && cost[from] + price < next[to])
                next[to] = cost[from] + price;
        }
        cost = next;
    }
    return cost[dst] == INF ? -1 : cost[dst];
}

Time O(k · E)Space O(n)

k + 1 rounds, each looking at every flight once. With E ≈ 5000 flights and k < 100 that is about half a million steps.

Remember

"At most k edges" → Bellman-Ford with k + 1 rounds and a copied array per round. Round i = best paths using at most i edges.

Watch out

Forgetting clone(): updating cost in place lets 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 all happen inside one round, so the example returns 400 instead of 700 (and 400 even for k = 0, where the answer is -1). Also, k counts stops, so the number of flights (rounds) is k + 1.

Pattern notes: Shortest Paths · Open on LeetCode

LC 1631Path With Minimum EffortMediumDijkstra on gridLeetCode
The problem in easy words

A hiker walks on a grid of heights from the top-left to the bottom-right cell, moving up, down, left or right. The effort of a route is its biggest single height difference between two neighbouring cells. Find the route with the smallest effort.

Example: [[1,2,2],[3,8,2],[5,3,5]] → 2, going down the left side: 1 → 3 → 5 → 3 → 5, every step is 2.

How to spot the pattern

"Minimum effort" from one corner to another on a grid with different costs per step: BFS no longer works (steps don't cost the same), so it's Dijkstra, like Network Delay Time (LC 743). The only twist is that a path's cost is a max, not a sum.

1Brute force — try every simple path

Backtrack through every path that doesn't revisit a cell, track the biggest step so far, and keep the best finish. Prune a path once it is no better than the best found.

int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
int best;

int minimumEffortPath(int[][] heights) {
    best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    walk(heights, 0, 0, 0, new boolean[heights.length][heights[0].length]);
    return best;
}

void walk(int[][] h, int i, int j, int effort, boolean[][] onPath) {
    if (effort >= best) return;                        // can't beat what we have
    if (i == h.length - 1 && j == h[0].length - 1) { best = effort; return; }
    onPath[i][j] = true;
    for (int[] d : DIRS) {
        int x = i + d[0], y = j + d[1];
        if (x >= 0 && y >= 0 && x < h.length && y < h[0].length && !onPath[x][y])
            walk(h, x, y, Math.max(effort, Math.abs(h[x][y] - h[i][j])), onPath);
    }
    onPath[i][j] = false;                              // backtrack: free the cell
}

Time exponentialSpace O(R · C)

The number of simple paths in a grid grows exponentially; even a 10 × 10 grid is too many, and the limit is 100 × 100.

2Optimal — Dijkstra where a path costs its biggest step
The idea

This is Dijkstra from LC 743, plus one change: new cost = max(cost so far, this step) instead of cost + step. Dijkstra still works, because taking one more step can never make a path's maximum smaller (just like adding a non-negative weight can't make a sum smaller).

The heap always expands the cell with the smallest effort, so the first time the bottom-right cell comes out of the heap, its effort is final.

int minimumEffortPath(int[][] heights) {
    int rows = heights.length, cols = heights[0].length;
    int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
    int[][] effort = new int[rows][cols];              // best known effort to reach a cell
    for (int[] row : effort) Arrays.fill(row, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    effort[0][0] = 0;
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);   // {effort, i, j}
    pq.add(new int[]{0, 0, 0});
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = pq.poll();
        int e = cur[0], i = cur[1], j = cur[2];
        if (e > effort[i][j]) continue;                // stale entry, skip
        if (i == rows - 1 && j == cols - 1) return e;  // first pop of the target is final
        for (int[] d : DIRS) {
            int x = i + d[0], y = j + d[1];
            if (x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= rows || y >= cols) continue;
            int ne = Math.max(e, Math.abs(heights[x][y] - heights[i][j]));   // MAX, not sum
            if (ne < effort[x][y]) {
                effort[x][y] = ne;
                pq.add(new int[]{ne, x, y});
            }
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Time O(R·C · log(R·C))Space O(R · C)

Each cell is improved a few times at most, and every heap operation costs a log. About 10,000 cells for the biggest grid: instant.

Remember

Dijkstra works for any path cost that never goes down as the path gets longer: a sum of non-negative weights, or a maximum. Just change the line that combines the costs.

Watch out

Using e + diff (sum) instead of max(e, diff) answers a different question. Also skip stale heap entries (e > effort[i][j]) and return when the target is popped, not when it is first pushed: the first push may not be the best.

Pattern notes: Shortest Paths · Open on LeetCode

LC 778Swim in Rising WaterHardDijkstra (minimax)LeetCode
The problem in easy words

An n × n grid holds the heights 0 … n²−1, each once. At time t the water level is t, and you can swim into a cell only if its height is ≤ t (swimming itself is instant). What is the earliest time you can get from the top-left to the bottom-right?

Example: [[0,2],[1,3]] → 3: the bottom-right cell itself is 3, so you must wait until t = 3.

How to spot the pattern

You need a path whose highest cell is as low as possible: "minimise the maximum along a path". That is exactly LC 1631 again, only the cost sits on the cells instead of the steps. Minimax path → Dijkstra with max, or binary search on the answer + BFS.

1Brute force — try t = 0, 1, 2, … until BFS gets through

For each time t, flood-fill from the start through cells with height ≤ t. The first t that reaches the corner is the answer.

int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};

int swimInWater(int[][] grid) {
    for (int t = grid[0][0]; ; t++)                  // try every time, smallest first
        if (canSwim(grid, t)) return t;
}

boolean canSwim(int[][] grid, int t) {               // BFS through cells with height <= t
    int n = grid.length;
    boolean[][] seen = new boolean[n][n];
    Queue<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.add(new int[]{0, 0});
    seen[0][0] = true;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int[] c = q.poll();
        if (c[0] == n - 1 && c[1] == n - 1) return true;
        for (int[] d : DIRS) {
            int x = c[0] + d[0], y = c[1] + d[1];
            if (x >= 0 && y >= 0 && x < n && y < n && !seen[x][y] && grid[x][y] <= t) {
                seen[x][y] = true;
                q.add(new int[]{x, y});
            }
        }
    }
    return false;
}

Time O(n⁴)Space O(n²)

Up to n² values of t, each a BFS over n² cells. With n ≤ 50 that is about 6 million steps, so it actually passes here; but it does not scale (n = 1000 would be 10¹² steps), and interviewers expect better.

2Optimal — Dijkstra on "highest cell so far"
The idea

This is the Dijkstra from LC 1631, with the key time to reach a cell = max(time so far, height of that cell). Always expand the cell you can reach the earliest; the moment the corner comes out of the heap, that time is the answer.

int swimInWater(int[][] grid) {
    int n = grid.length;
    int[][] DIRS = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
    boolean[][] done = new boolean[n][n];
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);   // {time, i, j}
    pq.add(new int[]{grid[0][0], 0, 0});
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = pq.poll();
        int t = cur[0], i = cur[1], j = cur[2];
        if (done[i][j]) continue;
        done[i][j] = true;
        if (i == n - 1 && j == n - 1) return t;
        for (int[] d : DIRS) {
            int x = i + d[0], y = j + d[1];
            if (x >= 0 && y >= 0 && x < n && y < n && !done[x][y])
                pq.add(new int[]{Math.max(t, grid[x][y]), x, y});   // wait for the higher cell
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

Time O(n² log n)Space O(n²)

n² cells, each pushed a few times into a heap of size O(n²); log(n²) = 2·log n.

3Also good — binary search on t

If you can finish at time t, you can finish at any later time too. That "no, no, …, no, yes, yes" shape is binary search on the answer (like Koko, LC 875): search t in [grid[0][0], n²−1] and test each guess with the BFS from step 1.

int swimInWater(int[][] grid) {
    int n = grid.length;
    int lo = grid[0][0], hi = n * n - 1;             // answer is somewhere in here
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
        if (canSwim(grid, mid)) hi = mid;            // works: try smaller
        else lo = mid + 1;                           // too early: need more water
    }
    return lo;
}
// canSwim(grid, t) is the same BFS as in step 1

Time O(n² log n)Space O(n²)

Remember

"Lowest possible maximum along a path" has two standard answers: Dijkstra with max, or binary search the answer + a yes/no BFS. (Union-find, adding cells from low to high until the corners connect, is a third.)

Watch out

The start cell counts too: begin with time grid[0][0], not 0. And the corner's own height matters: in [[0,2],[1,3]] the answer is 3 even though you could reach its neighbours at t = 1.

LC 1584Min Cost to Connect All PointsMediumMinimum spanning treeLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get points on a plane. Connecting two points costs their Manhattan distance |x1 − x2| + |y1 − y2|. Connect all points (every point reachable from every other) for the least total cost.

Example: [[0,0],[2,2],[3,10],[5,2],[7,0]] → 20.

How to spot the pattern

"Connect all points" with the "minimum total cost", and no start or end point: that is a minimum spanning tree (MST). Here every pair of points is an edge, so the graph is dense (about n²/2 edges), which favours Prim.

1Straightforward — Kruskal on all n² edges

The truly naive idea, trying every possible tree, is hopeless (there are nⁿ⁻² of them). The first real solution is Kruskal: list every pair as an edge, sort by cost, and take an edge whenever it joins two different groups (union-find, as in Redundant Connection, LC 684).

int minCostConnectPoints(int[][] points) {
    int n = points.length;
    List<int[]> edges = new ArrayList<>();                 // {cost, i, j} for EVERY pair
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
            edges.add(new int[]{dist(points, i, j), i, j});
    edges.sort((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);                     // cheapest first

    int[] parent = new int[n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i;
    int total = 0, used = 0;
    for (int[] e : edges) {
        int a = find(parent, e[1]), b = find(parent, e[2]);
        if (a == b) continue;                              // already connected: would make a loop
        parent[a] = b;
        total += e[0];
        if (++used == n - 1) break;                        // a tree has n - 1 edges
    }
    return total;
}

int find(int[] parent, int x) {
    while (parent[x] != x) x = parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];   // path halving
    return x;
}

int dist(int[][] p, int i, int j) {
    return Math.abs(p[i][0] - p[j][0]) + Math.abs(p[i][1] - p[j][1]);
}

Time O(n² log n)Space O(n²)

Correct and it passes for n = 1000, but it builds and sorts about 500,000 edges. We can avoid storing edges at all.

2Optimal — Prim with a plain array
The idea

Grow one tree from point 0. Keep cheapest[v] = the cheapest link from the tree to v. Each round, add the outside point with the smallest link, then let it offer cheaper links to the rest. This is the greedy "always take the cheapest safe edge" idea; the extra insight for dense graphs is to skip the heap: a linear scan for the minimum costs O(n), and there are no stored edges.

int minCostConnectPoints(int[][] points) {
    int n = points.length, total = 0;
    boolean[] inTree = new boolean[n];
    int[] cheapest = new int[n];                           // cheapest link from the tree to i
    Arrays.fill(cheapest, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    cheapest[0] = 0;                                       // start the tree at point 0
    for (int round = 0; round < n; round++) {
        int u = -1;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)                        // closest point not yet in the tree
            if (!inTree[i] && (u == -1 || cheapest[i] < cheapest[u])) u = i;
        inTree[u] = true;
        total += cheapest[u];
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) {                      // u joined: maybe v is closer now
            if (inTree[v]) continue;
            int d = Math.abs(points[u][0] - points[v][0]) + Math.abs(points[u][1] - points[v][1]);
            if (d < cheapest[v]) cheapest[v] = d;
        }
    }
    return total;
}

Time O(n²)Space O(n)

n rounds, each with two O(n) scans: about 2 million steps for n = 1000, with no edge list and no sorting.

Remember

MST: Kruskal (sort edges + union-find) when edges are given and few; Prim when the graph is dense or complete. For a complete graph, array Prim in O(n²) beats everything.

Watch out

A spanning tree has exactly n − 1 edges; stop there, and never take an edge between two points already in the same group (that makes a loop). The cost is Manhattan distance, not straight-line distance.

Pattern notes: Topological Sort, MST & More · Open on LeetCode

LC 332Reconstruct ItineraryHardEulerian path (Hierholzer)LeetCode
The problem in easy words

You have a pile of plane tickets [from, to]. Use every ticket exactly once in one trip starting from "JFK". If several trips work, return the one that is smallest in dictionary order. A valid trip always exists.

Example: [[JFK,KUL],[JFK,NRT],[NRT,JFK]] → [JFK, NRT, JFK, KUL]. Going to KUL first looks smaller, but then you are stuck with tickets left.

How to spot the pattern

"Use all the tickets (edges) exactly once" is an Eulerian path: a walk that covers every edge once. It is not a "visit every node" problem. Eulerian path has a neat linear-time algorithm, Hierholzer's.

1Brute force — backtracking in sorted order

Sort each airport's destinations. DFS, always trying the smallest unused ticket first; if you get stuck with tickets left, undo and try the next one. The first complete trip is the answer.

List<String> findItinerary(List<List<String>> tickets) {
    Map<String, List<String>> adj = new HashMap<>();
    for (List<String> t : tickets)
        adj.computeIfAbsent(t.get(0), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(t.get(1));
    for (List<String> dests : adj.values()) Collections.sort(dests);   // try smallest first
    List<String> route = new ArrayList<>(List.of("JFK"));
    fly("JFK", tickets.size(), adj, route);
    return route;
}

boolean fly(String from, int left, Map<String, List<String>> adj, List<String> route) {
    if (left == 0) return true;                           // every ticket used: done
    List<String> dests = adj.getOrDefault(from, new ArrayList<>());
    for (int i = 0; i < dests.size(); i++) {
        String to = dests.get(i);
        if (to == null) continue;                         // ticket already used
        dests.set(i, null);                               // use it
        route.add(to);
        if (fly(to, left - 1, adj, route)) return true;
        route.remove(route.size() - 1);                   // dead end: undo and try the next
        dests.set(i, to);
    }
    return false;
}

Time exponential (worst case)Space O(E)

Usually fast, but with up to 300 tickets and many dead ends (lots of tickets between the same few airports), the undo-and-retry can blow up.

2Optimal — Hierholzer: add airports when you get stuck
The idea

This is DFS from Intermediate, plus one insight: write an airport into the route only when you are stuck there, and write it at the front (post-order, then reverse). A dead end like KUL gets stuck first, so it ends up last in the route, and the loop JFK → NRT → JFK that was skipped gets spliced in before it. No undoing is ever needed.

A min-heap per airport makes sure we always take the smallest destination first, which gives the smallest trip.

List<String> findItinerary(List<List<String>> tickets) {
    Map<String, PriorityQueue<String>> adj = new HashMap<>();   // smallest destination on top
    for (List<String> t : tickets)
        adj.computeIfAbsent(t.get(0), k -> new PriorityQueue<>()).add(t.get(1));
    LinkedList<String> route = new LinkedList<>();
    visit("JFK", adj, route);
    return route;
}

void visit(String from, Map<String, PriorityQueue<String>> adj, LinkedList<String> route) {
    PriorityQueue<String> dests = adj.get(from);
    while (dests != null && !dests.isEmpty())
        visit(dests.poll(), adj, route);                  // use the ticket, keep flying
    route.addFirst(from);                                 // stuck here: prepend (post-order)
}

Time O(E log E)Space O(E)

Each ticket is pushed and polled once from a heap. The log comes from keeping destinations in order.

Remember

"Use every edge exactly once" → Hierholzer: DFS that consumes edges, and adds a node after its edges are used up, then reverse (or add to the front).

Watch out

Adding the airport before the loop (pre-order) gives [JFK, KUL, NRT, JFK] for the example, which is not a real trip. And poll the ticket (remove it) as you use it; just reading it lets you fly the same ticket forever.

LC 1192Critical Connections in a NetworkHardTarjan bridgesLeetCode
The problem in easy words

n servers are joined by two-way cables, and every server can reach every other. A cable is critical if cutting it would split the network. Return all critical cables (in any order).

Example: n = 4, cables [[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[1,3]] → [[1,3]]. Cables 0-1, 1-2, 2-0 form a triangle, so any one of them can be cut safely.

How to spot the pattern

"Which edges, if removed, disconnect the graph" is the textbook definition of a bridge. An edge is a bridge exactly when it is not on any cycle. Finding them all in one DFS is Tarjan's low-link trick.

1Brute force — cut each cable and check

For every cable: pretend it is gone, run a DFS from server 0, and count how many servers you reach. Fewer than n means the cable was critical.

List<List<Integer>> criticalConnections(int n, List<List<Integer>> connections) {
    List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int skip = 0; skip < connections.size(); skip++)   // cut one cable at a time
        if (reachable(n, connections, skip) < n)
            result.add(connections.get(skip));
    return result;
}

int reachable(int n, List<List<Integer>> connections, int skip) {
    List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (int e = 0; e < connections.size(); e++) {
        if (e == skip) continue;
        int a = connections.get(e).get(0), b = connections.get(e).get(1);
        adj.get(a).add(b);
        adj.get(b).add(a);
    }
    boolean[] seen = new boolean[n];
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(0));
    seen[0] = true;
    int count = 1;
    while (!stack.isEmpty())
        for (int v : adj.get(stack.pop()))
            if (!seen[v]) { seen[v] = true; count++; stack.push(v); }
    return count;
}

Time O(E · (V + E))Space O(V + E)

One full DFS per cable. With 10⁵ servers and 10⁵ cables that is about 10¹⁰ steps.

2Optimal — one DFS with discovery times and low-links
The idea

This is DFS from Intermediate, plus two numbers per node. disc[u] is when DFS first visited u. low[u] is the earliest visit time that u, or anything below it in the DFS, can reach using one "shortcut" edge back up. Then tree edge u–v is a bridge exactly when low[v] > disc[u]: nothing under v can climb back to u or above without that edge.

int[] disc, low;                  // disc = visit time, low = earliest time reachable
int timer = 0;
List<List<Integer>> bridges = new ArrayList<>();

List<List<Integer>> criticalConnections(int n, List<List<Integer>> connections) {
    List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (List<Integer> c : connections) {
        adj.get(c.get(0)).add(c.get(1));
        adj.get(c.get(1)).add(c.get(0));
    }
    disc = new int[n];
    low = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(disc, -1);                                 // -1 = not visited
    dfs(0, -1, adj);
    return bridges;
}

void dfs(int u, int parent, List<List<Integer>> adj) {
    disc[u] = low[u] = timer++;
    for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
        if (v == parent) continue;                         // don't walk the same cable back
        if (disc[v] == -1) {                               // tree edge: go deeper
            dfs(v, u, adj);
            low[u] = Math.min(low[u], low[v]);
            if (low[v] > disc[u])                          // v's subtree can't get above u
                bridges.add(List.of(u, v));
        } else {
            low[u] = Math.min(low[u], disc[v]);            // back edge: a shortcut up
        }
    }
}

Time O(V + E)Space O(V + E)

A single DFS: each node and each cable is looked at a constant number of times.

Remember

Bridge test: low[v] > disc[u]. Articulation point (critical node) test is the same with >=, plus a special rule for the root. Both come from one DFS that tracks disc and low.

Watch out

Skip only the edge back to the parent; otherwise every edge looks like a cycle and no bridge is found. For a back edge, use disc[v] (not low[v]) to update low[u]. And the test is strictly greater: >= would wrongly flag edges on cycles.
