LC 847Shortest Path Visiting All NodesHardBFS over (node, bitmask)LeetCode
The problem in easy words

An undirected, connected graph has n ≤ 12 nodes. Find the length of the shortest walk that visits every node. You may start and end anywhere, and you may reuse nodes and edges.

Example: graph = [[1,2,3],[0],[0],[0]] (node 0 in the middle of a star) → 4, e.g. 1 → 0 → 2 → 0 → 3.

How to spot the pattern

"Shortest" with equal-cost edges says BFS, but "visit all nodes" means the same node can be worth revisiting, so "which node am I on" is not enough. The tiny limit n ≤ 12 is the giveaway: 2¹² = 4096, so you can afford to remember which nodes are visited as a bitmask.

1Brute force — try every visiting order

Compute the BFS distance between every pair of nodes. Then try every order of visiting the nodes and add up the distances between consecutive ones; keep the smallest total.

int best;

int shortestPathLength(int[][] graph) {
    int n = graph.length;
    int[][] d = new int[n][n];                         // d[a][b] = BFS distance a -> b
    for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) d[s] = bfs(graph, s);
    best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    for (int s = 0; s < n; s++)                        // try every visiting order
        tryOrders(d, s, 1 << s, 0);
    return best;
}

void tryOrders(int[][] d, int last, int visited, int cost) {
    int n = d.length;
    if (visited == (1 << n) - 1) { best = Math.min(best, cost); return; }
    for (int next = 0; next < n; next++)
        if ((visited & (1 << next)) == 0)
            tryOrders(d, next, visited | (1 << next), cost + d[last][next]);
}

int[] bfs(int[][] graph, int s) {
    int[] dist = new int[graph.length];
    Arrays.fill(dist, -1);
    dist[s] = 0;
    Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>(List.of(s));
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll();
        for (int v : graph[u])
            if (dist[v] == -1) { dist[v] = dist[u] + 1; q.add(v); }
    }
    return dist;
}

Time O(n! · n)Space O(n²)

For n = 12 there are 12! ≈ 479 million orders. Too slow already, and n = 13 would be 13 times worse.

2Optimal — BFS where a state is (node, visited mask)
The idea

This is multi-source BFS (Rotting Oranges, LC 994), plus one insight: make the BFS node a pair (where I am, which nodes I have seen). The "seen" set is an int whose bit i means "node i visited". Start from every node at once with only its own bit set. The first state whose mask is all ones gives the answer.

Walking back through node 0 is fine: (0, 0011) and (0, 0111) are different states, so BFS doesn't block the revisit, but it never repeats the same state.

int shortestPathLength(int[][] graph) {
    int n = graph.length, full = (1 << n) - 1;
    boolean[][] seen = new boolean[n][1 << n];         // seen[node][mask]
    Queue<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {                      // start everywhere at once
        q.add(new int[]{i, 1 << i});
        seen[i][1 << i] = true;
    }
    for (int steps = 0; !q.isEmpty(); steps++) {
        for (int size = q.size(); size > 0; size--) {
            int[] cur = q.poll();
            int node = cur[0], mask = cur[1];
            if (mask == full) return steps;            // everyone visited
            for (int next : graph[node]) {
                int nm = mask | (1 << next);           // mark next as visited
                if (!seen[next][nm]) {
                    seen[next][nm] = true;
                    q.add(new int[]{next, nm});
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

Time O(2ⁿ · n²)Space O(2ⁿ · n)

There are n · 2ⁿ states (about 49,000 for n = 12), and each tries at most n neighbours: well under a million steps.

Remember

When "where you are" isn't enough to decide the future, add the missing info to the state and BFS over states. Small n (≤ 20) plus "visit all" → the extra info is a bitmask.

Watch out

A visited array per node is wrong here: the star needs node 0 three times. Mark seen[node][mask] instead. And n = 1 must return 0: the start state is already "all visited".

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

Stage 5 — Search spaces & DPBacktracking with strong pruning, DP on two strings, and the hardest DP shapes.

Backtracking with Pruning

This is the choose / explore / un-choose template from Intermediate (LC 46, LC 79, LC 131), but the search trees are now huge, so the whole game is pruning: cut a branch the moment it can no longer lead to an answer, and never solve the same sub-problem twice. Template: keep small lookup tables (used columns, used digits, how many brackets must still go) so "is this choice legal?" costs O(1), check before you recurse, and add a memo when different paths reach the same state. What is harder than Intermediate: the brute force is not "a bit slow", it is 99 or 951 or 225 steps, so the pruning rule is the solution.

LC 51N-QueensHardBacktracking + O(1) checksLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Place n queens on an n × n chess board so that no two attack each other: no two in the same row, the same column or the same diagonal. Return every such board, drawn as strings with 'Q' and '.'.

Example: n = 4 → 2 boards: [".Q..","...Q","Q...","..Q."] and ["..Q.","Q...","...Q",".Q.."]. n = 1 → [["Q"]].

How to spot the pattern

"Return all placements" and "no two may attack" means: build the answer piece by piece and throw away a partial board as soon as it breaks a rule. That is backtracking. The rule "one per row" also tells you the shape of the tree: level r of the recursion chooses the column for row r.

1Brute force — every column for every row, check at the end

Put exactly one queen in each row (that rule is free), try every column for each row, and only when all n rows are filled check whether any two queens clash.

List<List<String>> solveNQueens(int n) {
    List<List<String>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    place(0, new int[n], n, res);            // q[r] = column of the queen in row r
    return res;
}

void place(int row, int[] q, int n, List<List<String>> res) {
    if (row == n) {                          // board full: only now check it
        if (valid(q)) res.add(build(q));
        return;
    }
    for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {            // no checking on the way down
        q[row] = c;
        place(row + 1, q, n, res);
    }
}

boolean valid(int[] q) {                     // any two queens in a column or diagonal?
    for (int a = 0; a < q.length; a++)
        for (int b = a + 1; b < q.length; b++)
            if (q[a] == q[b] || Math.abs(q[a] - q[b]) == b - a) return false;
    return true;
}

List<String> build(int[] q) {                // turn columns into "..Q." strings
    List<String> board = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int c : q) {
        char[] row = new char[q.length];
        Arrays.fill(row, '.');
        row[c] = 'Q';
        board.add(new String(row));
    }
    return board;
}

Time O(nⁿ · n²)Space O(n)

At the limit n = 9 that is 9⁹ ≈ 387 million full boards, each checked with 36 pair tests: over 10 billion steps. Almost all of those boards were already broken after two rows.

2Optimal — check each queen as you place it, in O(1)
The idea

This is the Intermediate backtracking template (LC 46 Permutations: "pick an unused item for this slot") plus one extra insight: every diagonal has a fixed number: r − c on one direction, r + c on the other. Keep three boolean arrays (col, diag, anti) and a square is safe if all three are free. Check before recursing, so a bad partial board is never extended.

List<List<String>> solveNQueens(int n) {
    List<List<String>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    boolean[] col  = new boolean[n];
    boolean[] diag = new boolean[2 * n];     // index r - c + n (shifted, never negative)
    boolean[] anti = new boolean[2 * n];     // index r + c
    dfs(0, n, new int[n], col, diag, anti, res);
    return res;
}

void dfs(int r, int n, int[] q, boolean[] col, boolean[] diag, boolean[] anti,
         List<List<String>> res) {
    if (r == n) { res.add(build(q)); return; }       // every row has a safe queen
    for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
        if (col[c] || diag[r - c + n] || anti[r + c]) continue;  // prune: attacked
        q[r] = c;
        col[c] = diag[r - c + n] = anti[r + c] = true;           // choose
        dfs(r + 1, n, q, col, diag, anti, res);                  // explore
        col[c] = diag[r - c + n] = anti[r + c] = false;          // un-choose
    }
}
// build(q) is the same helper as in step 1

Time O(n!)Space O(n)

Row 0 has n choices, row 1 at most n − 1 safe ones, and so on, so the tree is at most n! leaves, and in practice far fewer. The three arrays turn "is this square attacked?" from a loop into three lookups. Checked for n = 1 to 9: 1, 0, 0, 2, 10, 4, 40, 92, 352 boards.

Remember

Backtracking gets fast when the "is this choice legal?" test is O(1) and done before recursing. For grids, label diagonals with r − c and r + c; that trick comes back in many board problems.

Watch out

r − c can be negative (row 0, column 3 gives −3), so shift it: diag[r − c + n] with an array of size 2n. And undo all three marks on the way back, or later branches see squares as attacked that are not.

Pattern notes: Recursion & Backtracking · Open on LeetCode

LC 37Sudoku SolverHardBacktracking + O(1) checksLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Fill the empty cells ('.') of a 9 × 9 Sudoku in place so that every row, every column and every 3 × 3 box contains the digits 1 to 9 exactly once. The puzzle has exactly one solution.

Example: the LeetCode board starting with row "53..7...." becomes the solved board starting with "534678912".

How to spot the pattern

"Fill the cells so that rules hold" with no clever formula is a constraint puzzle: guess, check, and undo a guess when it leads nowhere. It is the same shape as N-Queens (LC 51): one decision per empty cell, and three kinds of conflict (row, column, box) to test. You already know the row/column/box bookkeeping from Intermediate LC 36 Valid Sudoku.

1Brute force — fill everything, check at the end

Walk the 81 cells in order. For each empty cell try every digit 1 to 9, without looking at the rules. Only when the last cell is filled, check the whole board.

void solveSudoku(char[][] board) { fill(board, 0); }

boolean fill(char[][] b, int pos) {           // pos = 0..80, row = pos / 9, col = pos % 9
    if (pos == 81) return allValid(b);        // only now look at the rules
    int r = pos / 9, c = pos % 9;
    if (b[r][c] != '.') return fill(b, pos + 1);
    for (char d = '1'; d <= '9'; d++) {
        b[r][c] = d;
        if (fill(b, pos + 1)) return true;
    }
    b[r][c] = '.';
    return false;
}

boolean allValid(char[][] b) {                // LC 36 on a full board
    for (int i = 0; i < 9; i++) {
        boolean[] row = new boolean[10], col = new boolean[10], box = new boolean[10];
        for (int j = 0; j < 9; j++) {
            int x = b[i][j] - '0', y = b[j][i] - '0';
            int z = b[i / 3 * 3 + j / 3][i % 3 * 3 + j % 3] - '0';
            if (row[x] || col[y] || box[z]) return false;
            row[x] = col[y] = box[z] = true;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

Time O(9ᵐ · 81)Space O(m)

With m empty cells there are 9m fillings. The LeetCode example has 51 blanks: 951 is about 1048, which would never finish. It only works on a board with 4 or 5 blanks.

2Optimal — only try digits that are still legal
The idea

Same trick as N-Queens: keep row[r][d], col[c][d], box[k][d] tables (box number k = r / 3 * 3 + c / 3, from LC 36). Before placing a digit, ask the three tables; if any says "used", skip the digit. A wrong guess now fails at the very next cell it breaks, not 50 cells later. When a cell has no legal digit, return false and the caller tries its next digit.

boolean[][] row = new boolean[9][10], col = new boolean[9][10], box = new boolean[9][10];

void solveSudoku(char[][] board) {
    for (int r = 0; r < 9; r++)                  // record the given digits
        for (int c = 0; c < 9; c++)
            if (board[r][c] != '.') {
                int d = board[r][c] - '0';
                row[r][d] = col[c][d] = box[r / 3 * 3 + c / 3][d] = true;
            }
    solve(board, 0);
}

boolean solve(char[][] b, int pos) {
    if (pos == 81) return true;                  // every cell filled legally
    int r = pos / 9, c = pos % 9, k = r / 3 * 3 + c / 3;
    if (b[r][c] != '.') return solve(b, pos + 1);   // given digit: move on
    for (int d = 1; d <= 9; d++) {
        if (row[r][d] || col[c][d] || box[k][d]) continue;  // prune now
        b[r][c] = (char) ('0' + d);
        row[r][d] = col[c][d] = box[k][d] = true;            // choose
        if (solve(b, pos + 1)) return true;                  // solved: stop
        row[r][d] = col[c][d] = box[k][d] = false;           // un-choose
        b[r][c] = '.';
    }
    return false;                                // no digit fits: caller backs up
}

Time O(9ᵐ) worst case, fast in practiceSpace O(81)

The worst-case bound does not change on paper, but pruning cuts almost every branch after one or two cells, so a real puzzle solves in milliseconds. Returning true all the way up stops the search at the first solution and leaves the board filled.

Remember

"Search that stops at the first answer": make the recursion return boolean and bubble true up. Keep one "used" table per rule so every legality test is O(1). A known speed-up: fill the empty cell with the fewest legal digits first.

Watch out

Record the given digits in the tables before you start, or the solver will happily place a second 5 in row 0. And when you undo a guess, reset the cell to '.' as well as the three tables.

Pattern notes: Recursion & Backtracking · Open on LeetCode

LC 140Word Break IIHardBacktracking + memoLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get a string with no spaces and a dictionary of words. Add spaces to turn the string into a sentence where every piece is a dictionary word. Return all such sentences (words may be reused).

Example: s = "catsanddog", wordDict = ["cat","cats","and","sand","dog"] → ["cats and dog", "cat sand dog"]. s = "catsandog" with the same kind of dictionary → [].

How to spot the pattern

"Return all ways to split" means backtracking over "which word comes next". The hint for the memo: the rest of the string from index i has the same sentences no matter how you got to i ("cat|sand" and "cats|and" both land on "dog"). Same sub-problem, reached many times: remember it. It is Intermediate LC 139 Word Break, but returning the sentences instead of true/false.

1Brute force — try every dictionary prefix, recurse

From position start, try every end: if s[start..end) is a word, add it to the path and solve the rest. When start reaches the end, the path is a sentence.

List<String> wordBreak(String s, List<String> wordDict) {
    Set<String> dict = new HashSet<>(wordDict);
    List<String> res = new ArrayList<>();
    dfs(s, 0, dict, new ArrayList<>(), res);
    return res;
}

void dfs(String s, int start, Set<String> dict, List<String> path, List<String> res) {
    if (start == s.length()) { res.add(String.join(" ", path)); return; }
    for (int end = start + 1; end <= s.length(); end++) {
        String word = s.substring(start, end);
        if (!dict.contains(word)) continue;       // this prefix is not a word
        path.add(word);                           // choose
        dfs(s, end, dict, path, res);             // explore the rest
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);             // un-choose
    }
}

Time O(2ⁿ · n)Space O(n)

At LeetCode's limit of 20 letters this still passes (219 ≈ 500,000 splits). But it re-explores the same tail again and again, and dead ends are the worst case: "aaa…ab" (30 a's) with ["a","aa","aaa","aaaa"] took about 30 seconds to find zero sentences.

2Optimal — memo: start index → all sentences of the tail
The idea

Backtracking from step 1, plus one extra insight: make the function return the sentences for s[start..] instead of pushing them into a global list. Then the result only depends on start, so store it in a map and reuse it the next time any path reaches the same start. An empty list is stored too: "no sentence from here" is the most valuable thing to remember.

Map<Integer, List<String>> memo = new HashMap<>();

List<String> wordBreak(String s, List<String> wordDict) {
    return build(s, 0, new HashSet<>(wordDict));
}

// every sentence that spells s[start..]
List<String> build(String s, int start, Set<String> dict) {
    if (memo.containsKey(start)) return memo.get(start);  // solved before
    List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (start == s.length()) {
        out.add("");                                      // one way: the empty sentence
        return out;
    }
    for (int end = start + 1; end <= s.length(); end++) {
        String word = s.substring(start, end);
        if (!dict.contains(word)) continue;
        for (String rest : build(s, end, dict)) {         // sentences for the tail
            out.add(rest.isEmpty() ? word : word + " " + rest);
        }
    }
    memo.put(start, out);                                 // remember, even if empty
    return out;
}

Time O(n³ + total answer size)Space O(total answer size)

Each start index is solved once, with n substring checks, so the search itself is n² substring checks of up to n letters each. On top of that you pay for copying the sentences, which can be exponential if the answer really has that many (no algorithm can avoid writing the output). The dead-end input above now takes under a millisecond.

Remember

Backtracking + memo works when the recursion can return its result and that result depends only on a small key (here: the start index). Then "all sentences" is just LC 139's DP carrying lists instead of booleans.

Watch out

The base case must return a list with one empty string, not an empty list: an empty list means "no way", and every sentence would vanish. Then join with care, so you don't get a trailing space like "cat sand dog ".

Pattern notes: Recursion & Backtracking · Open on LeetCode

LC 301Remove Invalid ParenthesesHardBacktracking + countingLeetCode
The problem in easy words

A string has letters and brackets ( ). Remove the fewest brackets so that the brackets are balanced. Return every different string you can get that way (any order).

Example: "()())()" → ["(())()", "()()()"]. "(a)())()" → ["(a())()", "(a)()()"]. ")(" → [""].

How to spot the pattern

"Remove the minimum number" plus "return all results" means: first work out how many must go (a counting pass, like Beginner LC 20 Valid Parentheses), then backtrack over which ones, allowed to delete exactly that many. The count is the pruning rule.

1Brute force — try every subset of characters

Every answer is a subsequence of s. So try all 2n ways to keep or drop each character, keep the valid ones, and among them keep only the longest.

List<String> removeInvalidParentheses(String s) {
    int n = s.length(), bestLen = -1;
    Set<String> best = new HashSet<>();
    for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); mask++) {    // bit i = keep s[i]
        StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if ((mask >> i & 1) == 1) sb.append(s.charAt(i));
        String t = sb.toString();
        if (!isValid(t) || t.length() < bestLen) continue;
        if (t.length() > bestLen) { bestLen = t.length(); best.clear(); }
        best.add(t);
    }
    return new ArrayList<>(best);
}

boolean isValid(String t) {
    int open = 0;
    for (char c : t.toCharArray()) {
        if (c == '(') open++;
        else if (c == ')' && --open < 0) return false;  // ')' with nothing open
    }
    return open == 0;
}

Time O(2ⁿ · n)Space O(n)

At the limit of 25 characters that is 225 ≈ 33 million subsets, each built and checked in 25 steps: close to a billion operations, a time-out. Most of those subsets delete far more than needed.

2Optimal — count what must go, then DFS with that budget
The idea

Intermediate LC 22 Generate Parentheses taught "track the open count, never let it go negative". Add one extra insight: one scan tells you exactly how many '(' (left) and ')' (right) must be removed. A ')' that arrives with nothing open must go; the '(' still open at the end must go. Then DFS: at each bracket, either drop it (if that kind still has budget) or keep it (if the open count stays ≥ 0). A Set removes duplicate strings.

List<String> removeInvalidParentheses(String s) {
    int left = 0, right = 0;                  // how many '(' and ')' MUST go
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (c == '(') left++;
        else if (c == ')') {
            if (left > 0) left--;             // matches an earlier '('
            else right++;                     // nothing to match: extra ')'
        }
    }
    Set<String> res = new HashSet<>();        // removes duplicate answers
    dfs(s, 0, left, right, 0, new StringBuilder(), res);
    return new ArrayList<>(res);
}

void dfs(String s, int i, int left, int right, int open, StringBuilder sb, Set<String> res) {
    if (left < 0 || right < 0 || open < 0) return;           // prune: over budget or invalid
    if (i == s.length()) {
        if (left == 0 && right == 0 && open == 0) res.add(sb.toString());
        return;
    }
    char c = s.charAt(i);
    int len = sb.length();
    if (c == '(') dfs(s, i + 1, left - 1, right, open, sb, res);   // drop this '('
    if (c == ')') dfs(s, i + 1, left, right - 1, open, sb, res);   // drop this ')'
    sb.append(c);                                                  // keep c
    if (c == '(') dfs(s, i + 1, left, right, open + 1, sb, res);
    else if (c == ')') dfs(s, i + 1, left, right, open - 1, sb, res);
    else dfs(s, i + 1, left, right, open, sb, res);                // letters: always keep
    sb.setLength(len);                                             // un-choose
}

Time O(2ᵖ · n) worst, far less in practiceSpace O(n)

p is the number of brackets (at most 20). The budget means the DFS only ever builds strings with the minimum number of removals, and the open < 0 check kills invalid prefixes early. Cross-checked against step 1 on 5,000 random strings.

Remember

"Fewest removals, list all results": compute the minimum first with a greedy scan, then backtrack with that exact budget. The alternative is BFS by number of removals: level 0 is s, level 1 is every string with one bracket removed, and you stop at the first level that has a valid string.

Watch out

Duplicates: removing the ")" at index 3 or at index 4 of "()())()" gives the same string, so collect into a Set (or skip a bracket equal to the one before it). And ")(" must return [""], a list holding the empty string, not an empty list.

Pattern notes: Recursion & Backtracking · Open on LeetCode

DP on Strings

DP on strings is the table you built for LCS (LC 1143) in Intermediate, now used for Hard questions. One template covers this whole section: two strings → dp[i][j] = the answer for the prefixes s[0..i) and t[0..j). Make an (m+1) × (n+1) table. Row 0 and column 0 stand for an empty prefix (the base cases). Each cell looks only at the last letters s[i−1] and t[j−1] and reads cells that are already filled: diagonal dp[i−1][j−1] (both last letters used up), up dp[i−1][j] (s's last letter dropped or used), left dp[i][j−1] (t's last letter dropped or used). Fill row by row; the answer sits at dp[m][n]. What is harder than Intermediate: the base row and column are no longer all zeros, a * in a pattern turns into a move that can repeat (up again and again), and LC 32 has only one string, so the same "prefix that ends here" idea becomes a 1D dp[i]. In every diagram, yellow is the base, blue are the cells being read and green is the cell being computed.

LC 72Edit DistanceMediumTwo-string DPLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Turn word1 into word2. In one step you may insert a letter, delete a letter or replace a letter. What is the fewest steps?

Example: word1 = "horse", word2 = "ros" → 3: horse → rorse (replace h with r) → rose (delete r) → ros (delete e).

How to spot the pattern

Two strings and "minimum number of operations to convert one into the other", where each operation touches one letter. That is the template: the question for the whole strings shrinks to the same question for shorter prefixes. Three operations means three neighbours per cell.

1Brute force — decide the last letter, recursively

Look at the last letters of both prefixes. If they are equal, they cost nothing: drop both. If not, try all three operations on the last letter and keep the cheapest. This is already the template's recurrence, just without a table.

int minDistance(String word1, String word2) {
    return solve(word1, word2, word1.length(), word2.length());
}

// fewest edits to turn a[0..i) into b[0..j)
int solve(String a, String b, int i, int j) {
    if (i == 0) return j;                          // insert all j letters
    if (j == 0) return i;                          // delete all i letters
    if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1))
        return solve(a, b, i - 1, j - 1);          // last letters equal: free
    return 1 + Math.min(solve(a, b, i - 1, j - 1), // replace a's last letter
               Math.min(solve(a, b, i - 1, j),     // delete a's last letter
                        solve(a, b, i, j - 1)));   // insert b's last letter
}

Time O(3^(m+n))Space O(m + n)

Every mismatch branches three ways. Two 12-letter words with no letter in common already take about 377 million calls; LeetCode allows 500 letters. Yet there are only (m+1)(n+1) different (i, j) pairs.

2Optimal — fill the (m+1) × (n+1) table
The idea

This is LCS (LC 1143) from Intermediate with a different question in each cell. The extra insight: every operation is exactly one neighbour of the cell. Replace = diagonal, delete = up, insert = left, each costing 1. Equal last letters are free and just copy the diagonal.

State: dp[i][j] = fewest steps to turn word1[0..i) into word2[0..j).
Recurrence: letters equal: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i−1][j−1], dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]).
Base case: dp[i][0] = i (delete all i letters), dp[0][j] = j (insert all j letters).

int minDistance(String word1, String word2) {
    int m = word1.length(), n = word2.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];   // dp[i][j]: word1[0..i) -> word2[0..j)
    for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i;   // delete everything
    for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;   // insert everything
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            if (word1.charAt(i - 1) == word2.charAt(j - 1)) {
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1];               // free: diagonal
            } else {
                dp[i][j] = 1 + Math.min(dp[i - 1][j - 1],  // replace: diagonal
                               Math.min(dp[i - 1][j],      // delete: up
                                        dp[i][j - 1]));    // insert: left
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];
}

Time O(m · n)Space O(m · n)

Each cell is O(1) work. A row only reads the row above it, so two rows of length n + 1 are enough if memory matters.

Remember

"Cheapest way to turn one string into another" → dp[i][j] over prefixes, where each allowed operation is one neighbour: diagonal, up or left.

Watch out

The base row and column are not zeros: dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j. With zeros, ("abc", "") returns 0 instead of 3. And when the letters are equal, don't add 1.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

LC 97Interleaving StringMediumTwo-string DPLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Can s3 be made by shuffling s1 and s2 together, like riffling two card decks, where each string keeps its own letter order?

Example: s1 = "aabcc", s2 = "dbbca", s3 = "aadbbcbcac" → true. With s3 = "aadbbbaccc" → false.

How to spot the pattern

"Interleaving" of two strings with order kept. When the next letter of s3 could come from either string, you can't decide greedily; you must try both, and the same (letters used from s1, letters used from s2) situation comes back over and over. Two strings to walk through → dp[i][j].

1Brute force — where did the last letter come from?

The last letter of s3[0..i+j) was taken either from the end of s1[0..i) or from the end of s2[0..j). Try both, recursively.

boolean isInterleave(String s1, String s2, String s3) {
    if (s1.length() + s2.length() != s3.length()) return false;
    return can(s1, s2, s3, s1.length(), s2.length());
}

// can s3[0..i+j) be built from s1[0..i) and s2[0..j)?
boolean can(String a, String b, String c, int i, int j) {
    if (i == 0 && j == 0) return true;             // nothing left to build
    char last = c.charAt(i + j - 1);                 // last letter of s3's prefix
    if (i > 0 && a.charAt(i - 1) == last && can(a, b, c, i - 1, j))
        return true;                                 // it came from s1
    return j > 0 && b.charAt(j - 1) == last && can(a, b, c, i, j - 1);   // from s2
}

Time O(2^(m+n))Space O(m + n)

When both strings are full of the same letter, both branches are always open. With 14 a's in each and an s3 that fails at its first letter, that is 115 million calls; with 18 each it is 26 billion. LeetCode allows 100 letters each.

2Optimal — a boolean table over (i, j)
The idea

This is grid DP from Intermediate (Unique Paths, LC 62: you arrive from up or from left) on the template's table. The extra insight: s3 needs no third dimension. After using i letters of s1 and j of s2 you are exactly at s3[i + j], so the letter to explain is always s3[i+j−1].

State: dp[i][j] = s1[0..i) and s2[0..j) can be shuffled into s3[0..i+j).
Recurrence: dp[i][j] = (dp[i−1][j] and s1[i−1] == s3[i+j−1]) or (dp[i][j−1] and s2[j−1] == s3[i+j−1]).
Base case: dp[0][0] = true; if m + n != s3.length() the answer is false right away.

boolean isInterleave(String s1, String s2, String s3) {
    int m = s1.length(), n = s2.length();
    if (m + n != s3.length()) return false;          // letters must add up
    boolean[][] dp = new boolean[m + 1][n + 1];
    dp[0][0] = true;                                 // empty + empty = empty
    for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) {
            if (i == 0 && j == 0) continue;
            char last = s3.charAt(i + j - 1);
            boolean fromS1 = i > 0 && dp[i - 1][j] && s1.charAt(i - 1) == last;  // up
            boolean fromS2 = j > 0 && dp[i][j - 1] && s2.charAt(j - 1) == last;  // left
            dp[i][j] = fromS1 || fromS2;
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];
}

Time O(m · n)Space O(m · n)

Each cell does two O(1) checks. Only the row above is read, so one boolean row of length n + 1 also works.

Remember

If a third string's position is fixed by the other two (here i + j), it does not need its own dimension. A True cell means "this corner of the table is reachable".

Watch out

Check m + n == s3.length() first, or s1 = "a", s2 = "b", s3 = "a" reads past the end of s3. And greedy "take from s1 whenever it matches" fails as soon as both strings offer the same letter.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

LC 32Longest Valid ParenthesesHardPrefix DP / StackLeetCode
The problem in easy words

A string has only '(' and ')'. Find the length of the longest substring (no gaps) that is a correctly matched bracket string.

Example: ")()())" → 4 (the part "()()"). "(()" → 2. "" → 0.

How to spot the pattern

"Longest valid (well-formed) substring" of brackets. Matching brackets points to a stack (Valid Parentheses, LC 20, from Beginner). "Longest substring" over one string points to dp[i] = best answer for a part that ends exactly here. Both work; this card shows both.

1Brute force — every start, extend with a counter

From each start, walk right keeping balance = opens − closes. If it drops below 0, a ')' has no partner and nothing longer from this start can be valid. Whenever it is exactly 0, the part so far is valid.

int longestValidParentheses(String s) {
    int best = 0;
    for (int start = 0; start < s.length(); start++) {
        int balance = 0;                              // opens minus closes
        for (int end = start; end < s.length(); end++) {
            balance += s.charAt(end) == '(' ? 1 : -1;
            if (balance < 0) break;                   // a ')' with no partner
            if (balance == 0) best = Math.max(best, end - start + 1);
        }
    }
    return best;
}

Time O(n²)Space O(1)

With up to 3 · 10⁴ letters that is about 450 million steps on a string like "(((((…" (the counter never drops, so no early stop), too slow. The fully naive version, testing every substring separately with a stack, is O(n³).

2Optimal — dp[i] for the part ending at the end of the prefix
The idea

The template with one string: dp[i] is about the prefix s[0..i), and it only counts valid parts that end at its last letter. A valid part can only end in ')'. The extra insight is how to find its partner: jump over the valid block right before it (length dp[i−1]) to j = i − dp[i−1] − 2; if s[j] is '(' they pair up, and you glue on dp[j], the valid part ending just before the partner. The simple case "()" is the same formula with dp[i−1] = 0.

State: dp[i] = length of the longest valid part ending at s[i−1] (0 if none).
Recurrence: if s[i−1] == ')' and s[j] == '(' with j = i − dp[i−1] − 2 ≥ 0: dp[i] = dp[i−1] + 2 + dp[j].
Base case: dp[0] = dp[1] = 0. The answer is the largest dp[i], not dp[n].

int longestValidParentheses(String s) {
    int n = s.length(), best = 0;
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];       // dp[i]: longest valid part ENDING at s[i-1]
    for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
        if (s.charAt(i - 1) != ')') continue;        // '(' never ends one
        int j = i - dp[i - 1] - 2;                   // must be the partner '('
        if (j >= 0 && s.charAt(j) == '(') {
            dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + 2 + dp[j];           // inside + this pair + glued left
            best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
        }
    }
    return best;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Each dp[i] reads two earlier cells in O(1), so one pass is enough.

3Also optimal — a stack of indices with a "wall"

Push the index of every '('. A ')' pops its partner. The bottom of the stack always holds a wall: the index just before the current valid run (start with -1). After a pop, the run length is i − stack.peek(). If the pop empties the stack, this ')' had no partner and becomes the new wall.

s = ")()())" stack (bottom → top) best start [-1] 0 i=0 ')' pop -1, empty → [0] new wall 0 i=1 '(' push [0, 1] 0 i=2 ')' pop 1 [0] 2 − 0 = 2 2 i=3 '(' push [0, 3] 2 i=4 ')' pop 3 [0] 4 − 0 = 4 4 i=5 ')' pop 0, empty → [5] new wall 4
int longestValidParentheses(String s) {
    Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    stack.push(-1);                      // wall: index just before the current run
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        if (s.charAt(i) == '(') {
            stack.push(i);                   // wait for a partner
        } else {
            stack.pop();                     // partner found (or the wall is gone)
            if (stack.isEmpty()) stack.push(i);           // unmatched ')': new wall
            else best = Math.max(best, i - stack.peek()); // run since the top
        }
    }
    return best;
}

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Each index is pushed and popped at most once. (There is also an O(1)-space trick: count opens and closes left to right, then right to left, and record a length whenever they are equal.)

Remember

"Longest valid part" with one string → dp[i] = best part ending here, and the answer is the max over all i. For brackets: jump over the inner block to find the partner, then glue on what ends before it.

Watch out

Don't forget the glue + dp[j]: without it "()(())" gives 4 instead of 6. In the stack version, forgetting the initial -1 makes the first ')' pop from an empty stack and measures runs from the wrong place.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Stacks · Open on LeetCode

LC 115Distinct SubsequencesHardTwo-string DP (count)LeetCode
The problem in easy words

In how many different ways can you pick letters out of s, keeping their order, so that they spell t? Two ways are different if they use different positions of s.

Example: s = "rabbbit", t = "rabbit" → 3 (leave out the first, second or third b). s = "babgbag", t = "bag" → 5.

How to spot the pattern

Two strings, "subsequence" and "number of" ways. Subsequence of two strings is the template; "number of" means the cell adds its choices instead of taking a min or max.

1Brute force — use or skip each letter of s

Look at the last letter of s[0..i). You can always skip it. If it equals the last letter of t[0..j), you can also use it for that letter. Count both.

int numDistinct(String s, String t) {
    return count(s, t, s.length(), t.length());
}

// ways to pick t[0..j) out of s[0..i)
int count(String s, String t, int i, int j) {
    if (j == 0) return 1;                       // empty t: pick nothing, 1 way
    if (i == 0) return 0;                       // s used up but t is not
    int ways = count(s, t, i - 1, j);           // don't use s[i-1]
    if (s.charAt(i - 1) == t.charAt(j - 1))
        ways += count(s, t, i - 1, j - 1);      // use s[i-1] as t[j-1]
    return ways;
}

Time O(2^m)Space O(m)

Every matching letter splits the count in two. For s = 30 a's and t = 15 a's the recursion makes about 1.2 billion calls; LeetCode allows 1000 letters.

2Optimal — a counting table
The idea

This is LCS (LC 1143) from Intermediate turned into a counter. The extra insight: skipping s[i−1] (up) and using it for t[j−1] (diagonal) never produce the same pick, so you add them. And the base is not 0: the empty t can be picked from any prefix in exactly one way.

State: dp[i][j] = number of ways to pick t[0..j) out of s[0..i).
Recurrence: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + (s[i−1] == t[j−1] ? dp[i−1][j−1] : 0).
Base case: dp[i][0] = 1 for every i; dp[0][j] = 0 for j > 0.

int numDistinct(String s, String t) {
    int m = s.length(), n = t.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];   // dp[i][j]: ways t[0..j) hides in s[0..i)
    for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = 1;   // empty t: one way
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j];                 // skip s[i-1]: up
            if (s.charAt(i - 1) == t.charAt(j - 1))
                dp[i][j] += dp[i - 1][j - 1];        // use it: diagonal
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];
}

Time O(m · n)Space O(m · n)

One O(1) cell at a time. Middle cells can grow bigger than an int; Java just wraps them around, and because the cells are only ever added, the last cell still comes out right (LeetCode promises the answer fits in an int).

3Follow-up — one row, filled right to left

Row i only reads row i−1 (up and diagonal). Keep one array and walk j from right to left, so dp[j − 1] still holds the old row's value when you read it.

int numDistinct(String s, String t) {
    int n = t.length();
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];            // one row: dp[j] for the current i
    dp[0] = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i <= s.length(); i++) {
        for (int j = n; j >= 1; j--) {    // right to left: dp[j-1] is still row i-1
            if (s.charAt(i - 1) == t.charAt(j - 1)) dp[j] += dp[j - 1];
        }
    }
    return dp[n];
}

Time O(m · n)Space O(n)

Remember

Counting ways on two strings → same table, but add the choices. "Empty target" is 1 way, not 0.

Watch out

If column 0 is left as 0, every cell stays 0. In the one-row version, a left-to-right loop reads the new dp[j − 1] and counts the same letter of s twice: s = "a", t = "aa" would give 1 instead of 0.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

LC 44Wildcard MatchingHardTwo-string DP (pattern)LeetCode
The problem in easy words

A pattern p may contain '?' (exactly one letter, any letter) and '*' (any run of letters, even an empty one). Does p match the whole string s?

Example: s = "aa", p = "a" → false. p = "*" → true. s = "cb", p = "?a" → false. s = "adceb", p = "*a*b" → true.

How to spot the pattern

A text, a pattern and "matches the entire string", with a symbol that can cover any number of letters. You don't know how much each * should eat, so you would have to try all amounts, and the same (text prefix, pattern prefix) question repeats. Two strings → the template.

1Brute force — let the star eat one letter at a time

Look at the last pattern letter. A normal letter or '?' must match the last text letter. A '*' either matches nothing (drop it) or eats the last text letter and stays, ready to eat more.

boolean isMatch(String s, String p) {
    return match(s, p, s.length(), p.length());
}

// does s[0..i) match p[0..j)?
boolean match(String s, String p, int i, int j) {
    if (j == 0) return i == 0;                   // empty pattern: only empty text
    char pc = p.charAt(j - 1);
    if (pc == '*')
        return match(s, p, i, j - 1)             // * matches nothing
            || (i > 0 && match(s, p, i - 1, j)); // * eats s[i-1] and stays
    return i > 0 && (pc == '?' || pc == s.charAt(i - 1))
                 && match(s, p, i - 1, j - 1);   // one letter for one letter
}

Time exponentialSpace O(m + n)

Each star can stop at any point, and every choice is explored again for the stars before it. The text "b" + 21 a's against "a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*" already takes 1.8 million calls; LeetCode allows 2000 letters in each.

2Optimal — a boolean table, star = left or up
The idea

The template, plus one insight for the star: you never need to try "star eats 0, 1, 2, … letters" by hand. A '*' cell reads only left (star matches nothing) and up (star eats one more letter and stays). "Up" can repeat row after row, so chains of ups cover every length. '?' and equal letters read the diagonal.

State: dp[i][j] = s[0..i) matches p[0..j).
Recurrence: p[j−1] == '*': dp[i][j] = dp[i][j−1] || dp[i−1][j]; '?' or equal letters: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise false.
Base case: dp[0][0] = true; dp[0][j] is true only while p[0..j) is all stars; dp[i][0] = false for i > 0.

boolean isMatch(String s, String p) {
    int m = s.length(), n = p.length();
    boolean[][] dp = new boolean[m + 1][n + 1];  // dp[i][j]: s[0..i) matches p[0..j)
    dp[0][0] = true;
    for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)                 // empty text: only a run of *s
        dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 1] && p.charAt(j - 1) == '*';
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            char pc = p.charAt(j - 1);
            if (pc == '*')
                dp[i][j] = dp[i][j - 1]          // * matches nothing: left
                        || dp[i - 1][j];         // * eats s[i-1]: up
            else if (pc == '?' || pc == s.charAt(i - 1))
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1];     // one for one: diagonal
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];
}

Time O(m · n)Space O(m · n)

Every cell is O(1). The star's "any length" became a chain of single steps through the table.

3Follow-up — greedy with one saved star, O(1) space

Walk both strings. On a star, remember where it is and let it match nothing. On a mismatch, go back to the last star and let it eat one more letter. Only the last star matters: anything an earlier star could have eaten, the later star can eat too.

boolean isMatch(String s, String p) {
    int i = 0, j = 0, star = -1, mark = 0;       // star: index of the last '*' seen
    while (i < s.length()) {
        if (j < p.length() && (p.charAt(j) == '?' || p.charAt(j) == s.charAt(i))) {
            i++; j++;                            // plain match, move both
        } else if (j < p.length() && p.charAt(j) == '*') {
            star = j++; mark = i;                // star matches nothing for now
        } else if (star != -1) {
            j = star + 1; i = ++mark;            // mismatch: star eats one more letter
        } else {
            return false;                        // mismatch and no star to help
        }
    }
    while (j < p.length() && p.charAt(j) == '*') j++;   // leftover stars match ""
    return j == p.length();
}

Time O(m · n) worstSpace O(1)

Usually close to linear in practice. The DP is easier to get right in an interview; mention this as the follow-up.

Remember

A symbol that matches "any amount" = left (take none) or up (take one more, stay). No inner loop over lengths needed.

Watch out

Row 0 is not just dp[0][0]: s = "", p = "***" is true, and p = "*a" is false. Forgetting the leading-stars row makes every pattern that starts with * fail.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

LC 10Regular Expression MatchingHardTwo-string DP (pattern)LeetCode
The problem in easy words

A pattern may contain '.' (any one letter) and '*', which means zero or more copies of the letter just before it. Does the pattern match the whole string?

Example: s = "aa", p = "a" → false. p = "a*" → true. s = "ab", p = ".*" → true. s = "aab", p = "c*a*b" → true (zero c's, two a's, one b).

How to spot the pattern

Same signals as Wildcard Matching (LC 44): text, pattern, "entire string", and a star that repeats. The difference is in the words "preceding element": the star is glued to the letter before it, so x* is one two-letter unit.

1Brute force — zero copies, or one more copy

If the pattern ends in x*: either use it zero times (drop both letters) or, if the last text letter matches x, let it eat that letter and keep x* for more. Otherwise the last letters must match one for one.

boolean isMatch(String s, String p) {
    return match(s, p, s.length(), p.length());
}

// does s[0..i) match p[0..j)?
boolean match(String s, String p, int i, int j) {
    if (j == 0) return i == 0;
    if (p.charAt(j - 1) == '*') {
        char x = p.charAt(j - 2);                     // the letter that repeats
        if (match(s, p, i, j - 2)) return true;       // "x*" used zero times
        return i > 0 && same(s.charAt(i - 1), x)
                     && match(s, p, i - 1, j);        // "x*" eats s[i-1], stays
    }
    return i > 0 && same(s.charAt(i - 1), p.charAt(j - 1))
                 && match(s, p, i - 1, j - 1);        // one letter for one letter
}

boolean same(char c, char pc) { return pc == '.' || pc == c; }

Time exponentialSpace O(m + n)

LeetCode keeps both strings at 20 letters or fewer, so this plain recursion is actually accepted. It is still exponential: s = "baaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa" against ten "a*"s already makes 50 million calls, and at 40 letters it would never finish. Interviewers expect the table.

2Optimal — the same table, star jumps two columns
The idea

This is Wildcard Matching (LC 44, just above) plus one change. "x*" is one unit: zero copies jumps two columns left, dp[i][j−2]; one more copy goes up, dp[i−1][j], but only if s[i−1] matches x. '.' matches any letter, both on its own and as the x of .*.

State: dp[i][j] = s[0..i) matches p[0..j).
Recurrence: p[j−1] == '*': dp[i][j] = dp[i][j−2] || (same(s[i−1], p[j−2]) && dp[i−1][j]); otherwise dp[i][j] = same(s[i−1], p[j−1]) && dp[i−1][j−1].
Base case: dp[0][0] = true; dp[0][j] = dp[0][j−2] when p[j−1] == '*' (a run like "a*b*" can vanish).

boolean isMatch(String s, String p) {
    int m = s.length(), n = p.length();
    boolean[][] dp = new boolean[m + 1][n + 1];  // dp[i][j]: s[0..i) matches p[0..j)
    dp[0][0] = true;
    for (int j = 2; j <= n; j++)                 // empty text: "a*b*c*" can vanish
        dp[0][j] = p.charAt(j - 1) == '*' && dp[0][j - 2];
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) {
            char pc = p.charAt(j - 1);
            if (pc == '*') {
                char x = p.charAt(j - 2);                  // the repeated letter
                dp[i][j] = dp[i][j - 2]                    // zero copies: two left
                        || (same(s.charAt(i - 1), x) &&
                            dp[i - 1][j]);                 // one more copy: up
            } else {
                dp[i][j] = same(s.charAt(i - 1), pc)
                        && dp[i - 1][j - 1];               // one for one: diagonal
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[m][n];
}

boolean same(char c, char pc) { return pc == '.' || pc == c; }

Time O(m · n)Space O(m · n)

Each cell is O(1). LeetCode guarantees every '*' has a letter before it, so p.charAt(j − 2) is always safe.

Remember

When the star belongs to the letter before it, "zero copies" means skip two pattern letters (j − 2) and "one more copy" means up, guarded by a letter check.

Watch out

Unlike LC 44, the star is not "anything": "a*" only eats a's. Forgetting the same(s[i−1], x) check on the up move makes s = "ab", p = "a*" wrongly true. And don't skip row 0: s = "", p = "c*" is true.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

Advanced DP

Same recipe as the Intermediate DP section: say what the state means in words, write the recurrence from the last choice, set the base case, fill in order. The Hard problems below each add one new idea to a pattern you already know: a state machine with a transaction counter (stock problems, from LC 309), interval DP where you pick what happens last (Burst Balloons), and sort first, then a known DP with binary search to make it O(n log n) (envelopes, job scheduling). What is harder than Intermediate: finding the state is the whole problem, and the obvious state ("which balloon goes first") is often the one that does not work.

LC 123Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IIIHardDP state machineLeetCode
The problem in easy words

You get the price of a stock for each day. You may make at most two trades (buy then sell), and you must sell before you buy again. What is the biggest total profit?

Example: prices = [3,3,5,0,0,3,1,4] → 6 (buy at 0, sell at 3, then buy at 1, sell at 4). [1,2,3,4,5] → 4. [7,6,4,3,1] → 0.

How to spot the pattern

Stock prices day by day with a rule about what you may do next ("at most two transactions", "cooldown", "fee") is a state machine DP: each day you are in one of a few modes, and the rule decides which modes lead to which. LC 309 (Intermediate) had modes hold / sold / rest; here the modes also remember how many trades you have used.

1Brute force — try every split day

Two trades never overlap, so there is a day k where the first trade is over and the second one has not started. For every k, run the one-trade answer (LC 121: track the lowest price so far) on the left part and on the right part, and add them.

int maxProfit(int[] prices) {
    int n = prices.length, best = 0;
    for (int k = 0; k < n; k++) {             // first trade ends by day k,
        best = Math.max(best,                 // second trade starts from day k
            oneTrade(prices, 0, k) + oneTrade(prices, k, n - 1));
    }
    return best;
}

int oneTrade(int[] p, int lo, int hi) {       // LC 121 on p[lo..hi]
    int min = Integer.MAX_VALUE, best = 0;
    for (int i = lo; i <= hi; i++) {
        min = Math.min(min, p[i]);
        best = Math.max(best, p[i] - min);
    }
    return best;
}

Time O(n²)Space O(1)

With up to 105 days that is 1010 steps: a time-out. (A left-to-right and a right-to-left array of one-trade answers would make it O(n), but the state machine below is simpler and generalises to k trades.)

2Optimal — four running states, one pass
The idea

This is LC 309's state machine, plus one extra insight: put the number of trades into the state. Four modes, each "best money in my pocket if I am in this mode now":

State: buy1 = holding the 1st share, sell1 = done 1 trade, buy2 = holding the 2nd share, sell2 = done 2 trades.
Recurrence (each day, price p): buy1 = max(buy1, −p), sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p), buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 − p), sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p).
Base case: the buys start at "impossible" (−∞), the sells at 0. The answer is sell2 (doing fewer trades is covered, because a trade can buy and sell on the same day for 0).

int maxProfit(int[] prices) {
    int buy1 = Integer.MIN_VALUE, sell1 = 0;  // after 1st buy / after 1st sell
    int buy2 = Integer.MIN_VALUE, sell2 = 0;  // after 2nd buy / after 2nd sell
    for (int p : prices) {
        buy1  = Math.max(buy1, -p);           // buy the first share today
        sell1 = Math.max(sell1, buy1 + p);    // or sell it today
        buy2  = Math.max(buy2, sell1 - p);    // buy again, paid from profit 1
        sell2 = Math.max(sell2, buy2 + p);    // sell the second share
    }
    return sell2;
}

Time O(n)Space O(1)

Four numbers per day, one pass. Integer.MIN_VALUE is safe here because each buy is replaced by a real value (like −p) before anything is added to it.

Remember

Stock problems = state machine. List the modes you can be in, write "today's mode = best of (stay, or come from the mode before and pay/earn p)". A limit on trades just means more modes: buy1 → sell1 → buy2 → sell2.

Watch out

Two separate "best single trade" answers do not add up: taking the best trade and then the second-best trade can overlap in time. Also don't start buy1 at 0: that would mean you own a share for free.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

LC 188Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IVHardDP state machineLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Same as LC 123, but instead of two trades you may make at most k trades. Buy before you sell, and hold at most one share at a time.

Example: k = 2, prices = [2,4,1] → 2. k = 2, prices = [3,2,6,5,0,3] → 7 (buy 2 sell 6, buy 0 sell 3).

How to spot the pattern

"At most k transactions" where k is an input: the four variables of LC 123 become two arrays of length k + 1. Whenever a problem's state includes "how many times I have used something" (trades, skips, deletions), that count becomes an index of the DP.

1Brute force — on each day, do nothing or act

Recursion on (day, trades left, holding?). Each day you either do nothing, or buy (if not holding), or sell (if holding, using up one trade).

int maxProfit(int k, int[] prices) { return go(prices, 0, k, false); }

// best profit from day i on, with k sells left, holding a share or not
int go(int[] p, int i, int k, boolean holding) {
    if (i == p.length || k == 0) return 0;
    int skip = go(p, i + 1, k, holding);                              // do nothing today
    if (holding) return Math.max(skip, p[i] + go(p, i + 1, k - 1, false)); // sell
    return Math.max(skip, -p[i] + go(p, i + 1, k, true));                 // buy
}

Time O(2ⁿ)Space O(n)

Two branches per day. Just 30 days with k = 15 already took about 7 seconds; LeetCode allows 1,000 days. Note there are only n · k · 2 different arguments, which is the hint that a table will work.

2Optimal — buy[j] and sell[j] for every trade number j
The idea

LC 123 had the chain buy1 → sell1 → buy2 → sell2. Here the chain is k links long, so store it in two arrays and, for each price, walk the chain once.

State: buy[j] = best money while holding the share of trade j; sell[j] = best money after finishing j trades.
Recurrence: buy[j] = max(buy[j], sell[j−1] − p), sell[j] = max(sell[j], buy[j] + p).
Base case: sell[0] = 0 (no trades yet), every buy[j] starts "impossible". Answer: sell[k].

int maxProfit(int k, int[] prices) {
    int[] buy = new int[k + 1];               // buy[j]: holding the share of trade j
    int[] sell = new int[k + 1];              // sell[j]: finished j trades
    Arrays.fill(buy, Integer.MIN_VALUE / 2);  // "impossible", and safe to add p to
    for (int p : prices) {
        for (int j = 1; j <= k; j++) {
            buy[j]  = Math.max(buy[j], sell[j - 1] - p);  // start trade j
            sell[j] = Math.max(sell[j], buy[j] + p);      // finish trade j
        }
    }
    return sell[k];
}

Time O(n · k)Space O(k)

1,000 days × 100 trades = 100,000 updates. With k = 2 this is exactly the LC 123 solution. If k ≥ n / 2 the limit never bites, and you can use the "take every rise" greedy from LC 122 instead.

Remember

A counter in the state ("trades used", "deletions left") turns a few variables into an array indexed by the counter. Write the small version (k = 2) first, then generalise the pattern.

Watch out

Use Integer.MIN_VALUE / 2 as "impossible", not MIN_VALUE: then any small change to it (adding or subtracting a price) stays very negative, while MIN_VALUE − 1 wraps around to a huge positive number. And k counts trades (buy + sell pairs), not single actions.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

LC 312Burst BalloonsHardInterval DPLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Balloons in a row have numbers. When you burst balloon i you earn left neighbour × i × right neighbour (a missing neighbour counts as 1), and then its two neighbours become next to each other. Burst them all; what is the most coins you can earn?

Example: nums = [3,1,5,8] → 167: burst 1 (3·1·5 = 15), then 5 (3·5·8 = 120), then 3 (1·3·8 = 24), then 8 (1·8·1 = 8). [1,5] → 10.

How to spot the pattern

"Remove items one by one, and the cost depends on who is next to it at that moment" on a row of up to 300 items: the answer for a range [l, r] is built from smaller ranges, so it is interval DP (the family of LC 5 Longest Palindromic Substring). The small n (300) also hints at O(n³).

1Brute force — try every order

Pick any balloon to burst next, earn its coins, remove it from the list, recurse on what is left, and put it back.

int maxCoins(int[] nums) {
    List<Integer> b = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int x : nums) b.add(x);
    return go(b);
}

int go(List<Integer> b) {                     // try every balloon as the NEXT one
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < b.size(); i++) {
        int left = i > 0 ? b.get(i - 1) : 1;
        int right = i < b.size() - 1 ? b.get(i + 1) : 1;
        int x = b.remove(i);                  // burst it
        best = Math.max(best, left * x * right + go(b));
        b.add(i, x);                          // put it back
    }
    return best;
}

Time O(n! · n)Space O(n)

10 balloons already take a quarter of a second (10! = 3.6 million orders); 13 would take minutes, and LeetCode allows 300. Memo does not rescue this version cleanly: the state is "which balloons are left", and there are 2n of those.

2Optimal — choose which balloon bursts LAST in each range
The idea

Thinking "which one first" fails, because bursting a balloon glues its neighbours together, so the two sides are no longer independent. The extra insight: ask which balloon k bursts LAST between walls l and r. While k is still there, the left side (l, k) and the right side (k, r) can never touch, so they are two independent smaller problems. And when k finally bursts, its neighbours are exactly the walls: it earns a[l] · a[k] · a[r].

State: pad the array with a 1 at each end; dp[l][r] = most coins from bursting everything strictly between l and r.
Recurrence: dp[l][r] = max over l < k < r of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l]·a[k]·a[r].
Base case: dp[l][l+1] = 0 (nothing between). Fill by range length, short to long. Answer: dp[0][n+1].

int maxCoins(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] a = new int[n + 2];                 // pad with 1 on both ends
    a[0] = a[n + 1] = 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i + 1] = nums[i];
    // dp[l][r] = best coins from bursting everything strictly between l and r
    int[][] dp = new int[n + 2][n + 2];
    for (int len = 2; len <= n + 1; len++) {          // gap r - l, small to big
        for (int l = 0; l + len <= n + 1; l++) {
            int r = l + len;
            for (int k = l + 1; k < r; k++) {         // k bursts LAST in (l, r)
                dp[l][r] = Math.max(dp[l][r],
                    dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l] * a[k] * a[r]);
            }
        }
    }
    return dp[0][n + 1];
}

Time O(n³)Space O(n²)

About n³ / 6 ≈ 4.5 million steps for 300 balloons. Filling by length guarantees dp[l][k] and dp[k][r] (shorter ranges) are ready before dp[l][r] needs them.

Remember

When removing an item changes its neighbours, think backwards: the item removed last splits the range into two independent halves. Interval DP: dp[l][r] over a split point k, filled by increasing length.

Watch out

The walls l and r are not burst inside dp[l][r]; that is why the padded 1s work and why k runs strictly between them. Looping l from 0 upward with r inside (instead of by length) reads cells that are not filled yet.

Pattern notes: DP Patterns · Open on LeetCode

LC 354Russian Doll EnvelopesHardSort + LISLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Each envelope has a width and a height. One envelope fits inside another only if it is strictly smaller in both. What is the largest number of envelopes you can nest inside each other (like Russian dolls)? You can't rotate them.

Example: [[5,4],[6,4],[6,7],[2,3]] → 3 ([2,3] → [5,4] → [6,7]). [[1,1],[1,1],[1,1]] → 1.

How to spot the pattern

"Longest chain where each item is bigger than the one before" is Longest Increasing Subsequence (Intermediate LC 300). The twist is that "bigger" has two dimensions. Sorting by one dimension removes it, and LIS runs on the other.

1Brute force — sort by width, then O(n²) LIS

Sort by width so every envelope that can go inside i comes before it. Then do the LC 300 DP: dp[i] = longest chain ending with envelope i, checking every earlier envelope that is smaller in both.

int maxEnvelopes(int[][] envelopes) {
    int n = envelopes.length, best = 0;
    Arrays.sort(envelopes, (a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);   // by width
    int[] dp = new int[n];                            // longest chain ending at i
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        dp[i] = 1;
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
            if (envelopes[j][0] < envelopes[i][0] && envelopes[j][1] < envelopes[i][1])
                dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
        }
        best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);
    }
    return best;
}

Time O(n²)Space O(n)

Correct, but LeetCode has up to 105 envelopes: 5 × 109 pair checks, a time-out.

2Optimal — clever sort, then LIS with binary search
The idea

LC 300's O(n log n) follow-up (the tails array) works on one dimension. So sort by width, and run it on heights. The one extra insight is the tie-break: for equal widths, sort heights DESCENDING. Then two envelopes of the same width can never both be in an increasing run of heights, which is exactly the rule "same width can't nest".

int maxEnvelopes(int[][] envelopes) {
    // width up; for EQUAL widths, height DOWN
    Arrays.sort(envelopes, (a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? a[0] - b[0] : b[1] - a[1]);
    int[] tails = new int[envelopes.length];  // tails[k]: smallest last height
    int len = 0;                              //   of a chain of length k + 1
    for (int[] e : envelopes) {
        int h = e[1], lo = 0, hi = len;
        while (lo < hi) {                     // first tail >= h
            int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
            if (tails[mid] < h) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid;
        }
        tails[lo] = h;                        // replace, or extend when lo == len
        if (lo == len) len++;
    }
    return len;
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)

One sort, then one binary search per envelope. Searching for the first tail ≥ h (not > h) keeps the chain strictly increasing, so equal heights can't nest either.

Remember

A 2D "chain" problem: sort by one dimension to kill it, then run a 1D algorithm on the other. Choose the tie-break so that items that must not chain together (equal first dimension) can't form an increasing run.

Watch out

Sorting equal widths by height ascending is the classic bug: [[1,1],[2,2],[2,3]] would give heights 1, 2, 3 and answer 3, but [2,2] can't go inside [2,3]. The right answer is 2.

LC 1235Maximum Profit in Job SchedulingHardDP + binary searchLeetCode
The problem in easy words

Each job has a start time, an end time and a profit. You can't do two jobs that overlap in time (a job may start exactly when another ends). Pick jobs to get the largest total profit.

Example: startTime = [1,2,3,3], endTime = [3,4,5,6], profit = [50,10,40,70] → 120 (the job 1–3 for 50 and the job 3–6 for 70).

How to spot the pattern

"Choose non-overlapping intervals" is the Intermediate intervals family (LC 435), but "maximise profit" instead of "maximise count" breaks the greedy: a long job can be worth more than many short ones. So it is take or skip DP, like House Robber, where "the previous job I can combine with" is found by binary search on end times.

1Brute force — take or skip, scanning back for a compatible job

Sort jobs by end time. dp[i] = best profit using only the first i jobs. For job i, either skip it (dp[i−1]) or take it and add the best from the jobs that end before it starts, found by walking backwards.

int jobScheduling(int[] startTime, int[] endTime, int[] profit) {
    int n = profit.length;
    int[][] jobs = new int[n][];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) jobs[i] = new int[]{startTime[i], endTime[i], profit[i]};
    Arrays.sort(jobs, (a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]);         // by end time
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];                        // dp[i]: best using first i jobs
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        int[] job = jobs[i - 1];
        int j = i - 1;
        while (j > 0 && jobs[j - 1][1] > job[0]) j--; // walk back to a job that fits
        dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i - 1], dp[j] + job[2]);  // skip it, or take it
    }
    return dp[n];
}

Time O(n²)Space O(n)

The DP is already right; the backward walk is the slow part. With 5 × 104 jobs it can take about 1.25 × 109 steps (for example when every job overlaps every other one).

2Optimal — same DP, binary search for the compatible job
The idea

This is House Robber's "skip it, or take it plus the best from before", plus one extra insight: because jobs are sorted by end time, the jobs that end at or before job i's start form a prefix. So binary search on end times finds how many jobs fit before job i in O(log n).

State: dp[i] = best profit from the first i jobs (sorted by end).
Recurrence: dp[i] = max(dp[i−1], dp[j] + profit_i), where j = number of jobs whose end ≤ starti.
Base case: dp[0] = 0. Answer: dp[n].

int jobScheduling(int[] startTime, int[] endTime, int[] profit) {
    int n = profit.length;
    int[][] jobs = new int[n][];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) jobs[i] = new int[]{startTime[i], endTime[i], profit[i]};
    Arrays.sort(jobs, (a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]);         // by end time
    int[] dp = new int[n + 1];                        // dp[i]: best using first i jobs
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        int start = jobs[i - 1][0];
        // lo = how many of the first i-1 jobs end at or before 'start'
        int lo = 0, hi = i - 1;
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
            if (jobs[mid][1] <= start) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid;
        }
        dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i - 1],                   // skip job i
                         dp[lo] + jobs[i - 1][2]);    // take job i
    }
    return dp[n];
}

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)

The sort is O(n log n) and each of the n jobs does one O(log n) search. Checked against an all-subsets brute force on 20,000 random small inputs.

Remember

Weighted intervals: sort by end, take-or-skip DP, binary search for the last compatible item. The same trick works whenever "the previous item I can combine with" is a prefix of a sorted list.

Watch out

Sort by end, not start: dp[i] must mean "best among jobs that finish first". And a job ending at time 3 is compatible with one starting at 3, so search for end ≤ start, not < start.
